reports.title: Envíos aéreos de ayuda humanitaria a Venezuela (13 agosto 2026)
Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #2 (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
reports.body_text:
**A. SITUATION ANALYSIS**  
**Description of the crisis**

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession; with the first one reaching a 7.2 magnitude, and a second one of 7.5 magnitude taking place approximately 39 seconds later. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. USGS analysis confirmed the epicentre of the second earthquake to be approximately 17 km west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State1. Authorities have reported 1,463 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse2. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The earthquakes were also felt beyond Venezuela, including parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and northern Brazil, highlighting the exceptional geographic extent of the seismic event3.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone.

According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS) approximately 530,000 were exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. The scale of the disaster led to a significant expansion of international humanitarian presence in the country. On 15 July, the United Nations announced an addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), increasing financial requirements and expanding the number of people targeted for assistance for their overall humanitarian response to Venezuela (which extends beyond those affected by the earthquakes).

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira State, a popular beachside destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes. La Guaira also serves multiple critical functions for the country given very close proximity to the Capital, Caracas. It hosts the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, making it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people with secondary affectations and the extent of logistical capacity impacted.

As of 3 August, 6,125 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing.4 The United Nations interagency indicated that tens of thousands of people remained unaccounted for during the response period; while many families including from those having opened tracing requests with the RCRC system have reported having been able to reunite with their loved ones in the days and weeks following the disaster. Efforts to identify and notify direct family members of persons hospitalized and persons deceased also continue. It is expected for the death toll to continue to rise as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors has moved towards a focus on recovery, identification and dignified return of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures to their family members.5 Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) have now concluded their assignment. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and multiple RCRC Movement specialized teams such as the USAR teams of the Mexican RC, Colombian RC, Costa Rican RC who deployed in support of Venezuelan RC search & rescue efforts. The initial response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, and initial shelter provision has now shifted towards bridging emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.6

On 21 July, the Venezuelan President of the Presidential Commission for the Assessment of Infrastructure Habitability reported that 6,907 buildings had been inspected in La Guaira using the traffic light assessment methodology to determine the condition of structures. Of the total inspected, 3,237 received a green tag indicating that the infrastructure poses no risk; 1,785 structures received a yellow tag indicating restricted use; and 1,885 were classified with a red tag indicating high risk. Structures assigned yellow or red classifications are now undergoing a secondary more thorough assessment7.

Disruptions of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems caused by the earthquakes are undergoing repair to continue restoring functionality across the affected areas. Damaged roads and bridges have also affected movement to and within some affected areas; prompting authorities to relocate mobile bridges to facilitate access while repairs are finalized. Public transportation and airport operations are also under repair, with Maiquetia International Airport (which was severely damaged) expected to resume use for commercial cargo flights in the coming weeks. Commercial international passenger flights remain operating mostly in and out of Valencia airport, located approximately 2 hours out of the capital. Humanitarian cargo donated by Governments bilaterally to the Venezuelan Authorities, and through humanitarian actors, continues to flow in country through air, sea and land shipments.

In terms of essential services, healthcare capacity has been particularly including given the mass scale needs following the rapid onset emergency (trauma injuries), as well as given rates of chronic illness among displaced communities and affectations to water supply and sanitation services. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been assigned as temporary shelters while authorities assign free permanent housing units and/or transitional single-family homes until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. To this end, Venezuelan authorities have already provided 240 permanent housing units to affected families; and while land & public housing infrastructure is evaluated and attributed for the assignment of additional seismic resistant units entirely free of charge, they have also enabled a parallel option for affected families who prefer to buy existing homes from the private market (whereby 80% of the price is subsidized by the government and the 20% remaining be granted on 25-year-loans extended by the local banking system.)

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, as well as mental health and psychosocial support. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, displacement from damaged homes, and exposure to destroyed environments and recovery operations contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected population.

The earthquakes have resulted in grave humanitarian needs while exacerbating existing vulnerabilities, which increases the severity and complexity of the situation for the affected communities. This context reinforces the need for a response that addresses immediate lifesaving needs while supporting early recovery and strengthening community resilience.

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #6 (August 12, 2026)
reports.body_text:
**FAST FACTS**

- On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela in rapid succession, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
- Official figures have so far confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 24,477 people currently displaced.
- Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

**Our Response**

- International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,819 consultations since July 1.
- On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to impacted communities. To date, we have provided 3,263 consultations through the EMT.
- Our teams have delivered 390,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting an estimated 4,000 people.
- Our teams have provided 759 MHPSS consultations.

reports.title: Situation Report No.9: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 August 2026
reports.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

• Seven weeks after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response continues to sustain emergency operations while transitioning toward early recovery. Current efforts are focused on maintaining essential health services, rehabilitating affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and delivering health services through a comprehensive approach, while mitigating public health risks and ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment.

• Health service recovery and critical care capacity are advancing, with rehabilitation planning progressing in priority facilities and intensive care and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, while assessments in Caracas and Miranda continue to identify critical gaps in equipment and human resources.

• Public health surveillance and immunization systems are being reinforced, with expanded epidemiological analysis and digital reporting, enhanced laboratory diagnostic capacity, and more than 31,000 vaccine doses administered; national vaccine supply security was further supported through a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line.

• Efforts advanced toward the provision of comprehensive care, focusing on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, noncommunicable diseases, and rehabilitation. This included dissemination of the national mental health protocol, training of transitional camp focal points, continuity of oncology care through three designated centers, and attention to emerging needs such as assessing rehabilitation center capacities and training on amputee management and wound care.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, most recently delivering targeted emergency medical supplies – including specialized kits, medicines, and high-complexity surgical instruments – to the Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere in Petare, Sucre.

• PAHO/WHO continues to support the health response through its Regional Response Team, covering key areas such as emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory services, WASH, immunization, risk communication, and Emergency Medical Teams (EMT) coordination. Additional experts in entomology and infection prevention and control are being deployed.

reports.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #6: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 10 August 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
reports.body_text:
On 9 August, AMDA dispatched a Japanese nurse for the ongoing quake response efforts in Venezuela.

Venezuela suffered extensive damage following two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude that struck in succession on 24 June 2026. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), the earthquakes have claimed 5,546 lives and injured 16,740 people. More than 1,500 aftershocks have also been recorded in the affected areas, as of 31 July.

For more than a month, AMDA has been providing medical support in Caraballeda, La Guaira, one of the areas hardest hit by the earthquakes, where numerous buildings collapsed. Following the conclusion of activities by AMDA’s Japanese doctor and nurse on 31 July, the AMDA team, comprising local medical professionals and coordinators, continued to provide care at a temporary clinic in Caraballeda, with local volunteers and other organizations supporting the affected community.

Among those who visited the clinic between 27-30 July was a mother who brought her baby in, stating that she was concerned about her child’s cough and diarrhea. The doctors reassured her that symptoms were nothing to worry about after examining the infant. There was also a patient with severe insect bites stemming from sleeping outdoors after losing one’s house.

On the afternoon of 30 July, the team met with His Excellency Yasushi Sato, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Japan to Venezuela, at the Ambassador's official residence. During the meeting, they reported on AMDA's activities to date, the situation on the ground and plans for future assistance.

On 31 July, 208 patients (well above the usual number) visited the temporary clinic, including 127 who received dental care at a special dental clinic set up that day. After the weekend, the clinic returned to its regular schedule on 3 August, seeing 74 patients that day, 37 on 4 August, and 93 on 5 August.

Respiratory conditions and symptoms, including cough, bronchospasm, and bronchitis, were particularly common. There were also cases in which chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes had worsened. A patient with suspected cholecystitis was referred to a nearby hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Although numerous natural disasters have been occurring in different locations around the world, AMDA will continue doing what it can to save those affected by them.

reports.title: UNFPA Situation Report: Earthquakes in Venezuela (24 June – 7 August 2026)
reports.body_text:
Venezuela continues to face significant humanitarian needs following the earthquakes of 24 June 2026. The most urgent needs among affected populations include healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health (SRH); food and safe water; mental health and psychosocial support; shelter; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV).

The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies. Currently, 24,477 people are residing in 107 transitional shelters, where overcrowding, limited privacy in sleeping and bathroom facilities, and inadequate lighting are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, girls, and adolescents.

Numerous health facilities in affected areas have sustained structural damage, while others are facing shortages of medicines, equipment, and health personnel, placing additional strain on an already overstretched health system. UNFPA is supporting the continuity of life-saving maternal, newborn, and obstetric care through its support to maternity wards in 16 hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda. UNFPA is also providing on-the-job training for health personnel and delivering critical medical equipment and supplies, including 62 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health Kits, which will support the needs of approximately 2,250 people.  
  
UNFPA and its implementing partners are also delivering SRH and GBV services across four transitional shelters. To date, 4,327 people have received prenatal care, family planning services, psychosocial support, GBV case management, and dignity kits. In addition, 4,186 people have been reached through SRH and GBV awareness-raising and information sessions.

UNFPA is appealing for US$10 million to support the emergency response to the earthquakes in Venezuela. To date, US$4 million has been mobilized, leaving a 60 per cent funding gap. Additional support is urgently needed to sustain the delivery of life-saving SRH and GBV services to affected populations.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #21 (7 al 10 de agosto 2026)
reports.body_text:
El Reporte de Situación No. 21 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, correspondiente al período del 7 al 10 de agosto de 2026.

## Aspectos destacados

- El 10 de agosto, OIM inició la distribución de artículos no alimentarios en Mare II y Algarín, tras completar actividades de registro y verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II y comunidades adyacentes.
- OIM y su socio Ven Da Tu Mano mantuvieron los servicios móviles de salud y salud mental en los campamentos transitorios. Las atenciones acumuladas alcanzaron **3.267 en el Polideportivo José María Vargas y 2.864 en César Nieves**, mientras se reforzó la vigilancia de enfermedades diarreicas.
- Entre el 17 de julio y el 7 de agosto, las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios apoyadas por OIM y la Fundación Vivienda Popular alcanzaron un acumulado de **2.244 kits** en La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito Capital y Carabobo. El campamento transitorio Playa Grande cerró el 10 de agosto.

## Actividades de OIM

OIM mantuvo la gestión de cinco campamentos transitorios durante el período, incluidos tres sitios cogestionados con el Consejo Noruego para Refugiados. Las actividades incluyeron la coordinación de servicios, el registro de población, la verificación de hogares y el seguimiento de necesidades. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para **751 personas de 202 grupos familiares**, mientras se dio seguimiento a movimientos de población en Campo de Golf.

La verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II permitió iniciar las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios en Mare II y Algarín el 10 de agosto. OIM y la Fundación Vivienda Popular también apoyaron la provisión de artículos no alimentarios en sitios y comunidades gestionados por las autoridades. El 7 de agosto se entregaron **70 kits** en el campamento transitorio del Colegio Olivia Andrade, en La Guaira.

OIM y Ven Da Tu Mano continuaron prestando servicios móviles de salud y salud mental, incluida la atención de enfermedades crónicas y necesidades de salud mental asociadas a la emergencia. En César Nieves, los equipos de salud respondieron a un incidente que afectó aproximadamente a **20 personas adultas y 12 niños y niñas**, brindando atención médica, seguimiento del estado de hidratación y fortaleciendo la vigilancia de enfermedades diarreicas.

OIM amplió la verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II y comunidades adyacentes, y continuó actualizando los registros de población en César Nieves y José María Vargas. También continuaron las evaluaciones de necesidades en asentamientos comunitarios y alojamientos formales de La Guaira, Miranda y Carabobo.

Las actividades de protección incluyeron la articulación para facilitar el acceso a servicios de gestión de casos, salud, asistencia legal y protección especializada. En José María Vargas, **40 mujeres** participaron en sesiones informativas sobre violencia contra mujeres y niñas y salvaguarda. OIM también facilitó espacios de coordinación interagencial para actualizar la cobertura y los horarios de atención, fortalecer los mecanismos de derivación y dar seguimiento a los movimientos de población.

## Respuesta prevista de OIM

OIM prevé:

- Completar las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios en las comunidades priorizadas alrededor de Mare Abajo II.
- Atender las brechas de infraestructura identificadas en Mare Abajo II, particularmente el drenaje de las nuevas duchas y el ajuste de los anclajes de las carpas.
- Mantener la vigilancia y el seguimiento médico de las enfermedades diarreicas y apoyar la continuidad del tratamiento de la hipertensión, la diabetes y otras enfermedades crónicas.
- Fortalecer las rutas de derivación para servicios de salud mental, asistencia legal y protección especializada.
- Completar la verificación de hogares en las comunidades priorizadas y ampliar las evaluaciones de necesidades y el seguimiento de movimientos de población en Carabobo y otras localidades afectadas.
- Mantener actualizada la información sobre los servicios disponibles, los horarios de atención y los mecanismos de derivación en los campamentos transitorios.
- Fortalecer los mecanismos accesibles de información y retroalimentación comunitaria.

  • El 10 de agosto, OIM inició la distribución de artículos no alimentarios en Mare II y Algarín, tras completar actividades de registro y verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II y comunidades adyacentes.
  • OIM y su socio Ven Da Tu Mano mantuvieron los servicios móviles de salud y salud mental en los campamentos transitorios. Las atenciones acumuladas alcanzaron 3.267 en el Polideportivo José María Vargas y 2.864 en César Nieves, mientras se reforzó la vigilancia de enfermedades diarreicas.
  • Entre el 17 de julio y el 7 de agosto, las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios apoyadas por OIM y la Fundación Vivienda Popular alcanzaron un acumulado de 2.244 kits en La Guaira, Miranda, Distrito Capital y Carabobo. El campamento transitorio Playa Grande cerró el 10 de agosto.

Actividades de OIM

OIM mantuvo la gestión de cinco campamentos transitorios durante el período, incluidos tres sitios cogestionados con el Consejo Noruego para Refugiados. Las actividades incluyeron la coordinación de servicios, el registro de población, la verificación de hogares y el seguimiento de necesidades. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para 751 personas de 202 grupos familiares, mientras se dio seguimiento a movimientos de población en Campo de Golf.

La verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II permitió iniciar las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios en Mare II y Algarín el 10 de agosto. OIM y la Fundación Vivienda Popular también apoyaron la provisión de artículos no alimentarios en sitios y comunidades gestionados por las autoridades. El 7 de agosto se entregaron 70 kits en el campamento transitorio del Colegio Olivia Andrade, en La Guaira.

OIM y Ven Da Tu Mano continuaron prestando servicios móviles de salud y salud mental, incluida la atención de enfermedades crónicas y necesidades de salud mental asociadas a la emergencia. En César Nieves, los equipos de salud respondieron a un incidente que afectó aproximadamente a 20 personas adultas y 12 niños y niñas, brindando atención médica, seguimiento del estado de hidratación y fortaleciendo la vigilancia de enfermedades diarreicas.

OIM amplió la verificación de hogares en Mare Abajo II y comunidades adyacentes, y continuó actualizando los registros de población en César Nieves y José María Vargas. También continuaron las evaluaciones de necesidades en asentamientos comunitarios y alojamientos formales de La Guaira, Miranda y Carabobo.

Las actividades de protección incluyeron la articulación para facilitar el acceso a servicios de gestión de casos, salud, asistencia legal y protección especializada. En José María Vargas, 40 mujeres participaron en sesiones informativas sobre violencia contra mujeres y niñas y salvaguarda. OIM también facilitó espacios de coordinación interagencial para actualizar la cobertura y los horarios de atención, fortalecer los mecanismos de derivación y dar seguimiento a los movimientos de población.

OIM prevé:

  • Completar las distribuciones de artículos no alimentarios en las comunidades priorizadas alrededor de Mare Abajo II.
  • Atender las brechas de infraestructura identificadas en Mare Abajo II, particularmente el drenaje de las nuevas duchas y el ajuste de los anclajes de las carpas.
  • Mantener la vigilancia y el seguimiento médico de las enfermedades diarreicas y apoyar la continuidad del tratamiento de la hipertensión, la diabetes y otras enfermedades crónicas.
  • Fortalecer las rutas de derivación para servicios de salud mental, asistencia legal y protección especializada.
  • Completar la verificación de hogares en las comunidades priorizadas y ampliar las evaluaciones de necesidades y el seguimiento de movimientos de población en Carabobo y otras localidades afectadas.

reports.body_text:
Situation Report No. 21 provides an update on IOM's response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 7 to 10 August 2026.

## Highlights

- On 10 August, IOM launched the distribution of non-food items in Mare II and Algarín following household registration and verification activities in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities.
- IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano maintained mobile health and mental health services in temporary accommodation sites. Cumulative services reached **3,267 consultations at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and 2,864 consultations in César Nieves**, while surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases was reinforced.
- From 17 July to 7 August, NFI distributions supported by IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular reached a cumulative total of **2,244 kits** in La Guaira, Miranda, Capital District and Carabobo. The Playa Grande temporary accommodation site closed on 10 August.

## IOM activities

IOM maintained the management of five temporary accommodation sites during the reporting period, including three sites co-managed with the Norwegian Refugee Council. Activities included service coordination, population registration, household verification and needs monitoring. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for **751 people from 202 households**, while population movements in Campo de Golf were monitored.

Household verification in Mare Abajo II supported the launch of NFI distributions in Mare II and Algarín on 10 August. IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular also supported the provision of NFIs in sites and communities managed by the authorities. On 7 August, **70 kits** were distributed at the Colegio Olivia Andrade temporary accommodation site in La Guaira.

IOM and Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing mobile health and mental health services, including care for chronic conditions and mental health needs associated with the emergency. In César Nieves, health teams responded to an incident affecting approximately **20 adults and 12 children**, providing medical care, monitoring hydration status and strengthening surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases.

IOM expanded household verification in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities and continued updating population records in César Nieves and José María Vargas. Needs assessments in community settlements and formal accommodation sites also continued in La Guaira, Miranda and Carabobo.

Protection activities included coordination of access to case management, health, legal assistance and specialized services. At José María Vargas, **40 women** participated in information sessions on violence against women and girls and safeguarding. IOM also facilitated inter-agency coordination to update service coverage and schedules, strengthen referral mechanisms and monitor population movements.

## IOM planned response

IOM will:

- Complete NFI distributions in prioritized communities surrounding Mare Abajo II.
- Address identified infrastructure gaps in Mare Abajo II, particularly drainage for newly installed showers and adjustments to tent anchoring systems.
- Continue health surveillance and medical follow-up for diarrhoeal diseases and support continuity of treatment for hypertension, diabetes and other chronic conditions.
- Strengthen referral pathways for mental health, legal assistance and specialized protection services.
- Complete household verification in prioritized communities and expand needs assessments and population movement monitoring in Carabobo and other affected locations.
- Maintain updated information on available services, operating schedules and referral mechanisms in temporary accommodation sites.
- Strengthen accessible community information and feedback mechanisms.

reports.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #08, 10 August 2026
reports.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

**Situation Update**

- A month after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, the World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide food assistance to communities impacted by the devastation. This unprecedented response, tailored to different needs in each affected area, has already reached more than 120,000 people and, with proper funding, hopes to reach a total of half a million over the next two months.
- Following needs assessments, WFP has expanded the scope of its assistance from assistance in temporary shelters, community kitchens and communities in the most populated cities, to remote communities in La Guaira, where residents have retained cooking capacities, but whose livelihoods have been severely affected.
- WFP's response extends well beyond La Guaira. The operation plan spans seven states, considering both families directly displaced or affected in their homes, and those whose livelihoods were disrupted by the earthquake — people whose sources of income collapsed overnight.

Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #20 (4 to 6 August 2026)
reports.body_text:
Situation Report No. 20 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 4 to 6 August 2026.

## **Highlights**

Between 4 and 6 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). During the reporting period, the **Shelter, Land and Site Coordination (SLSC) Cluster** was formally activated, co-led by IOM and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), strengthening response coordination in the affected areas.

Since 3 August, IOM has expanded its response to **13 communities in Morón (Carabobo State)**, providing assistance to **373 households (1,232 people)** affected by the earthquakes through the distribution of essential relief items and other humanitarian assistance activities.

IOM-supported teams have delivered **7,641 medical consultations to 6,753 earthquake-affected people** through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities.

## **IOM Activities**

IOM and the Norwegian Refugee Council (**NRC**) continued the co-management of five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service coordination, population registration and site management activities.

During the reporting period, household registration and verification activities continued across temporary accommodation sites. In Mare Abajo II, the household registration process was reinforced to support distributions scheduled for the following week. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for **760 people from 209 households**, while updated registration data at Campo de Golf identified **359 people**, including **10 persons with disabilities, four pregnant women and three lactating women**.

IOM also expanded its response to **13 communities in Morón (Carabobo)**, where **373 households (1,232 people)** received essential relief items.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water and sanitation through monitoring of water treatment systems, water quality surveillance, expansion of sanitation infrastructure and strengthened waste management activities. Improvements continued in Mare Abajo II to enhance access to safe water and sanitation, while water and sanitation systems remained operational in Campo de Golf.

IOM and its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams. During the reporting period, **99 consultations** were conducted in Cesar Nieves, while mobile services at Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex reached a cumulative total of **2,678 consultations**. In addition, IOM delivered training sessions to **29 humanitarian workers**, including staff from HIAS and IOM mental health, psychological support and CCCM teams. Training topics included Psychological First Aid (PFA), community outreach approaches and institutional methodologies for delivering mental health and psychological support services. To date, IOM-supported interventions have provided **7,641 medical consultations to 6,753 earthquake-affected people**.

IOM continued registration and information management activities through the Unified Information Management System (**IMS**) in temporary accommodation sites. During the reporting period, Displacement Tracking Matrix (**DTM**) teams continued data collection in earthquake-affected communities in **La Guaira and Morón (Carabobo)**. In addition, shelter needs assessments were conducted in **Guatire (Miranda)**. To date, IOM has characterized **51 earthquake-affected accommodation sites**.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention, prevention of violence against women and girls, and community information mechanisms. During the reporting period, information sessions were conducted for women, adolescents and community leaders, while case management and referrals continued for individuals requiring legal assistance, mental health support and other specialized services. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, information sessions reached **71 women**.

As co-lead of the **Shelter, Land and Site Coordination (SLSC) Cluster** together with IFRC, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, distribution planning, sectoral needs monitoring and coordination among humanitarian actors in temporary accommodation sites. In Mare Abajo II, coordination efforts focused on preparing distributions planned for the following week, including household registration follow-up and logistical planning.

In PSEA, IOM conducted awareness-raising activities and distributed information materials to **24 community leaders** in Campo de Golf and Cesar Nieves. In addition, refresher sessions were delivered to **25 humanitarian workers** to reinforce understanding of standards of conduct, free-of-charge assistance and reporting mechanisms.

## **IOM Planned Response**

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure, service delivery, WASH interventions, shelter assistance and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (**CCCM**) activities in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM will also continue providing health, mental health, psychological support and protection services while strengthening referral mechanisms, case management and access to documentation for people with specific protection needs.

In addition, IOM will maintain mobility monitoring, registration activities, information management, shelter needs assessments and coordination with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning.

reports.body_text:
El Reporte de Situación No. 20 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, cubriendo el período comprendido entre el 4 y el 6 de agosto de 2026.

## **Aspectos destacados**

Entre el 4 y el 6 de agosto, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación y gestión de campamentos, salud, protección, Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (WASH), gestión de información y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS). Durante el período, se formalizó la activación del **Clúster de Alojamiento, Tierra y Coordinación de Sitios (SLSC, por sus siglas en inglés)**, coliderado por la OIM y la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR), fortaleciendo la coordinación de la respuesta en las zonas afectadas.

Desde el 3 de agosto, la OIM amplió su respuesta a **13 comunidades en Morón (estado Carabobo)**, brindando asistencia a **373 hogares (1.232 personas)** afectados por los terremotos mediante la distribución de artículos esenciales y otras acciones de apoyo humanitario.

Los equipos apoyados por la OIM han realizado **7.641 consultas médicas a 6.753 personas afectadas** mediante servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

## **Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM y el Consejo Noruego para Refugiados (NRC, por sus siglas en inglés) continuaron la cogestión de cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande y César Nieves, apoyando la coordinación de servicios, el registro de población y la gestión operativa de los sitios.

Durante el período continuaron las actividades de registro y verificación de hogares en los campamentos transitorios. En Mare Abajo II se reforzó el proceso de registro de grupos familiares para apoyar las distribuciones programadas para la siguiente semana. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para **760 personas pertenecientes a 209 grupos familiares**, mientras que en Campo de Golf el registro actualizado identificó **359 personas**, incluidas **10 personas con discapacidad, cuatro mujeres embarazadas y tres personas lactantes**.

Asimismo, la OIM amplió su respuesta a **13 comunidades en Morón (Carabobo)**, donde se asistió a **373 hogares (1.232 personas)** mediante distribuciones de artículos esenciales.

En WASH, la OIM continuó ampliando el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento mediante el seguimiento a la operación de sistemas de potabilización, monitoreo de calidad del agua, ampliación de infraestructura sanitaria y fortalecimiento de actividades de gestión de residuos. En Mare Abajo II continuaron las mejoras para ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, mientras que en Campo de Golf permanecieron operativos los sistemas de agua y saneamiento.

La OIM y su socio implementador Ven Da Tu Mano continuaron prestando servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico mediante equipos móviles. Durante el período se realizaron **99 consultas** en César Nieves y las jornadas móviles en el Polideportivo José María Vargas alcanzaron un acumulado de **2.678 consultas**. Asimismo, la OIM impartió capacitaciones dirigidas a **29 trabajadores humanitarios**, incluyendo personal de HIAS y de los equipos de salud mental, apoyo psicológico y CCCM de la OIM, abordando Primeros Auxilios Psicológicos (PAP), abordaje comunitario y metodologías institucionales para la prestación de servicios de salud mental y apoyo psicológico. A la fecha, las intervenciones apoyadas por la OIM han permitido realizar **7.641 consultas médicas a 6.753 personas afectadas**.

La OIM continuó las actividades de registro y gestión de información mediante el Sistema Unificado de Gestión de Información (IMS) en los campamentos transitorios. Durante el período, equipos de la Matriz de Seguimiento de Desplazamiento (DTM, por sus siglas en inglés) continuaron el levantamiento de información en comunidades afectadas por los terremotos en **La Guaira y Morón (Carabobo).** Asimismo, se realizaron evaluaciones de necesidades de alojamiento en **Guatire (Miranda)**. A la fecha, la OIM ha caracterizado **51 alojamientos afectados por los terremotos**.

En protección, la OIM continuó brindando asistencia legal, gestión de casos, actividades de protección infantil, prevención de la trata de personas, prevención de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas y mecanismos de información comunitaria. Durante el período se realizaron sesiones informativas dirigidas a mujeres, adolescentes y lideresas comunitarias, mientras continuó la atención y derivación de casos que requirieron asistencia legal, salud mental y otros servicios especializados. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, las sesiones informativas alcanzaron a **71 mujeres**.

Como colíder del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales junto con ACNUR, la OIM continuó apoyando la coordinación operativa, la planificación de distribuciones, el seguimiento de necesidades sectoriales y la articulación entre actores humanitarios en los campamentos transitorios. En Mare Abajo II se coordinó la preparación de distribuciones previstas para la siguiente semana, incluyendo el seguimiento al registro de hogares y la organización logística de la asistencia.

En PEAS, la OIM realizó actividades de sensibilización y distribución de materiales informativos con **24 lideresas comunitarias** en Campo de Golf y César Nieves. Asimismo, desarrolló sesiones de refrescamiento con **25 trabajadores humanitarios** para reforzar la comprensión de los estándares de conducta, la gratuidad de la asistencia y los mecanismos de denuncia.

## **Respuesta Prevista de la OIM**

La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la infraestructura, la prestación de servicios, las intervenciones WASH, el apoyo en alojamiento y las actividades de Coordinación y Gestión de Campamentos (CCCM) en los campamentos transitorios.

La OIM también continuará prestando servicios de salud, salud mental, apoyo psicológico y protección, al tiempo que fortalecerá los mecanismos de derivación, la gestión de casos y el acceso a documentación para personas con necesidades específicas de protección.

Asimismo, mantendrá el monitoreo de movilidad, las actividades de registro, la gestión de información, las evaluaciones de necesidades de alojamiento y la coordinación con autoridades y organizaciones implementadoras para apoyar una planificación de la respuesta basada en evidencia.

El Reporte de Situación No. 20 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, cubriendo el período comprendido entre el 4 y el 6 de agosto de 2026.

Aspectos destacados

Entre el 4 y el 6 de agosto, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación y gestión de campamentos, salud, protección, Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (WASH), gestión de información y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS). Durante el período, se formalizó la activación del Clúster de Alojamiento, Tierra y Coordinación de Sitios (SLSC, por sus siglas en inglés), coliderado por la OIM y la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (FICR), fortaleciendo la coordinación de la respuesta en las zonas afectadas.

Desde el 3 de agosto, la OIM amplió su respuesta a 13 comunidades en Morón (estado Carabobo), brindando asistencia a 373 hogares (1.232 personas) afectados por los terremotos mediante la distribución de artículos esenciales y otras acciones de apoyo humanitario.

Los equipos apoyados por la OIM han realizado 7.641 consultas médicas a 6.753 personas afectadas mediante servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

Actividades de la OIM

La OIM y el Consejo Noruego para Refugiados (NRC, por sus siglas en inglés) continuaron la cogestión de cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande y César Nieves, apoyando la coordinación de servicios, el registro de población y la gestión operativa de los sitios.

Durante el período continuaron las actividades de registro y verificación de hogares en los campamentos transitorios. En Mare Abajo II se reforzó el proceso de registro de grupos familiares para apoyar las distribuciones programadas para la siguiente semana. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para 760 personas pertenecientes a 209 grupos familiares, mientras que en Campo de Golf el registro actualizado identificó 359 personas, incluidas 10 personas con discapacidad, cuatro mujeres embarazadas y tres personas lactantes.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 32**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**07 August 2026**  
**Time: 2:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Nearly 212,000 people affected by the earthquakes have accessed humanitarian assistance and essential services** through a coordinated multi-sector response involving humanitarian organizations, United Nations agencies, communities, and national and local authorities.
- As of 03 August, authorities reported **6,125 deaths and 60,992 people that received care at hospitals**, **and 16,740 injuries** as a result of the earthquakes.
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency to address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months**.

**Situation overview**  
 Venezuela continues to face the consequences of the two major earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the north-central region of the country on 24 June at 18:00 local time, causing significant humanitarian impacts and damage to infrastructure. The first earthquake, measuring 7.2, was centered along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). According to a recent update from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the second earthquake, measuring 7.5, had its epicenter 17 kilometers west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State.

As of 03 August, authorities reported **6,125 deaths and 16,740 injuries resulting from the earthquakes**. They also reported that 60,992 people received care at hospitals and 43,679 homes were evaluated, out of which 6,433 are at high risk. According to national authorities, 16,51% of the total rubble has been cleared. A preliminary assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure at approximately **US$37 billion**, while preliminary estimates from UNDP place direct physical damages at US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.

The government response continues to focus on assisting affected populations and managing temporary displacement sites. According to the latest report given by authorities on 26 July, **107 temporary camps remain operational, with a capacity for 28,223 people and a current occupancy of 24,477 people.** Of those accommodated, 12,752 people are in **La Guaira**, 9,092 in the **Distrito Capital**, 1,958 in **Miranda**, and 675 in **Aragua**.

More than one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response continues to expand across the affected states. **As of 06 August, nearly 212,000 people had access to essential services and humanitarian assistance** through the joint efforts of communities, humanitarian organizations, United Nations entities, donor partners, and national and local authorities.

**Note**

> ***The report will be published on a weekly basis. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation:*** [***345W Preparedness and Response***](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12Tdck_8iHPTcj6BRDeYMwkp1lwS_-rYq/view?usp=sharing)

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 32**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**07 de agosto de 2026**  
**Hora: 2:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Cerca de 212.000 personas afectadas por los terremotos (54% mujeres y niñas) han accedido a asistencia humanitaria y servicios esenciales** mediante una respuesta multisectorial coordinada entre organizaciones humanitarias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas, comunidades y autoridades nacionales y locales.
- Hasta el 03 de agosto, las autoridades reportaron **6.125 personas fallecidas, 60.992 personas atendidas en hospitales y 16.740 heridas a causa de los terremotos**.
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los**  
    **próximos seis meses.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela continúa enfrentando las consecuencias de los dos sismos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio a las 18:00 hora local en la región centro-norte del país, los cuales provocaron importantes impactos humanitarios y daños en infraestructura. El primer sismo, de magnitud 7,2, tuvo su epicentro en el eje San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). De acuerdo con una actualización reciente del Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos (USGS), el segundo sismo, de magnitud 7,5, tuvo su epicentro a 17 kilómetros al oeste de Catia La Mar, frente a las costas del estado La Guaira.

Hasta el 03 de agosto, las autoridades reportaron **6.125 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas a causa de los terremotos.** Asimismo, informaron que 60.992 personas han sido atendidas en hospitales y 43.679 viviendas han sido evaluadas, de las cuales 6.433 son de alto riesgo. Según las autoridades nacionales, 16,51% del total de escombros han sido recogidos. Una evaluación preliminar de la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas para la Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres (UNDRR) estima daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura por aproximadamente **US$37.000 millones**, mientras que estimaciones preliminares del PNUD sitúan los daños físicos directos en US$6.700 millones, equivalentes al 6% del PIB.

La respuesta gubernamental continúa centrada en la atención de la población afectada y la gestión de los campamentos transitorios. Según el último informe presentado por las autoridades el 26 de julio, permanecen habilitados **107 campamentos transitorios, con capacidad para 28.223 personas y una ocupación de 24.477 personas.** Del total de la población alojada, 12.752 personas se encuentran en **La Guaira**, 9.092 en el **Distrito Capital**, 1.958 en **Miranda** y 675 en **Aragua**.

Más de un mes después de los terremotos, la respuesta humanitaria continúa ampliándose en los estados afectados. Al 6 de agosto, cerca de 212.000 personas (54% mujeres y niñas) accedieron a servicios esenciales y asistencia humanitaria a través del trabajo conjunto de comunidades, organizaciones humanitarias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas, socios donantes y autoridades.

**Nota**

> ***El informe se publicará de manera semanal. Agradecemos a las organizaciones socias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas y donantes por sus valiosos aportes, y les invitamos a continuar reportando sus actividades de respuesta a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos a través de la plataforma 345W. Para más detalles sobre cómo reportar y la herramienta, puede consultar la presentación:*** [***345W Preparación y respuesta***](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12Tdck_8iHPTcj6BRDeYMwkp1lwS_-rYq/view?usp=sharing)***.***

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
reports.body_text:
**FAST FACTS**

- On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela consecutively, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
- Official figures have confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 17,907 people who have lost their homes.
- The earthquakes have compounded pre-existing humanitarian vulnerabilities, leaving millions of people with limited access to healthcare services, clean water, food and other basic services.

**Our Response**

- International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,336 consultations since beginning operations on July 1.
- On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an [Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility](https://internationalmedicalcorps.org/program/emergency-response-preparedness/emergency-medical-team/) to provide free medical services to affected communities. To date, we have provided 3,109 consultations through the EMT.
- Our teams have delivered 290,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting some 3,820 people.
- Our teams have so far provided 463 mental health consultations.

Our team is continuing to provide services to about 130 patients per day at the EMT. As patient loads have grown, we have been able to keep up with the demand by training and hiring locally recruited staff who are now managing EMT operations as we rotate out international personnel. The integration of local staff has helped to ensure we have the human resources necessary to scale up our response in La Guaira as needs evolve, and to transition our response programming responsibly and sustainably.

International Medical Corps is also delivering medical and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services through three mobile medical units (MMUs) in La Guaira that have provided 3,336 patient consultations to date. As needs within affected communities evolve, International Medical Corps will continue to coordinate closely with national and international partners to ensure that services are targeted to areas where they will have the greatest impact.

reports.body_text:
**Highlights**

- UNICEF continued to scale up its humanitarian response across earthquake-affected areas, supporting the continuity of essential health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, and education services for children and families in temporary camps and affected communities.
- To date, UNICEF has reached 25,483 people with primary health care, 22,424 children, adults, and pregnant women with routine and catch-up vaccinations, 9,412 people with critical WASH supplies, 5,804 children and caregivers with nutrition services, and 6,134 children, adolescents, and caregivers with child protection services, including MHPSS.
- UNICEF is supporting the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), leading the WASH and education sectors. The PDNA will inform recovery priorities and help accelerate the restoration of essential services.
- In addition to its US$137.6 million 2026 HAC appeal, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to sustain critical interventions and support the implementation of the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum.

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
Context

Five weeks after the June 24 earthquakes in Venezuela, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026).

- Toll: 5,546 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Rescuers describe no longer searching for survivors, and international search and rescue missions are scaling back. There are critical information gaps related to missing persons.
- Children: CECODAP estimates that over 1,400 children and adolescents remain at significant risk of harm due to the earthquake.
- Displacement: As of July 26, 107 transitional camps for affected populations are housing 24,477 people (87% capacity). Most displaced people remain concentrated in Caracas and La Guaira.
- Education: According to civil society organizations, over 900 schools have been affected, including 18 school facilities that have totally collapsed and 40 that have severe structural damage. 120 teachers have been reported dead.
- Economic effects and reconstruction costs: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion. Government and private sector banking institutions are exploring credit programs for housing repair and replacement.
- Humanitarian funding request: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake.
- Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).

reports.title: Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response appeal raises more than $7.5 million for life-saving aid
reports.body_text:
*With support from generous Canadians and the Government of Canada, our members are reaching more than 40,000 people with critical assistance*

After back-to-back earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, Canadians rallied to support people affected through the Humanitarian Coalition’s Venezuela Earthquake Response. With the Government of Canada’s matching fund, the appeal raised more than **$7.5 million** from June 25 to July 14, 2026.

"We’re very moved by the generosity of Canadians," said Tiffany Baggetta, Executive Director of the Humanitarian Coalition. “Every dollar given and every dollar matched will help our members deliver life-saving relief to families affected by the Venezuela earthquakes. We’re extremely grateful to our donors, our community and media partners, and the Government of Canada for standing with communities as they continue to face the devastating impacts of displacement and destruction.”

In temporary camps and affected communities, the Humanitarian Coalition’s 12 member organizations are working tirelessly to provide essential support, such as:

- **Emergency food assistance** for families living in temporary shelters and other affected communities.
- **Safe water, sanitation and hygiene services**, including water trucking, handwashing stations, water treatment supplies and hygiene promotion activities.
- **Shelter and essential household items**, such as shelter kits, mattresses and kitchen supplies for families who have lost their homes and belongings.
- **Health services**, including mental health and psychosocial support, community health activities and rehabilitation services for people injured by the earthquakes.
- **Protection services** for families, including child-friendly spaces and psychosocial support.
- **Nutrition programs**, such as malnutrition screening for children, treatment and referral for acute malnutrition cases, and nutrition counselling.
- **Support for people with disabilities** and those recovering from serious injuries.

As humanitarian needs in Venezuela remain high, the Humanitarian Coalition is continuing to accept donations for the[ **Venezuela Emergency Response**](https://donate.humanitariancoalition.ca/ui/RS262E/donations/start).

**Notes:**

The Humanitarian Coalition is immensely grateful to the following supporters and charitable partners for their contributions to the Venezuela Emergency Response: Bell Media, CanadaHelps, Canadaland, Canadian Affairs, CanadianSME, CHOQFM, Cogeco Média, Corus, Fairchild Radio, Golden West Media, Jazz 91.1 FM, Métro, Rabble, Rogers tv, SJC, The Free Press, The Globe and Mail, The Walrus, TLN Media Group and Venezuelan Canadian Society of British Columbia.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #19 (31 de julio al 3 de agosto 2026)
reports.body_text:
El Reporte de Situación No. 19 presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, cubriendo el período comprendido entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto de 2026.

## Aspectos destacados

Entre el 31 de julio y el 3 de agosto, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación y gestión de campamentos, salud, protección, Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (WASH), gestión de información y Prevención de la Explotación y el Abuso Sexual (PEAS).

Durante el período, la OIM distribuyó **245 lonas plásticas, 234 lámparas solares, 234 bidones plegables, 235 sets de cocina, 227 kits de higiene y 74 mosquiteros** para atender necesidades prioritarias de alojamiento y enseres domésticos de familias afectadas por los terremotos.

A la fecha, los equipos apoyados por la OIM han realizado **7.615 consultas médicas a 6.733 personas afectadas** mediante servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

La OIM inició la caracterización de asentamientos comunitarios afectados por los terremotos, alcanzando **20 asentamientos en La Guaira, uno en Miranda y uno en Carabobo**, ampliando el monitoreo de necesidades y desplazamiento fuera de los campamentos transitorios.

## Actividades de la OIM

La OIM continuó la cogestión de cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Polideportivo José María Vargas, Playa Grande y César Nieves, apoyando la prestación de servicios, el registro de población, los mecanismos de información comunitaria y la coordinación operativa.

En Campo de Golf continuó la asignación de nuevas carpas familiares, la ampliación de iluminación solar y la adecuación de espacios comunitarios y de atención. En Mare Abajo II inició el abordaje comunitario para promover los servicios disponibles, identificar necesidades y fortalecer los canales de comunicación con la población alojada, mientras continuaron las actividades de registro y verificación de grupos familiares. En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se mantuvieron servicios esenciales para **796 personas pertenecientes a 221 grupos familiares**, incluyendo registro, orientación comunitaria, conectividad y restablecimiento de contacto familiar.

Durante el período, la OIM distribuyó **245 lonas plásticas, 234 lámparas solares, 234 bidones plegables, 235 sets de cocina, 227 kits de higiene y 74 mosquiteros**. A la fecha, la OIM ha entregado **4.987 sets de cocina, 4.580 lonas plásticas, 3.441 lámparas solares, 3.313 bidones plegables, 2.527 kits de higiene, 2.384 baldes, 1.066 mosquiteros y 822 kits de refugio para emergencias** a familias afectadas por los terremotos.

En WASH, la OIM continuó ampliando el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento mediante la activación de un sistema de agua potable en Campo de Golf, actividades de monitoreo de calidad del agua, cloración, mejoras de infraestructura sanitaria y apoyo a la gestión de residuos. A la fecha, la OIM ha distribuido **3.313 bidones plegables de 10 litros, 285 bidones semiplegables de 10 litros y 2.527 kits de higiene**.

La OIM y su socio implementador Ven Da Tu Mano continuaron prestando servicios de salud, salud mental y apoyo psicológico mediante equipos móviles. Durante el período se realizaron **90 consultas** en César Nieves, mientras que las jornadas móviles en el Polideportivo José María Vargas alcanzaron un acumulado de **2.509 consultas**. A la fecha, las intervenciones apoyadas por la OIM han permitido realizar **7.615 consultas médicas a 6.733 personas afectadas**.

La OIM continuó las actividades de registro y gestión de información mediante el Sistema Unificado de Gestión de Información (IMS) en los cinco campamentos transitorios. Durante el período, inició el levantamiento de información en asentamientos comunitarios afectados por los terremotos, logrando caracterizar **20 asentamientos en La Guaira, uno en Miranda y uno en Carabobo**, mientras equipos de la Matriz de Seguimiento de Desplazamiento (DTM) realizaron evaluaciones adicionales en Carabobo.

En protección, la OIM continuó brindando asistencia legal, gestión de casos, actividades de protección infantil, prevención de la trata de personas, prevención de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas y mecanismos de información comunitaria. Asimismo, inició actividades de abordaje comunitario en Mare Abajo II y apoyó la coordinación de una jornada de documentación que permitió a **182 personas** acceder a servicios de cedulación.

Como colíder del Grupo de Trabajo de Infraestructura y Alojamientos Temporales junto con ACNUR, la OIM continuó apoyando la coordinación operativa, el mapeo de servicios, la gestión de información y la planificación conjunta en los campamentos transitorios.

En PEAS, la OIM realizó sesiones de refrescamiento con **24 trabajadores humanitarios**, distribuyó **1.000 volantes informativos y mensajes clave** al equipo de NFI y llevó a cabo actividades de sensibilización con **15 lideresas comunitarias** y **17 trabajadores humanitarios** en Playa Grande.

## Respuesta Prevista de la OIM

La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la infraestructura, la prestación de servicios, las intervenciones WASH, el apoyo en alojamiento y las actividades de Coordinación y Gestión de Campamentos (CCCM) en los campamentos transitorios.

La OIM también continuará prestando servicios de salud, salud mental, apoyo psicológico y protección, al tiempo que fortalecerá los mecanismos de derivación para asistencia especializada.

Asimismo, mantendrá el monitoreo de movilidad, las actividades de registro, la gestión de información, las evaluaciones en asentamientos comunitarios y la coordinación con autoridades y organizaciones implementadoras para apoyar la planificación de una respuesta basada en evidencia.

reports.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #19 (31 July to 3 August 2026)
reports.body_text:
The nineteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 31 July to 3 August 2026.

## Highlights

Between 31 July and 3 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA).

During the reporting period, IOM distributed **245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets** to address priority shelter and household needs of earthquake-affected families.

To date, IOM-supported teams have delivered **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people** through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities.

IOM initiated the characterization of earthquake-affected community settlements, reaching **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, expanding needs and displacement monitoring beyond temporary accommodation sites.

## IOM Activities

IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination.

At Campo de Golf, the allocation of new family tents, expansion of solar lighting and improvement of community and service spaces continued. At Mare Abajo II, community outreach activities began to promote available services, identify needs and strengthen communication channels with site residents, while household registration and verification activities continued. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for **796 people from 221 households**, including registration, community orientation, connectivity and restoring family links.

During the reporting period, IOM distributed **245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets** to earthquake-affected families. To date, IOM has delivered **4,987 kitchen sets, 4,580 plastic tarpaulins, 3,441 solar lamps, 3,313 collapsible water containers, 2,527 hygiene kits, 2,384 buckets, 1,066 mosquito nets and 822 emergency shelter kits**.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water and sanitation services through the activation of a potable water system at Campo de Golf, water quality monitoring, chlorination activities, sanitation infrastructure improvements and waste management support. To date, IOM has provided **3,313 collapsible 10-liter water containers, 285 semi-collapsible 10-liter water containers and 2,527 hygiene kits**.

IOM and its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued delivering health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams. During the reporting period, **90 consultations** were conducted in Cesar Nieves, while mobile health services at Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex reached a cumulative total of **2,509 consultations**. To date, IOM-supported interventions have provided **7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people**.

IOM continued registration and information management activities through the unified Information Management System (IMS) across the five temporary accommodation sites. During the reporting period, IOM initiated data collection in earthquake-affected community settlements, characterizing **20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo**, while Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) teams conducted additional assessments in Carabobo.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention, violence against women and girls prevention and community information services. Community outreach activities were launched in Mare Abajo II, and IOM supported the coordination of a documentation campaign that enabled **182 people** to access national identification services.

As co-lead of the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group together with UNHCR, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, service mapping, information management and joint planning across temporary accommodation sites.

In PSEA, IOM conducted refresher sessions with **24 humanitarian workers**, distributed **1,000 informational leaflets and key messages** to NFI teams, and carried out awareness activities with **15 community leaders** and **17 humanitarian workers** in Playa Grande.

## IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure, service delivery, WASH interventions, shelter support and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM will also continue delivering health, mental health, psychological support and protection services while strengthening referral pathways for specialized assistance.

In addition, IOM will maintain mobility monitoring, registration activities, information management, community settlement assessments and coordination with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning.

reports.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #05 (Reporting period: 24 – 31 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

• Since 05 July, an inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator has been deployed in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination and lead efforts to identify connectivity gaps and operational requirements for targeted humanitarian response support. A new inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator will assume the role on 03 August and continue supporting the response.

• The inter-agency LTC Telecoms Coordinator is working with UN OCHA, Comisión Nacional de Telecomunicaciones (CONATEL), Compañía Anónima Nacional Teléfonos de Venezuela (CANTV), Movistar, Digitel, G-Network, emergency.lu, Grupo Telefónica, and other partners to deploy connectivity solutions in the most affected areas.

• Through the Internet for Communities solution, GNetwork’s fibre internet connection will remain free for all users at Polideportivo, César Nieves, and a third site until the end of the year or until the emergency ends. This helps address immediate concerns related to service contracts and recurring connectivity costs.

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Country Appeal (July - December 2026)
reports.body_text:
Venezuela is facing a major humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June 2026. The states most affected include La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Falcón and neighbouring areas.

The loss of livelihoods, disruption of health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of gender-based violence and harmful coping mechanisms, especially among women, girls and adolescents.

The health system is under severe strain. Many health facilities have sustained structural damage and are facing critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and personnel, while disruptions to electricity, water supply and supply chains continue to hamper service delivery.

To respond to the crisis, UNFPA is seeking US$10 million to scale up life-saving sexual and reproductive health services and strengthen gender-based violence prevention and response across the affected areas.

UNFPA is targeting 64,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, including emergency obstetric care, antenatal and postnatal care, neonatal care, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, family planning services, clinical management of rape, and essential reproductive health information.

In addition, UNFPA is aiming to reach 57,780 people through gender-based violence prevention and response programmes, providing case management, psychosocial support, psychological first aid, the distribution of dignity kits, and awareness sessions on risk mitigation and available support services for survivors.

As humanitarian needs continue to grow, these interventions are critical to protecting the health, rights and dignity of those most at risk, preventing further loss of life, and ensuring continued access to essential care as affected communities recover and rebuild.

Needs Assessment Report: Venezuela - Assessment findings on the state of health services and urgent humanitarian needs in La Guaira, Miranda, and Distrito Capital following the June 2026 earthquakes (July 2026)
reports.body_text: Following the June 2026 earthquakes in Venezuela, Project HOPE and its local subsidiary, Proyecto Esperanza, conducted a needs assessment across 12 health facilities and 160 households in Distrito Capital, Miranda, and La Guaira to evaluate health service capacity, WASH conditions, and community protection needs. The assessment found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support services, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure, and protection mechanisms, despite generally strong community knowledge of disease prevention and existing health system capacity. Findings indicate that humanitarian response efforts should prioritize restoring essential health supplies and infrastructure, strengthening WASH systems, expanding mental health and protection services, and addressing barriers that prevent communities and health facilities from translating existing knowledge into effective practices.
