reports.title: Situation Report No.7: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 23 July 2026
reports.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

• More than three weeks after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, affecting at least seven states, the emergency response remains active. While the most acute phase of rescue, trauma care and immediate postdisaster surgery has eased, priorities are now focused on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, supporting temporary camps and preventing public health risks.

• The health response continues transitioning from emergency care to early recovery, prioritizing restoration of integrated health service networks, continuity of specialized care, and implementation of the Ministry of Health’s National Mental Health Response Plan.

• Integrated epidemiological surveillance continues to reinforce early detection, laboratory verification and environmental risk monitoring. PAHO/WHO supported the roll-out of a real-time surveillance dashboard and the delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen national preparedness.

• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through the deployment of its Regional Response Team, covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory, WASH, immunization, risk communication and community engagement, and EMT coordination. In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO is also supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with fourteen EMTs now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua, increasing clinical capacity in the affected areas.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response through the delivery of computers to strengthen on-site epidemiological surveillance and body bags for the dignified management of the deceased, and through the coordination of in-kind donations from seven partners, most recently from Direct Relief: water purification tablets covering 20 days of chlorinated supply, medicines, and hygiene kits. A second distribution of TESK and IEHK kits to 18 health facilities and 36 transitional camps is planned.

reports.title: Un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela, las comunidades comienzan a recuperarse
reports.body_text:
CARACAS – Un mes después de que devastadores terremotos sacudieran Venezuela, las comunidades afectadas están demostrando una notable resiliencia mientras las familias comienzan a recuperarse del desastre, reconstruyendo sus rutinas diarias y apoyándose mutuamente en un camino aún incierto hacia la recuperación.

En los sitios temporales de acogida y los barrios afectados, lideresas y líderes comunitarios, voluntarios, autoridades y trabajadores humanitarios están ayudando a las familias a acceder a asistencia, reconectarse con servicios esenciales y dar los primeros pasos para reconstruir sus vidas. Aunque las necesidades siguen siendo significativas, los esfuerzos conjuntos están contribuyendo a restablecer la estabilidad y la esperanza para miles de personas afectadas por el desastre.

Aprovechando su larga trayectoria de presencia en Venezuela, ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, ha apoyado a las familias a acceder a apoyo psicosocial, recibir asistencia legal, reemplazar documentos de identidad perdidos y conectarse con servicios especializados. Asimismo, ha proporcionado artículos esenciales y asistencia en los sitios temporales de acogida, en el marco de la respuesta más amplia del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y en estrecha coordinación con las autoridades nacionales y locales.

“Un mes después, seguimos inspirados por la fortaleza, la solidaridad y la determinación de las comunidades afectadas”, afirmó Kristin Halvorsen, Representante a cargo de ACNUR en Venezuela. “Las personas que han perdido sus hogares, seres queridos y medios de vida ya están ayudándose mutuamente a reconstruir. Nuestra prioridad es acompañarlas durante todo el proceso de recuperación, garantizando que las personas más vulnerables reciban la protección, asistencia y apoyo que necesitan para seguir adelante con dignidad y esperanza”.

Como organización líder del Clúster de Protección, ACNUR está contribuyendo a identificar y apoyar a las personas que enfrentan mayores riesgos tras el desastre, entre ellas mujeres, niñas y niños, personas mayores, personas con discapacidad, refugiadas, solicitantes de asilo, retornadas y miembros vulnerables de las comunidades de acogida. Las evaluaciones rápidas realizadas junto con socios permitieron identificar preocupaciones clave relacionadas con el impacto psicológico, la pérdida de documentación, el desplazamiento, la separación familiar y la limitada privacidad en los albergues colectivos.

Hasta la fecha, ACNUR y sus socios han brindado más de 4.000 servicios de protección en sitios temporales de acogida en La Guaira, incluyendo información y orientación, asistencia legal, primeros auxilios psicológicos, apoyo relacionado con documentación y derivaciones a servicios especializados. Más de 2.500 mujeres y niñas han recibido asistencia en materia de protección, mientras que se han realizado más de 400 derivaciones para atención médica, protección infantil, apoyo psicosocial y otros servicios especializados.

La pérdida de documentos de identidad sigue siendo un desafío importante para muchas familias afectadas. Sin documentación, las personas pueden enfrentar obstáculos para acceder a servicios de salud, educación, apoyo de vivienda y otros servicios esenciales. Desde los terremotos, ACNUR ha proporcionado más de 320 servicios de orientación y asistencia relacionados con documentación y está apoyando a las autoridades en los esfuerzos de registro y gestión de datos para ayudar a identificar necesidades y facilitar la asistencia.

ACNUR también ha movilizado artículos de emergencia provenientes de suministros preposicionados y puentes aéreos humanitarios, aportando más de 55 toneladas métricas de artículos, incluidos sistemas de iluminación solar, carpas para la provisión de servicios de protección, mosquiteros y otros artículos esenciales para apoyar a las familias que viven en sitios temporales de acogida y comunidades afectadas. La organización también está proporcionando apoyo técnico para mejorar la seguridad, la accesibilidad y la privacidad de las personas más vulnerables.

“Estamos profundamente agradecidos por la solidaridad demostrada por gobiernos, donantes, socios humanitarios y personas de todo el mundo en apoyo a las personas de Venezuela”, señaló Halvorsen. “Su apoyo ha permitido una respuesta rápida en un momento crítico, ayudando a las familias afectadas a acceder a servicios de protección, información, asistencia de emergencia y apoyo especializado. A medida que avanza la recuperación, el apoyo continuo será fundamental para garantizar que las personas permanezcan conectadas con los servicios que necesitan, que los riesgos emergentes de protección sean identificados de manera temprana y que nadie quede atrás”.

Para las personas sobrevivientes de los terremotos, la recuperación no consiste únicamente en reconstruir viviendas, sino también en fortalecer los vínculos que permiten a las comunidades sanar. En conversaciones con varias familias afectadas, todas expresaron su deseo de reconstruirse y recuperarse, con la esperanza de volver a encontrar la estabilidad necesaria para construir un futuro.

Un mes después del desastre, el impacto humanitario sigue siendo grave. Las autoridades informan de más de 5.000 personas fallecidas, más de 16.000 heridas y casi 18.000 que han perdido sus hogares. Más de 850 edificios han resultado afectados, incluidos 190 que colapsaron, mientras miles de familias continúan viviendo en sitios temporales de acogida o con familiares y comunidades de acogida mientras avanzan los esfuerzos de recuperación.

Las Naciones Unidas y sus socios humanitarios han lanzado una adenda de 298 millones de dólares estadounidenses al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026 para atender las necesidades derivadas de los terremotos de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses. El plan complementa las actividades humanitarias en curso y busca apoyar a las comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en protección, alojamiento, salud, educación, agua y saneamiento, seguridad alimentaria y recuperación temprana.

Más de 850 edificios han resultado afectados, incluidos 190 que colapsaron, mientras miles de familias continúan viviendo en sitios temporales de acogida o con familiares y comunidades de acogida mientras avanzan los esfuerzos de recuperación.

Las Naciones Unidas y sus socios humanitarios han lanzado una adenda de 298 millones de dólares estadounidenses al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026 para atender las necesidades derivadas de los terremotos de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses. El plan complementa las actividades humanitarias en curso y busca apoyar a las comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en protección, alojamiento, salud, educación, agua y saneamiento, seguridad alimentaria y recuperación temprana.

reports.title: Miles de niños y niñas siguen enfrentando múltiples riesgos un mes después de los devastadores terremotos en Venezuela
reports.body_text:
El desplazamiento, la interrupción de los servicios y las múltiples réplicas afectan a los más vulnerables mientras las comunidades intentan recuperarse de los efectos del desastre

**CARACAS/CIUDAD DE PANAMÁ/NUEVA YORK, 24 de julio de 2026 –** Un mes después de que dos poderosos terremotos azotaran la costa centro-norte de Venezuela, niños, niñas y familias continúan enfrentando los impactos causados por los sismos, entre ellos el desplazamiento, los daños a la infraestructura y las interrupciones de los servicios básicos.

Actualmente, casi 23.100 personas permanecen en los campamentos transitorios habilitados en La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda y Aragua. UNICEF está trabajando para llegar a aproximadamente 470.000 personas, incluyendo 169.000 niños y niñas, con asistencia para salvar vidas, lo que incluye servicios en salud, nutrición, agua, saneamiento e higiene, protección infantil, educación y protección social.

"Un mes después de los terremotos, niños, niñas y familias aún enfrentan las consecuencias de esta devastadora catástrofe. Más allá del daño visible, el miedo, la incertidumbre y las alteraciones causadas por el desplazamiento pueden tener impactos duraderos en el bienestar de la niñez", dijo **el representante de UNICEF en Venezuela, Manuel Rodríguez Pumarol**. "El apoyo continuo es esencial para asegurar que los niños, niñas y adolescentes tengan acceso a agua segura, atención médica, protección y los servicios que necesitan para recuperarse".

Los terremotos, que alcanzaron magnitudes de 7,2 y 7,5, causaron más de 5.390 muertes, dejaron más de 16.700 personas heridas y registraron más de 1.400 réplicas.

Las evaluaciones de daños continúan revelando la magnitud del impacto, con al menos 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 que colapsaron por completo. Los daños a las instalaciones de salud y a cientos de escuelas están interrumpiendo servicios esenciales para miles de niños, mientras que las continuas réplicas siguen generando riesgos para las familias que viven en los refugios temporales.

Los niños y niñas afectados por la emergencia enfrentan mayores probabilidades de experimentar angustia psicológica, violencia, negligencia, explotación y separación familiar, lo que agrava los riesgos para su seguridad y bienestar. Las condiciones de hacinamiento, la interrupción de la rutina y la incertidumbre prolongada pueden aumentar aún más estas amenazas, especialmente para los niños y niñas más vulnerables.

UNICEF está trabajando con el Gobierno, el sistema de las Naciones Unidas y socios humanitarios para ofrecer servicios que salvan vidas y garantizan el acceso a salud, nutrición, agua, saneamiento e higiene, y protección infantil. Hasta la fecha, UNICEF ha distribuido más de 82 toneladas métricas de suministros de emergencia, incluyendo kits de salud, equipo de purificación y almacenamiento de agua, y materiales para el desarrollo infantil temprano y recreativo.

A medida que los esfuerzos de recuperación entran en una nueva fase, UNICEF hace un llamado a donantes y socios para que mantengan el apoyo a los niños, niñas y familias afectados por los terremotos, pero se estima que se requieren 65,7 millones de dólares estadounidenses para responder al impacto humanitario de los terremotos en los próximos meses.

En los campamentos temporales y en comunidades afectadas, UNICEF, junto con sus socios:

- Ha proporcionado agua segura a más de 8.900 personas mediante la distribución diaria de 80.000 litros de agua en tres campamentos de transición en La Guaira, y ha distribuido suministros esenciales de higiene para apoyar hasta 29.000 personas.
- En coordinación con el Ministerio de Salud, UNICEF apoyó a equipos móviles de salud en la provisión de servicios de atención primaria, incluyendo vacunaciones, a más de 21.000 personas, entre ellas niños, niñas y mujeres embarazadas. UNICEF también suministró medicamentos esenciales a 198 centros de salud, con la capacidad de brindar servicios de atención primaria a unas 49.000 personas.
- Más de 5.000 personas han recibido servicios de nutrición, incluyendo detección aguda de desnutrición, suplementación con micronutrientes, asesoría nutricional y apoyo en la lactancia materna para mujeres embarazadas y lactantes.
- UNICEF estableció espacios amigables para la infancia en campamentos transitorios en La Guaira, con los que ha llegado a más de 4.000 niños, niñas, adolescentes y cuidadores con apoyo psicosocial, actividades recreativas, manejo de casos y servicios especializados de protección infantil.
- UNICEF también apoya las Evaluaciones de Necesidades Post-Desastre en sectores clave, incluyendo WASH, salud, nutrición y educación, para ayudar a acelerar la restauración de servicios sociales esenciales para niños, niñas y sus familias en las áreas afectadas.

"A medida que las familias comienzan a recuperarse, los niños y niñas deben permanecer en el centro de la respuesta", dijo **Rodríguez Pumarol**. "Las próximas semanas serán críticas y un apoyo sostenido puede ayudar a evitar que la emergencia de hoy se convierta en una crisis a largo plazo para la niñez".

reports.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #07, 23 July 2026
reports.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquake: One month update – 24 July 2026
reports.body_text:
One month following the devastating earthquakes of June 24, Venezuela continues to grapple with the aftermath, facing profound grief as thousands mourn the loss of family, friends, and everything they owned. ​

This sudden natural disaster that affected particularly the coastal state of La Guaira, near Caracas, has transitioned into a complex, protracted crisis characterized by massive population displacement, severe infrastructural damage, and deep psychological trauma. In La Guaira and Caracas, the urgent needs include access to clean water, adequate shelter, mental health care, and protection. ​

The official death toll has reached 5,398, with 16,740 individuals injured, 17,907 displaced, and 6,462 rescued from the rubble. The structural devastation is staggering; 190 buildings have officially collapsed, while over 895 structures, including schools, vital public infrastructure, and hospitals, have suffered severe damage and are at risk of collapse. ​

Thousands are currently residing in makeshift Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites or sleeping in tents adjacent to their damaged homes. In Maiquetía (La Guaira), approximately 3,000 individuals are camping on the pavement directly in front of 20 severely damaged and unstable buildings. Similarly, in Avenida Bolívar (Caracas), another 3,000 individuals are living on the streets, stripped of proper shelter and basic services. ​

In response to the crisis, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) currently operates four mobile clinics providing Primary Health Care, Mental Health support, Health Promotion, and WASH activities across the most affected areas: three in La Guaira (Maiquetía, Catia La Mar, and Tamaguarena) and one in Caracas (Avenida Bolívar). These clinics offer primary healthcare, clean water, and emergency mental health interventions to families who have lost everything. In the past month, MSF medical teams have conducted 2,217 medical consultations.

The injuries sustained extend beyond physical; families still searching for loved ones beneath the rubble, along with the shock of sudden homelessness and displacement, have given rise to a psychological crisis. To address these mental health challenges, MSF has integrated mental health support into its mobile response, providing: 113 individual mental health, 323 group therapy sessions, 1,402 psycho-education sessions. With local infrastructure severely compromised, MSF teams are implementing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) intervention: ​

- Installed a 5,000-liter water bladder in Playa Verde to serve as a reliable clean water source.
- Initiated the ongoing chlorination of four primary water distribution sites alongside continuous water purification monitoring.
- Distributed 5,000 bottles of emergency drinking water to families living on the streets.

Over the past month, MSF has donated approximately 8.5 tons of emergency medical supplies. This extensive logistical effort has supported immediate, life-saving operations and addressed the healthcare needs of an estimated 10,000 patients. MSF teams continue to provide disinfectants and Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) materials not only to active hospitals but also to overwhelmed local morgues, ensuring safety, hygiene, and dignity amid unprecedented loss.

reports.title: Venezuela earthquakes 1 month: protect girls from a second crisis
reports.body_text:
Following the twin earthquakes that killed more than [5,300](https://reliefweb.int/OCHA:%20https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-28-21-july-2026-time-0900-pm) people in Venezuela, children, especially girls, are now facing a rising risk of gender-based violence, disruption to essential services including menstrual health care, and increasingly uncertain access to education.

More than [23,000 ](https://reliefweb.int/OCHA:%20https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-28-21-july-2026-time-0900-pm)people still live in transitional camps across Venezuela.

Among them, girls and adolescents face risks that go beyond the immediate emergency.

## Overcrowded shelters increase violence risk

In some camps, overcrowded shelters without separate toilets or private spaces for women and girls increase exposure to violence and abuse.

Thousands of families are not in official camps at all, having set up makeshift shelters in public squares and open spaces near their damaged homes, with little access to clean water, food or protection services.

Fear of overcrowding and lack of privacy is pushing some families to stay in informal settlements rather than move to organised sites.

“I’d rather be in a plaza where I know the people around me than go somewhere huge where you don’t know who comes in and who goes out,” said Andreina, a 26-year-old mother who has been living in a public square with her husband and young daughter since 25 June.

“During emergencies, the protective environment for children weakens. Caregivers are under immense stress, and it is in these moments that trafficking networks and other perpetrators take advantage,” said Yesica Serrano, Plan International’s Regional Child Protection Advisor for Humanitarian Action, speaking from Caracas.

“The emergencies do not affect all children in the same way. Girls, especially adolescent girls face greater exposure to sexual exploitation, violence and domestic work, while adolescent boys face risks of recruitment by criminal groups,” Serrano added.

Adolescent girls who have been separated from their families, or whose caregivers have died or been hospitalised, face the sharpest exposure of all.

## Significant challenges accessing menstrual health supplies

Another major concern is the access to menstrual health supplies. Without adequate materials and private facilities, adolescent girls face barriers to accessing other forms of support available in the camps, compounding their isolation at exactly the moment they are most vulnerable.

“People are focused on finding food, water, torches and basic resources. But no one is thinking about what women need: sanitary towels, toilet paper, the basics,” said Andrea, a 17-year-old volunteer with a Plan International partner organisation.

## Disrupted education

Although Venezuelan schools are currently in their summer break, the earthquake cut the last school year short for thousands of children.

With several school buildings now being used to house displaced families, there is no certainty that classes will resume when the new school year is due to begin in September, putting at uncertainty the availability of one of the few safe spaces that help them recover.

## Hidden toll on children’s health

The physical and mental health of children and adolescents is increasingly affected by conditions in the areas hardest hit by the disaster.

Plan’s local partners in Venezuela report that physical complaints with no clear cause are appearing more and more, alongside signs of post-traumatic stress and a constant sense of insecurity, and on closer listening, they reveal weeks of disrupted sleep, jumpiness and accumulated fear.

“When it gets windy, I run into my room and hide, and I get scared,” says nine-year-old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only 5, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: “I was on the beach, and a tsunami was chasing me.”

Michele, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: “They’re scared, they’re frightened. Right now, the children need psychological support to help them.”

“At this stage of the emergency, children’s mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don’t address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible,” explains Yesica Serrano.

## Recovery funding must address all these risks from the outset

One month on, the challenge is no longer only humanitarian relief. Communities now face a longer recovery process that will determine whether girls return safely to school, regain access to protection services, manage their menstrual health with dignity and remain protected from exploitation and abuse in the months ahead.

The risk is that once global attention shifts elsewhere, girls will be left facing the consequences of this disaster alone. Plan International warns that recovery funding must go beyond rebuilding infrastructure.

Protecting girls, restoring education and strengthening community support systems are essential investments from the outset if we are to prevent a long-term crisis and ensure a more resilient recovery for Venezuela’s children and communities.

Plan International has been providing emergency assistance to communities since the first days after the earthquakes, working with local partner organisations across affected states.

The response includes protection services for children, with a focus on adolescent girls, psychosocial support, safe spaces in schools and communities, hygiene kits and essential household items, emergency education activities and primary health care.

Venezuela response appeal

“At this stage of the emergency, children’s mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don’t address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible,” explains Yesica Serrano.

Recovery funding must address all these risks from the outset

One month on, the challenge is no longer only humanitarian relief. Communities now face a longer recovery process that will determine whether girls return safely to school, regain access to protection services, manage their menstrual health with dignity and remain protected from exploitation and abuse in the months ahead.

The risk is that once global attention shifts elsewhere, girls will be left facing the consequences of this disaster alone. Plan International warns that recovery funding must go beyond rebuilding infrastructure.

Protecting girls, restoring education and strengthening community support systems are essential investments from the outset if we are to prevent a long-term crisis and ensure a more resilient recovery for Venezuela’s children and communities.

Plan International has been providing emergency assistance to communities since the first days after the earthquakes, working with local partner organisations across affected states.

The response includes protection services for children, with a focus on adolescent girls, psychosocial support, safe spaces in schools and communities, hygiene kits and essential household items, emergency education activities and primary health care.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 30**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**23 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

**Note**

> ###### Starting with this edition, the report will be published on a weekly basis. The next edition will be released on 30 July. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: [345W Preparedness and Response](https://drive.google.com/file/d/12Tdck_8iHPTcj6BRDeYMwkp1lwS_-rYq/view?usp=sharing).

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 30**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**23 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.

**Nota**

> ###### A partir de esta edición, el informe se publicará de manera semanal. La próxima edición será publicada el jueves 30 de julio. Agradecemos a las organizaciones socias, entidades de las Naciones Unidas y donantes por sus valiosos aportes, y les invitamos a continuar reportando sus actividades de respuesta a la emergencia ocasionada por los terremotos a través de la plataforma 345W. reports.title: Thousands of children continue to face multiple risks one month after devastating earthquakes in Venezuela
reports.body_text:
**CARACAS/PANAMA CITY/NEW YORK, 24 July 2026 –** One month after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela’s north-central coast, children and families continue to face the lasting impacts of displacement, damaged infrastructure and disruption to essential services.

Nearly 23,100 people are currently in temporary camps across La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda and Aragua. UNICEF is working to reach approximately 470,000 people, including 169,000 children, with life-saving assistance across health, nutrition, water and sanitation, child protection, education and social protection.

“One month after the earthquakes, children and families are still dealing with the consequences of this devastating disaster. Beyond the visible damage, the fear, uncertainty and disruption caused by displacement can have lasting impacts on children’s well-being,” said UNICEF Representative in Venezuela, Manuel Rodriguez Pumarol. “Continued support is essential to ensure children have access to safe water, health care, protection and the services they need to recover.”

The earthquakes, measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude, killed more than 5,390 people, injured over 16,700 and triggered more than 1,400 aftershocks.

Damage assessments continue to reveal the scale of the impact, with at least 856 buildings affected, including 190 that collapsed entirely. Damage to health facilities and hundreds of schools is disrupting essential services for thousands of children, while continued aftershocks are sustaining risks for families living in temporary shelters.

Children affected by emergencies face heightened risks of psychological distress, violence, neglect, exploitation and family separation which compounds risk to their safety and wellbeing. Overcrowded conditions, disruption to routine and prolonged uncertainty can further increase these risks, particularly for the most vulnerable children.

UNICEF is working with the Government, the United Nations system and humanitarian partners to deliver life-saving and protective services across health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, and child protection. To date, UNICEF has distributed more than 82 metric tons of emergency supplies, including health kits, water purification and storage equipment, and early childhood development and recreational materials.

As recovery efforts enter a new phase, UNICEF is calling on donors and partners to sustain support for children and families affected by the earthquakes, but an estimated US$65.7 million is required to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes in the months ahead.

In temporary camps and affected communities, UNICEF and partners have:

- Provided safe water to more than 8,900 people through the daily distribution of 80,000 litres of water across three transitional camps in La Guaira, and distributed essential hygiene supplies to support up to 29,000 people.
- In coordination with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF supported mobile health teams in providing primary healthcare services, including vaccinations, to more than 21,000 people, including children and pregnant women. UNICEF also supplied 198 health facilities with essential medicines, with the capacity to provide primary healthcare services to up to 49,000 people.
- Reached more than 5,000 people with nutrition services, including acute malnutrition screening, micronutrient supplementation, nutrition counselling, and breastfeeding support for pregnant and lactating women.
- Established child-friendly spaces in transitional camps in La Guaira, reaching more than 4,000 children, adolescents, and caregivers with psychosocial support, recreational activities, case management, and specialized child protection services.
- UNICEF is also supporting Post-Disaster Needs Assessments (PDNAs) across key sectors, including WASH, health, nutrition, and education, to help accelerate the restoration of essential social services for children and their families in affected areas.

“As families begin recovering, children must remain at the centre of the response,” said Pumarol. “The weeks ahead will be critical and sustained support can help prevent today's emergency from becoming a longer-term crisis for children.”

\#####

reports.title: Envíos aéreos de ayuda humanitaria a Venezuela (24 julio 2026)
El Programa Mundial de Alimentos alcanza a más de 100.000 personas con asistencia tras los terremotos en Venezuela
reports.body_text:
CARACAS – Un mes después de que dos poderosos terremotos sacudieran el centro-norte de Venezuela, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) continúa brindando asistencia alimentaria a las comunidades afectadas por la devastación. Esta respuesta sin precedentes, adaptada a las diferentes necesidades de cada zona afectada, ya ha alcanzado a más de 100.000 personas y, con la financiación adecuada, espera llegar a medio millón en los próximos dos meses.

En las primeras 72 horas de la emergencia, WFP puso en marcha una serie de diagnósticos que ya han sido completados en más de 80 comunidades de siete estados afectados. Estos han permitido orientar la respuesta con base en información sobre acceso a alimentos, funcionamiento de los mercados, cadenas de suministro y riesgos de protección. Este trabajo se ha realizado en estrecha coordinación con el Gobierno de Venezuela y los socios humanitarios.

"Ninguna familia afectada está viviendo esta catástrofe de la misma manera, y la asistencia debe moverse tan rápido como cambian las condiciones sobre el terreno", afirmó Stephanie Hochstetter, Representante de WFP en Venezuela. "Estábamos aquí antes de los terremotos, y nos quedamos con las y los venezolanos, junto a las autoridades locales y nuestros socios, el tiempo que sea necesario para que las familias afectadas puedan volver a ponerse en pie".

**Una respuesta adaptada a las condiciones y necesidades de cada comunidad**

WFP está ajustando su asistencia a las circunstancias específicas de cada comunidad:

- Comidas calientes para personas en albergues y comedores comunitarios: comidas completas con proteínas, vegetales y agua, preparadas en el lugar como parte de un esfuerzo coordinado entre múltiples socios.
- Raciones listas para consumir para personas sin medios para cocinar: dirigidas a quienes aún están en movimiento o refugiándose donde se sienten seguros. Estas raciones no requieren preparación y cubren tres días de necesidades alimentarias por persona.
- Canastas de alimentos para hogares cuyas viviendas siguen siendo habitables, pero cuyos medios de vida y acceso a los mercados se han visto afectados: consisten en alimentos básicos secos que cubren el 75 por ciento de las necesidades alimentarias mensuales de una familia.
- Cupones electrónicos prepagados en zonas donde los mercados están funcionando: permiten a las familias priorizar sus necesidades más urgentes y, al mismo tiempo, apoyan la recuperación de la economía local.

**Ampliando la respuesta de emergencia mientras se atienden las necesidades existentes en todo el país**

WFP busca alcanzar hasta 500.000 personas durante los primeros tres meses de la respuesta. La organización también actúa como columna vertebral logística de la respuesta humanitaria, movilizando suministros de socorro hacia comunidades de difícil acceso en apoyo a toda la comunidad humanitaria.

Los servicios logísticos de WFP han apoyado a organizaciones no gubernamentales y agencias de las Naciones Unidas, con el transporte de 261 toneladas métricas de asistencia y el almacenamiento de más de 1.300 metros cúbicos de suministros, incluidos artículos relacionados con albergue, salud, protección, recuperación temprana y agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH).

La asistencia se entrega en coordinación con la respuesta del Gobierno de Venezuela y como complemento a ella, junto a socios humanitarios y organizaciones de la sociedad civil presentes sobre el terreno.

**Brecha de financiación**

WFP solicita 80 millones de dólares para sostener y ampliar su respuesta. Sin contribuciones oportunas de los donantes, la expansión de las operaciones y la capacidad de seguir adaptando la asistencia a las necesidades cambiantes de las comunidades se verán limitadas.

\# # #

**Nota para los editores:**

[Aquí](https://multimedia.wfp.org/Share/rdy64s56nee55g23godbc2u614dtqgc5?FR_=1&W=1526&H=948) se puede acceder a material de vídeo con calidad de emisión.

Se puede acceder a fotografías en alta resolución [aquí](https://multimedia.wfp.org/Share/asobbfj2wcg85w2l17554o44ff4c4045).

El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas es la mayor organización humanitaria del mundo dedicada a salvar vidas en emergencias y a utilizar la asistencia alimentaria para allanar el camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad de las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos del cambio climático.

Síguenos en X, antes Twitter, e Instagram @WFP\_Venezuela @wfp\_venezuela

**Contacto**

**Para obtener más información, póngase en contacto con (dirección de correo electrónico: nombre.apellido@wfp.org):**

Tayra Pinzón, WFP/Panamá, móvil: +507 6346-3497

Marianela GONZÁLEZ, WFP/Venezuela, móvil: +58 414-3775967

reports.title: WFP reaches more than 100,000 people with assistance since Venezuela earthquakes
reports.body_text:
CARACAS – A month after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, the World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide food assistance to communities impacted by the devastation. This unprecedented response, tailored to different needs in each affected area, has already reached more than 100,000 people and, with proper funding, hopes to reach a total of half a million over the next two months.

Within 72 hours of the emergency, WFP launched a series of assessments that have now been completed across more than 80 communities in seven affected states. These have helped shape WFP’s response based on indicators involving access to food, market functionality, and supply chains and protection risks., These efforts have been undertaken in close coordination with the Government of Venezuela and humanitarian partners.

“No two affected families are living through this catastrophe the same way, and assistance must move as fast as conditions on the ground change,” said Stephanie Hochstetter, WFP Representative in Venezuela. “We were here before the earthquakes, and we will stay with Venezuelans, and alongside the local authorities and partners, for as long as it takes for families to get back on their feet”.

**A response built around real, changing conditions**

WFP is tailoring its support to each community’s specific circumstances and needs:

- Hot meals for people in shelters and community kitchens: Full meals with protein, vegetables, and water, prepared on site as part of a coordinated multi-partner effort.
- Ready-to-eat rations for people without the means to cook: For those still on the move or sheltering wherever they feel safe. These rations require no preparation and cover three days of food needs per person.
- Family food baskets for households whose homes remain habitable, but whose livelihoods and access to markets have been disrupted: this takes the form of dry staples covering 75 percent of a family's monthly food needs.
- Pre-paid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning: this enables families to prioritize their most urgent needs while supporting local economic recovery.

**Scaling the emergency response while continuing to address pre-existing needs across the country**

WFP aims to reach up to 500,000 people over the response's first three months. The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response; moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities in support of the wider humanitarian community. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies, with 261 metric tons transported and over 1,300 m³ stored — spanning shelter, health, protection, early recovery, and WASH supplies.

Assistance is being delivered in coordination with, and as a complement to, the Government of Venezuela's response and alongside humanitarian and civil-society partners on the ground.

**Funding gap**

WFP is appealing for USD 80 million to sustain and scale its response. Without timely donor contributions, the pace of expansion and the ability to continue tailoring assistance to evolving needs will be constrained.

\# # #

reports.title: IFRC: Un mes después de los terremotos de Venezuela, la atención en salud, el apoyo psicosocial y el acceso a agua potable son prioridad urgente
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
reports.body_text:
**Caracas, Ciudad de Panama, Ginebra, 23 de julio de 2026** — Un mes después de los dos terremotos que sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela, la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) y la Cruz Roja Venezolana (CRV) han identificado tres áreas críticas para la asistencia humanitaria en el corto y mediano plazo: la atención primaria en salud, el cuidado de la salud mental y el acceso a agua potable.

La IFRC y la CRV concentran ahora sus esfuerzos en la distribución de ayuda humanitaria, la prestación de servicios de salud y la realización de nuevas evaluaciones de necesidades. Sus hallazgos señalan que muchas familias todavía dependen del agua embotellada para beber, asearse y cocinar. El acceso al saneamiento también sigue siendo limitado, lo que eleva el riesgo de brotes de enfermedades en las zonas donde se aloja la población desplazada. Miles de personas con enfermedades crónicas no han recuperado del todo la continuidad de su tratamiento, una interrupción que amenaza su bienestar y puede añadir presión al sistema de salud. Los sobrevivientes conviven también con ansiedad, miedo, tristeza e insomnio mientras atraviesan el duelo por la pérdida de sus seres queridos, sus trabajos y sus medios de vida.

*“A un mes de los devastadores terremotos que sacudieron nuestro país, reafirmamos nuestro compromiso con los venezolanos. Hemos activado todos los mecanismos de cooperación del Movimiento Internacional de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja para fortalecer y complementar nuestra respuesta, y seguiremos aquí para quienes más lo necesitan”.* Dijo el presidente de la Cruz Roja Venezolana, Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva. “*Apuntamos a una operación de 24 meses para seguir acompañando a la población; las necesidades han ido cambiando y nuestra respuesta se ha ajustado para servir más y mejor.”*

Desde el minuto uno, los equipos locales de la Cruz Roja han estado al lado de las personas afectadas: primero instalando un hospital de campaña, acompañando el rescate de sobrevivientes y reconectando a familias que habían perdido el rastro de sus seres queridos; y ahora, con la distribución de ayuda humanitaria y el refuerzo de la atención primaria en salud a través de una clínica de emergencia en La Guaira.

Esta clínica, instalada por la IFRC y gestionada por la Cruz Roja Española, refuerza el hospital de campaña de la Cruz Roja Venezolana. Operará durante cuatro meses y ya presta servicios de salud y apoyo psicosocial que beneficiarán a cerca de 30.000 personas. Una de ellas es Gabriel Cipriani, quien perdió a familiares cercanos cuando su edificio colapsó y vive con una condición neurológica que requiere medicación constante. Para él, que la Cruz Roja siga ahí es la diferencia entre continuar su tratamiento o interrumpirlo: *"Saber que puedo contar con una doctora de la Cruz Roja me hizo sentir que no estoy solo, que hay una mano que está conmigo. Eso te da seguridad, te da confianza".*

En las próximas semanas y meses, la prioridad de la IFRC y la CRV será sostener esa atención de salud y ampliar el acceso a agua segura mientras se sientan las bases de la recuperación: reforzar la vigilancia epidemiológica para prevenir brotes, mantener el apoyo psicosocial y el tratamiento de enfermedades crónicas, y empezar a acompañar a las familias en la recuperación de sus medios de vida. La asistencia se ajustará a medida que las necesidades cambien, con especial atención a quienes corren mayor riesgo: la niñez, las personas mayores, las mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, y las personas con enfermedades crónicas o discapacidad.

*"El desastre está lejos de terminar. Continuar con las distribuciones de artículos esenciales y cuidar del bienestar de la población y de la salud pública es y seguirá siendo una prioridad en el mediano plazo; pero más adelante también lo será garantizar que las personas recuperen sus medios de vida y sus actividades de generación de ingresos",* dijo la directora regional de la IFRC para las Américas, Loyce Pace. *"Un desastre como este exige una asistencia multisectorial, integral y de largo aliento. La IFRC está comprometida con la Cruz Roja Venezolana y con la población venezolana para hacerlo posible, y por eso abogamos por un financiamiento sostenido y flexible, capaz de acompañar a las familias durante todo su proceso de recuperación".*

El financiamiento tiene una cifra concreta. La IFRC lanzó un llamamiento de emergencia para recaudar 50 millones de francos suizos para asistir a 300.000 personas durante dos años. A un mes del desastre, cuenta con un 25,19 por ciento de cobertura. A medida que las necesidades de la población incrementan y se hacen más complejas, los recursos deberían crecer al mismo ritmo.

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #3 (23 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
**1. Context**   
  
Three weeks after the 24 June earthquakes, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026).   
  
**Toll:** 5,278 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Of the confirmed dead, 7% remain unidentified, mainly due to missing fingerprint records and identity system gaps.   
  
**Displacement:** As of July 21, 107 transitional camps for affected populations have a total capacity of 27,822 people and current occupancy of 23,587 people. As of July 20, 41 camps are in Caracas, 28 in La Guaira, 28 in Miranda, and 10 in Aragua. Of the total camp population, 12,474 people are in La Guaira, 8,554 in Caracas, 1,877 in Miranda, and 682 in Aragua. These numbers are a snapshot, as the population in shelters changes constantly.   
  
**Debris:** An estimated 1 million tons of debris has resulted from the earthquake. Of this, only 6,700 tons has been cleared in La Guaira so far, representing just 1% of the total.   
  
**Humanitarian funding request**: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding appeal required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake Limited humanitarian operational presence: OCHA's own access assessment finds that Aragua, Carabobo, and Yaracuy have a relatively limited humanitarian operational presence. These states are accessible; the gap is a lack of resources. Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).   
**Economic constraints**: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion (internal field sourcing).

reports.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Situation Report #8 (July 22, 2026)
reports.body_text:
**Project HOPE continues to expand its humanitarian response across northern Venezuela. The team is significantly increasing access to healthcare for displaced and affected communities by operating eight mobile medical units (MMU), which are providing primary and maternal healthcare services in shelters and underserved communities. Project HOPE also continues to provide additional clinical support at health facilities in Distrito Capital and Miranda, with expansion underway to facilities in La Guaira. To reduce the risk of secondary public health emergencies, Project HOPE is also connecting families to mental health support, providing essential medicines, distributed additional hygiene kits through complementary funding, and recently launched a water trucking initiative.**

**Situation Overview**

**Humanitarian needs remain high as communities transition from the immediate aftermath of the earthquakes into a prolonged recovery phase.** While debris removal and damage assessments continue, thousands of displaced people remain in temporary shelters with persistent needs for healthcare, safe water, sanitation, and protection services. Overcrowded living conditions, intermittent rainfall, and disruptions to essential services continue to increase the risk of infectious disease transmission. At the same time, health facilities face the pressure of a continued increase in demand for services, including for acute injuries and routine health needs that were interrupted by the disaster. As operations evolve, humanitarian partners are increasingly focused on restoring access to primary healthcare and strengthening local health services to support communities through recovery.

reports.title: IFRC: Un mois après les séismes au Venezuela, les soins de santé, le soutien psychosocial et l'accès à l'eau potable demeurent des priorités urgentes
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
reports.body_text:
**Caracas, Panama, Genève, 23 juillet 2026** — Un mois après les deux séismes qui ont frappé le centre-nord du Venezuela, la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) et la Croix-Rouge vénézuélienne (CRV) ont identifié trois domaines critiques nécessitant une assistance humanitaire à court et à moyen terme : les soins de santé primaires, la santé mentale et l'accès à l'eau potable.

L'IFRC et la CRV concentrent désormais leurs efforts sur la distribution de l'aide humanitaire, la fourniture de services de santé et la réalisation d'évaluations complémentaires des besoins. Leurs constatations montrent que de nombreuses familles dépendent encore de l'eau en bouteille pour boire, cuisiner et assurer leur hygiène. L'accès aux services d'assainissement reste également limité, ce qui accroît le risque de flambées de maladies dans les zones où vivent les personnes déplacées. Des milliers de personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques n'ont pas encore retrouvé un accès régulier à leurs traitements, une interruption qui menace leur santé et exerce une pression supplémentaire sur le système de santé. Les survivants vivent également avec l'anxiété, la peur, la tristesse et les troubles du sommeil, tout en faisant le deuil de leurs proches, de leur emploi et de leurs moyens de subsistance

*« Un mois après les séismes dévastateurs qui ont secoué notre pays, nous réaffirmons notre engagement envers le peuple vénézuélien. C'est pourquoi nous lançons un appel en faveur d'un financement durable et flexible, capable d'accompagner les familles tout au long de leur relèvement. »*

Un mois après la catastrophe, cet appel est financé à hauteur de 25,19 %. À mesure que les besoins des populations évoluent et deviennent plus complexes, les ressources nécessaires pour y répondre doivent augmenter au même rythme.

reports.title: IFRC: One month after Venezuela's earthquakes, health care, psychosocial support and safe water remain urgent priorities
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
reports.body_text:
**Caracas, Panama City, Geneva 23 July 2026** — One month after the two earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the Venezuelan Red Cross (VRC) have identified three critical areas for humanitarian assistance in the short and medium term: primary health care, mental health care and access to safe drinking water.

The IFRC and the VRC are now focusing their efforts on distributing humanitarian aid, delivering health services and carrying out further needs assessments. Their findings show that many families still depend on bottled water to drink, wash and cook. Access to sanitation also remains limited, raising the risk of disease outbreaks in the areas where displaced people are staying. Thousands of people with chronic conditions have yet to fully regain continuity of treatment — an interruption that threatens their wellbeing and can add further strain to the health system. Survivors are also living with anxiety, fear, sadness and sleeplessness as they grieve the loss of loved ones, of their jobs and of their livelihoods.

*"One month on from the devastating earthquakes that shook our country, we reaffirm our commitment to the Venezuelan people. We have activated every cooperation mechanism of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement to strengthen and complement our response, and we will remain here for those who need it most,"* said Luis Manuel Farías Villanueva, President of the Venezuelan Red Cross. *"We are planning a 24-month operation to keep standing with people; needs have been changing, and our response has adjusted to serve more people and to serve them better."*

From the very first minute, local Red Cross teams have been alongside the people affected: first setting up a field hospital, supporting the rescue of survivors and reconnecting families who had lost track of their loved ones; and now, distributing humanitarian aid and strengthening primary health care through an emergency clinic in La Guaira.

The clinic, set up by the IFRC and managed by the Spanish Red Cross, reinforces the Venezuelan Red Cross field hospital. It will operate for four months and is already delivering health and psychosocial services that will benefit close to 30,000 people. One of them is Gabriel Cipriani, who lost close relatives when his building collapsed and lives with a neurological condition that requires constant medication. For him, the Red Cross remaining there is the difference between continuing his treatment and having it interrupted: *"Knowing I can count on a Red Cross doctor made me feel that I am not alone, that there is a hand with me. That gives you security, it gives you confidence."*

In the coming weeks and months, the priority for the IFRC and the VRC will be to sustain that health care and expand access to safe water while laying the foundations for recovery: strengthening epidemiological surveillance to prevent outbreaks, maintaining psychosocial support and treatment for chronic conditions, and beginning to accompany families as they rebuild their livelihoods. Assistance will be adjusted as needs change, with particular attention to those at greatest risk: children, older people, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and people with chronic illnesses or disabilities.

*"This disaster is far from over. Continuing to distribute essential items and safeguarding people's wellbeing and public health is, and will remain, a priority in the medium term — but further ahead it will also mean making sure people recover their livelihoods and their income-generating activities,"* said Loyce Pace, IFRC Regional Director for the Americas\*. "A disaster like this one calls for assistance that is multisectoral, comprehensive and sustained over time. The IFRC is committed to the Venezuelan Red Cross and to the people of Venezuela in making that possible — and that is why we are calling for sustained, flexible funding, able to accompany families throughout their recovery."\*

That funding has a concrete figure. The IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal to raise 50 million Swiss francs to assist 300,000 people over two years. One month on from the disaster, it is 25.19 per cent funded. As people's needs evolve and grow more complex, the resources to meet them should grow at the same pace.

Johannes Chinchilla, +584 222 550278

Susana Arroyo Barrantes, +507 6999-3199

Tommaso Della Longa +41 (0) 79 708 4367 | Scott Craig +41 (0) 79 76 370 3575

reports.title: Venezuela: One month after the earthquakes, humanitarian funding falls far short
reports.body_text:
*One month after the devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela, thousands of people are still living in temporary shelters while trying to rebuild their lives. International attention and financial support must be stepped up, without forgetting those who already needed humanitarian assistance, said the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)*.


[Venezuela](https://reliefweb.int/themes?categoryId=118) Published 23. Jul 2026

Up to 1.3 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance in the areas affected by the earthquakes, over 700,000 more people than before the earthquakes struck. The Humanitarian Response Plan has been revised to include the earthquake response, increasing requirements by nearly 50 per cent. The amended plan aims to support 6.2 million people over an initial six-month response period. Yet the plan is currently only 39 per cent funded.

"The first month after a disaster often brings global solidarity and attention. The real test now is whether that support continues after the headlines start to fade," said Elena Vicario, NRC’s country director in Venezuela. "Families who lost homes, livelihoods and access to essential services cannot rebuild their lives on short-lived commitments."

Prior to the earthquakes, over one quarter of the population was in need of humanitarian assistance and humanitarian organisations were already responding to significant needs, including protection, education, health, water and sanitation, and livelihoods across the country. The revised response plan integrates these existing priorities with emergency earthquake assistance within a single framework.

"We welcome the rapid mobilisation of resources following the earthquakes, but this funding must complement, not replace, support for existing humanitarian needs. Donors should ensure funding is sustained, reaches all sectors, and strengthens the capacities that already exist in Venezuela. Local communities, organisations, and long-standing humanitarian actors have the knowledge and access needed to reach affected populations, and new support should reinforce their work,” said Vicario.

After the earthquakes, nearly 24,000 children have had their education disrupted, further increasing the number of children in need of education support. So far, the education sector is only under 5 per cent funded, after years of underfunding from the international community, which has left education needs consistently unmet.

“For children living in temporary shelters, the emergency is far from over,” said Liliana Largo, NRC’s education programme development manager. “The routines that once provided stability and protection have been disrupted, and emotions such as fear emerge, affecting their ability to concentrate and learn. Temporary learning spaces and psychosocial support are critical in helping children rebuild a sense of normality and wellbeing, and must be treated as a core part of the emergency response."

NRC’s emergency response has evolved significantly over the past month. The organisation began by assessing needs in 16 temporary shelters. During the first month, NRC assisted more than 2,400 displaced people, distributing hygiene kits and other essential items to affected families, while also providing psychosocial support sessions for children, and legal counselling for people who have lost civil documentation and property ownership records.

"One month on, people affected by the earthquakes are still living with uncertainty every day. The humanitarian community now faces a choice: sustain the response and help communities recover or allow funding shortfalls to turn this disaster into a longer-term crisis. The world must not look away," said Vicario.

**Notes to editors**

- Photos and videos from Venezuela are available for use [here](https://visuals.nrc.no/?c=15116&k=5b02ed739f).
- Within two weeks of the earthquakes, the [2026 Humanitarian Response Plan](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes) (HRP) was amended to incorporate earthquake-related needs.
- The revised HRP seeks to reach 6.2 million people, including 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes)).
- Before the earthquakes, 596,000 people living in the municipalities affected by the earthquakes were included in the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan. 751,000 additional people were included in the plan to address humanitarian needs caused by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/terremotos-venezuela-adenda-al-plan-de-respuesta-humanitaria-2026-enes)).
- Total funding requirements increased from 632 million US Dollars to 931.3 million US dollars, including 298 million US Dollars for earthquake response activities ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), Financial Tracking Service).
- As of 22 July, the Humanitarian Response Plan for Venezuela is 39.2 per cent funded, with 365.1 million US dollars received against requirements of 931.3 million US dollars ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), Financial Tracking Service).
- The education sector accounts for approximately 10.2 per cent of the total humanitarian appeal (94.5 million US dollars), yet as of 22 July it has received only 1.1 per cent of total funding reported, leaving the sector just 4.7 per cent funded and facing a funding gap of more than 90 million US dollars ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/countries/242/summary/2026), [Financial Tracking Service](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1517/summary)).
- In 2025 the education sector was 20.3 per cent funded, while in 2024 it was 7.7 per cent funded ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1277/summary)).
- The school year in Venezuela ends in July. Educational authorities have begun working on reorganising the academic calendar, and we welcome these efforts.
- NRC will continue to support the efforts of the authorities and the wider humanitarian response, in line with the principles of neutrality and impartiality.
- In the Capital District alone, 432 schools – around a third of all schools – have been affected by the earthquakes ([UNICEF](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/unicef-venezuela-humanitarian-situation-report-no3-earthquake-02-july-2026)).
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), 34 schools are currently serving as temporary shelters.
- According to [Education Cannot Wait](https://www.educationcannotwait.org/news-stories/press-releases/education-cannot-wait-launches-emergency-response-help-children-return), learning has been disrupted for nearly 24,000 students.
- Since 8 July, NRC has reached more than 200 children aged 5 to 16 with educational activities. The response is ongoing, and NRC hopes to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where 600 children can receive educational kits and psychosocial support.
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005, providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four border states (Bolívar, Zulia, Apure and Táchira). NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela and seven local partners. NRC’s teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, with a plan to provide water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

  • Since 8 July, NRC has reached more than 200 children aged 5 to 16 with educational activities. The response is ongoing, and NRC hopes to set up 10 temporary learning spaces where 600 children can receive educational kits and psychosocial support.
  • NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005, providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four border states (Bolívar, Zulia, Apure and Táchira). NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela and seven local partners. NRC’s teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, with a plan to provide water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.

**Situation Report No. 29**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**22 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,463 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,398 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**22 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.463 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.398 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.
