reports.title: Venezuela Earthquakes: Pregnant Women and New Mothers Face Growing Health Risks as about 130 Babies Born Every Day
reports.body_text:
**CARACAS, 23 July 2026 –** Thousands of pregnant women and new mothers require access to healthcare, nutritious food and safe shelter one month after two devastating earthquakes damaged health facilities and displaced [about 21,000 people ](https://news.un.org/es/story/2026/07/1541700https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-17-july-2026)in Venezuela, Save the Children said.

 T[he UN estimates ](https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-26-june-6-july-2026)there are 36,700 pregnant women who have been affected by the earthquakes, 4,000 of whom are expected to give birth in the next month, equivalent to about 130 babies born every day.\[1\]

 The twin earthquakes, of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5, struck on 24 June, destroying and damaging dozens of health facilities and disrupting essential maternal and child healthcare services. Women have told Save the Children staff that some obstetricians and paediatricians were among the over 5,000 people killed in the disaster, leaving families uncertain where to seek care for themselves and their children.

 In La Guaira, which was hardest hit, the main maternity hospital remains closed and, while basic care is available, complicated cases must be referred to Caracas.

 Many pregnant women, caregivers, and their children who lost their homes are now living in temporary shelters where access to antenatal care, nutritious food, and clean water and sanitation is limited. At the same time, many are coping with the traumatic loss of loved ones.

 Research shows that high levels of stress and anxiety during pregnancy may affect a baby's brain development and immune system, increasing the risk of preterm birth or even miscarriage. Babies [exposed to elevated maternal stress](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/infa.12499) during pregnancy may also show more fear, sadness and distress at three months of age than those born to mothers who experienced less stress. Limited access to nutritious food, uncontrolled infant formula donations, and reduced antenatal care during pregnancy also heightens the risk of malnutrition in infants and increases the risk of preterm birth and low birth weight.

 **Yohana, \* 23,** who is pregnant with her first child and relies on glasses to see, was alone at home in one of the hardest-hit parts of La Guaira when the earthquake hit, causing her building to collapse. She managed to escape by breaking a window, although she could not get her glasses until later, adding to her panic.

 *“I went out barefoot, just wearing my house clothes,”* said Yohana\*. *“I lost my glasses...I couldn't see, or at least I could see less.”*

 *“When the whole house collapsed, I was scared. At that moment, I didn’t feel that I had hurt \[my stomach\], but with all the chaos, I wasn’t sure if I’d gotten hurt or not. But honestly, all I was thinking about was getting out alive.”*

 **Yohana\*** received a healthcare checkup at a mobile clinic run by Save the Children partner, Paluz in La Guaira.

 Meanwhile, newborn babies and infants living in sodden tents are falling sick from damp conditions or are at risk of mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue during the country’s rainy season. Some mothers living in temporary shelters say that along with feeling stressed and anxious, being able to buy nappies and other essential supplies for their babies is challenging.

 **Yennifer\*, 23,** who is breastfeeding her four-month-old baby, **Carmen\*,** struggled to take care of her own health after the earthquake. Carmen’s\* paediatrician was also killed in the earthquake.

 *“I couldn’t eat and I had a lot of headaches. I couldn't sleep because it felt like I was shaking. It was difficult for me, and any movement put me on alert and I felt very uneasy.”*

 *“Since \[Carmen’s\*\] paediatrician passed away, that's a big worry, because now how am I going to find someone to treat her because there's no money either,”* Yennifer\* said.

 *“Everything feels overwhelming and I can’t rest”.*

 **Fatima Andraca, Save the Children’s Country Director in Venezuela said:**

 *“Every day about 130 babies are born to mothers in Venezuela whose lives have been turned upside down by the earthquake and who are dealing with huge amounts of stress. Many are bringing their newborns into a world of uncertainty, displacement and disrupted healthcare services.*

 *“We’re hearing worrying reports of young babies becoming sick in camps where families are sleeping on damp mattresses exposed to rain and poor sanitation. At the same time, women are grieving loved ones, coping with trauma and worrying about where they can access healthcare after losing trusted obstetricians and paediatricians.*

 *"Pregnancy and caring for a newborn can be challenging under any circumstances. No mother should have to navigate those challenges while living in a tent, mourning losses and worrying about whether her child can access the healthcare they need.”*

 Save the Children said it is imperative that pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding women, and their children, are prioritised in the humanitarian response and recovery in Venezuela through urgent coordination, adequate funding, and targeted actions.

Save the Children is calling on international governments, donors and humanitarian partners to ensure that pregnant and breastfeeding women affected by the earthquake have continuous access to quality antenatal, delivery and postnatal care, skilled infant and young child feeding support, nutritious food, safe shelter, clean water and sanitation, and essential newborn supplies, both now and in the months ahead.

 Save the Children is on the ground in Venezuela, working with authorities and local partners providing primary healthcare through mobile clinics, distributing hygiene kits, clean water and essential supplies. Save the Children is also supporting parents and caregivers to access services for small and nutritionally at-risk babies under six months to help them survive and thrive, including nutrition assessments for babies, and breastfeeding counselling and mental health support for caregivers. The organisation is also exploring potential support to maternal and paediatric services in coordination with national health authorities.

 Save the Children has been working in Venezuela since 2019. Since the humanitarian crisis started to rapidly deteriorate a few years ago, Save the Children has been scaling up its response through local partners to support the increasing number of children in need. Save the Children is delivering health, nutrition, education, child protection, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene and food security and livelihoods support.

*Ends*

 \*Names changed for anonymity

 We have multimedia content available here:

 Interviews - [www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPNE94A](https://www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPNE94A)

 Photos & B-ROLL -www.contenthubsavethechildren.org/Package/2O4C2SPAIDCE

 **Notes to editors**

 \[1\] UNFPA estimated that 4,000 women will give birth in the next month, as of its 8 July 2026 update. [ https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-24-26-june-2026](https://www.unfpa.org/resources/flash-update-earthquakes-venezuela-24-26-june-2026) . This is just over 130 births a day.

**For more information**

Aisha Majid, Data Media Manager (in Madrid), Aisha.majid@savethechildren.org

Out of hours (BST) contact, media@savethechildren.org.uk

reports.body_text:
**A. SITUATION ANALYSIS**  
**Description of the crisis**

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 1,000 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira, a popular destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes.

As of 15 July, 4,829 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing1. It is expected for these figures to continue to rise in coming days as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors moves towards a focus on recovery, identification and return to family members of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG)2. International search and rescue deployments are progressively concluding, with several Movement teams having completed their missions. A response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, shelter provision and efforts to bridge emergency relief to recovery and reconstruction efforts continues under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.3 A comprehensive technical evaluation of structures is underway by respective authorities to identify homes that can be repaired and those that are too dangerous to return to. Evaluation of safe areas to build permanent housing for those affected is also taking place. Damage to residences, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure also disrupted the functioning of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems, as well as public transportation and airport operations. Damaged roads and bridges have also restricted access and affected movement to and within some affected areas. The healthcare capacity has been particularly affected, with limited supply of water systems. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been repurposed as temporary shelters until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. Damage to water systems has further affected the availability of basic services.

Moreover, it is important to note that the main affected area, La Guaira, fulfils multiple critical functions for the country. Its proximity to the Capital, Caracas, the presence of the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, makes it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected.

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations.

Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement. The exact death toll remains uncertain; however, the United States Geological Survey estimated that between 15,000 and 30,000 people were killed. The current earthquake has therefore affected communities with lived and intergenerational memories of one of Venezuela’s most severe disasters.

Damage to water systems has further affected the availability of basic services.

Moreover, it is important to note that the main affected area, La Guaira, fulfils multiple critical functions for the country. Its proximity to the Capital, Caracas, the presence of the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, makes it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people and logistical capacity affected.

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with thousands of injured, many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, and with families displaced after the destruction or severe damage of their homes. Beyond these physical impacts, the earthquakes have also had significant effects on the mental health and psychosocial well-being of affected people. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, uncertainty regarding housing and recovery, and exposure to damaged environments and recovery operations has contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected populations.

Notably, La Guaira’s geographical location is prone to various types of emergencies. In December 1999, torrential rainfall triggered catastrophic landslides, flash floods and debris flows across the then State of Vargas—now La Guaira—causing widespread destruction and displacement. The exact death toll remains uncertain; however, the United States Geological Survey estimated that between 15,000 and 30,000 people were killed. The current earthquake has therefore affected communities with lived and intergenerational memories of one of Venezuela’s most severe disasters.

reports.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #15 (20 to 21 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
The fifteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 20 to 21 July.

## Highlights

Between 20 and 21 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management.

To date, IOM has reached **8,542 unique individuals through 15,460 instances of assistance and services**, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, protection, health and WASH.

IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed **3,055 kitchen sets, 2,590 tarpaulins, 2,039 buckets, 1,676 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits** to affected households.

## IOM activities

IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM maintained essential services for 316 families and supported registration activities. Coordination and registration continued at César Nieves and Playa Grande, while preparations were finalized at Tanaguarena Golf Course for the installation of additional infrastructure.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water storage and hygiene items. To date, **1,552 collapsible water containers, 1,009 hygiene kits and 92 semi-collapsible water containers** have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano have provided **5,552 medical consultations**, including general and specialized care, medication distribution and psychological support. Mobile health and MHPSS services remained operational at José María Vargas and César Nieves.

IOM continued household registration and population data updates across five camps and conducted a mobility intentions survey in José María Vargas, César Nieves and Playa Grande to identify needs, displacement patterns and intentions to return or relocate.

In protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support and referrals to specialized services, with **130 people assisted and supported to date**.

## IOM planned response

IOM will continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC, assistance distributions and infrastructure improvements, while strengthening WASH, health, mental health and protection services.

It will also strengthen camp and mobility monitoring, multisectoral assessments inside and outside the sites, and coordination with authorities and partners.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #15 (20 al 21 de julio 2026)
reports.body_text:
El decimoquinto Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 20 al 21 de julio.

## Aspectos destacados

Entre el 20 y el 21 de julio, la OIM continuó su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas mediante intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, salud, protección, WASH y gestión de información.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 8.542 personas únicas mediante 15.460 asistencias y servicios, principalmente en alojamiento y coordinación de campamentos transitorios, protección, salud y WASH.

La OIM y su socio Fundación Vivienda Popular han distribuido 3.055 sets de cocina, 2.590 lonas, 2.039 baldes, 1.676 lámparas solares y 819 kits de refugio a hogares afectados.

## Actividades de la OIM

La OIM continuó gestionando y coordinando cinco campamentos transitorios en La Guaira y avanzó la transición operativa de tres de ellos al Consejo Noruego para los Refugiados (NRC).

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, mantuvo servicios esenciales para 316 familias y apoyó actividades de registro. En César Nieves y Playa Grande continuaron la coordinación y los registros, mientras que en el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena finalizaron los preparativos para instalar infraestructura adicional.

En WASH, continuó ampliando el acceso a artículos para almacenamiento seguro de agua e higiene. A la fecha, se han distribuido 1.552 bidones plegables, 1.009 kits de higiene y 92 bidones semiplegables.

La OIM y su socio Ven Da Tu Mano han realizado 5.552 atenciones médicas, incluidas consultas generales y especializadas, entrega de medicamentos y apoyo psicológico. Los servicios móviles de salud y SMAPS continuaron operativos en José María Vargas y César Nieves.

La OIM mantuvo el registro y actualización de información poblacional en cinco campamentos y realizó una encuesta sobre intenciones de movilidad en José María Vargas, César Nieves y Playa Grande para identificar necesidades, patrones de desplazamiento e intenciones de retorno o reubicación.

En protección, continuó brindando orientación, asistencia legal, apoyo en documentación y derivaciones a servicios especializados, con 130 personas atendidas y acompañadas a la fecha.

## Respuesta planificada de la OIM

La OIM continuará la transición operativa de tres campamentos a NRC, las distribuciones y mejoras de infraestructura, y reforzará los servicios de WASH, salud y salud mental y protección.

Asimismo, fortalecerá el monitoreo de los campamentos y de la movilidad, las evaluaciones multisectoriales dentro y fuera de los sitios y la coordinación con autoridades y socios.

reports.title: Venezuela - Meeting Minutes, Earthquake Response, Caracas, July 20, 2026
Comité de Emergencia Español: un mes después de los terremotos en Venezuela la ayuda es más necesaria que nunca
reports.body_text:
El Comité de Emergencia Español reitera el llamamiento para mantener la ayuda a las decenas de miles de personas afectadas por los terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela hace un mes. El desafío sigue siendo incalculable tras los seísmos que dejaron más de 5.069 muertos y más de 16.740 personas heridas, además de miles de familias afectadas y comunidades con daños severos. Los esfuerzos se centran ahora en que la población pueda retomar la vida cotidiana con seguridad: volver a entornos habitables, recuperar servicios básicos, reabrir espacios comunitarios y educativos y reducir la exposición a riesgos que amenazan la salud de miles de familias.

**La situación es crítica ya que las necesidades humanitarias son enormes.**

El trabajo de las **8 ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español** que están respondiendo a esta emergencia, **Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision,** continúa y se centra en estos momentos en la atención a la población en situación más vulnerable, incluídos niños, y niñas, proporcionando alimentos, agua y asistencia económica, protección y refugio, atención médica y psicosocial, prevención de brotes epidémicos y apoyo educativo para la infancia, principalmente.

“Un mes después de los terremotos el reto al que se enfrentan las ONG internacionales especialistas en ayuda humanitaria del Comité de Emergencia es que las familias puedan volver a una rutina segura sin que la emergencia se transforme en una crisis sanitaria. Evitar enfermedades y acompañar la recuperación física y emocional es ahora determinante”, **señala la directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira.**

**Llamamiento a mantener la solidaridad**

El **Comité de Emergencia Español, activado el 25 de junio**, canaliza la solidaridad de la sociedad española para apoyar la respuesta de las organizaciones en coordinación con entidades locales y socios sobre el terreno, especialmente en las zonas más afectadas, con La Guaira entre los estados con mayor impacto, y con efectos directos e indirectos en varios territorios del país.

“Ahora empieza el trabajo más largo: evitar una crisis sanitaria, sostener la atención médica y ayudar a las familias a recuperar su vida. La solidaridad de ciudadanos y empresas españolas ha sido enorme, pero debe mantenerse para que el pueblo venezolano pueda poco a poco recuperar una cierta normalidad. También para sanar en la manera de lo posible el trauma social de la terrible pérdida de miles de personas”, **agrega Sara Barbeira.**

**Retomar la vida cotidiana: una prioridad humanitaria**

Un mes después de los terremotos, las necesidades evolucionan y se vuelve clave impulsar una recuperación temprana que permita unas condiciones de vida digna y reducir riesgos secundarios. Para ello una de las prioridades de las ONG es garantizar **agua limpia, saneamiento e higiene** para prevenir enfermedades asociadas a la falta de letrinas, la contaminación del agua y la gestión deficiente de residuos.

Las ONG que forman parte del Comité de Emergencia están centradas en apoyar soluciones de alojamiento temporal y mejoras en refugios, así como en reforzar la **atención sanitaria** y el acceso a medicamentos esenciales, priorizando la atención primaria. También la atención psicosocial, especialmente para niños, niñas y familias que han sufrido pérdidas, desplazamiento o exposición a situaciones traumáticas, es fundamental. La **salud mental** de las personas afectadas es una de las grandes prioridades en esta fase.

La protección de los **grupos poblaciones más vulnerables** es una de las claves de esta respuesta, protegiendo frente a violaciones de sus derechos y promoviendo entornos más seguros. El foco se mantiene en quienes corren mayor riesgo tras el desastre, especialmente las niñas, adolescentes y mujeres, que se encuentran más expuestas a la violencia, la explotación y la interrupción de sus servicios de salud.

La respuesta también incluye la puesta en marcha de **Espacios Seguros para la Infancia** para que los niños y niñas tengan un entorno seguro donde retomar rutinas que favorezcan su bienestar emocional, y de espacios temporales de aprendizaje para que puedan continuar con su educación y recuperar la normalidad.

La recuperación también requerirá ampliar la cobertura hacia **comunidades receptoras** y estados que están recibiendo población desplazada, donde las vulnerabilidades preexistentes y la presión sobre los servicios básicos podrían agravar las necesidades humanitarias.

reports.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #4: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 22 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
reports.body_text:
As of 22 July, AMDA’s relief team has been working to provide aid to those affected by the earthquakes that devastated Venezuela on 24 June.

AMDA has been based in Caraballeda, La Guaira, one of the hardest-hit locations since the start of the quake response efforts. The below is the summary of its activities between 14-19 July:

■14 July

AMDA’s second relief team (comprising a Venezuelan physician and a nurse based in Peru) arrived in Venezuela on 14 July to join the ongoing quake response in Caraballeda.

Since the following day, the team began providing medical care at a temporary clinic in cooperation with local healthcare professionals and volunteers. Because the clinic was run by volunteers, AMDA’s medical team played a vital role in maintaining the clinic's services, as staff allocation of volunteers changed from day to day.

The AMDA team worked from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. each day and provided medical consultations to approximately 50 to 100 patients daily.

■18 July

On 18 July, one Japanese nurse arrived at Valencia Airport in Venezuela to join the advance team. The nurse was dispatched to respond to the ongoing humanitarian needs even though more than three weeks had passed since the earthquake struck.

Upon arrival, the nurse traveled approximately two hours by car to Caracas, the capital, to meet local partners for further coordination of aid work scheduled to begin the following day.

Meanwhile, the AMDA team on the ground continued providing medical assistance at the temporary clinic in La Guaira.

■19 July

On 19 July, AMDA’s aid workers took part in events to celebrate Children's Day in Venezuela, all of which were held in La Guaira.

At an event organized by the Blue Cross of Santa María University, medical assistance was provided alongside a play area for children. AMDA’s Japanese nurse supported the event by providing basic medical services, including blood pressure checks.

AMDA also joined another community event, "Lluvia de Sonrisas" (Rain of Smiles), organized by local medical professionals. In addition to medical consultations in internal medicine, pediatrics and other specialties, the event featured the distribution of relief supplies, games for children, and street performances, which attracted many children and their families.

AMDA distributed snacks, drinks and toys, while the aforementioned nurse worked together with a local psychologist to hold a colouring activity for children. (The colouring books used in it were donated by the Ohara Art Foundation in Japan, with which AMDA has concluded a comprehensive partnership agreement.)

Through these events, AMDA was able to provide not only medical support but also moments of joy and comfort for children and families facing difficult circumstances.

All this while, on the same day, AMDA’s second medical team (comprising a Venezuelan doctor and a nurse based in Peru) continued providing medical care at the temporary clinic.

The relief work will continue for the time being.

reports.title: Los terremotos en Venezuela dejan una huella invisible en la salud de la niñez
reports.body_text:
A casi un mes de los terremotos que sacudieron a Venezuela el 24 de junio, la organización humanitaria y de desarrollo Plan International advierte que la salud física y mental de niñas, niños y adolescentes se ve cada vez más afectada por las condiciones en las zonas más golpeadas por el desastre. Las condiciones inadecuadas de vivienda, la acumulación de escombros y cambio en los arreglos de cuidado están profundizando el impacto emocional del desastre en la niñez y sus familias.

Según el reporte de la agencia de Naciones Unidas responsable de coordinar la respuesta humanitaria ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-26-19-july-2026-time-0900-pm)), 107 campamentos transitorios albergan actualmente a más de 23.800 personas, cerca del 86% de su capacidad total, mientras que más de 17.900 personas continúan sin vivienda. Al 19 de julio, las cifras oficiales reportaban 5.208 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.

Las organizaciones socias de Plan International que responden en el terreno reportan que las molestias físicas sin causa clara aparecen cada vez con más frecuencia, junto con señales de estrés postraumático y una sensación constante de inseguridad, y que, al escuchar con más atención, revelan semanas de sueño interrumpido, sobresaltos y miedo acumulado.

“Cuando hace brisa yo me meto para el cuarto y me escondo y me asusto”, cuenta Victoria, de nueve años, en La Guaira. Naomi, de solo cinco años, describe cómo las pesadillas recurrentes le interrumpen el sueño: “Yo estaba en la playa y un tsunami me estaba persiguiendo”.

Michelle, madre de tres niñas de 25 años, resume lo que ve cada día: “Están asustadas, tienen miedo. La niñez ahorita necesita apoyo psicológico que les ayude”.

Yesica Serrano, asesora regional de Protección de la Niñez en Acción Humanitaria de Plan International, se encuentra actualmente en Venezuela y advierte que esta fase de la emergencia exige tanta atención como la primera.

“Cuando pasa el impacto inmediato del terremoto, el efecto no desaparece: se queda con niñas, niños y adolescentes, tanto en el cuerpo como en la mente. Un dolor de cabeza, un dolor de estómago, dificultad para dormir o miedo a los ruidos fuertes pueden ser señales de angustia que la niñez no logra expresar con palabras. En esta etapa de la emergencia, la salud mental de la niñez ya no puede tratarse como una respuesta secundaria. Si no atendemos el bienestar físico y emocional en conjunto, la recuperación será imposible”, afirmó Serrano.

Ella agrega que este impacto no se ve igual en todas las edades.

“Niñas, niños y adolescentes de distintas edades y etapas de desarrollo no siempre tienen las palabras o los medios para explicar lo que sienten, y no siempre lo demuestran de la misma manera. Las niñas y los niños más pequeños pueden dejar de comer, tener dificultad para dormir, presentar episodios de llanto sin razón aparente o sobresaltarse con facilidad, mientras que las y los adolescentes son más propensos a aislarse, a estar más callados, a mostrarse más agresivos o a alejarse de quienes los rodean. Estar conscientes de estas señales y actuar sobre ellas, junto con la atención médica, es tan urgente como reconstruir un techo”.

Niñas, niños y adolescentes continúan siendo agrupados en una sola categoría en la recolección de datos y las evaluaciones de necesidades, aun cuando enfrentan las crisis de manera distinta y se exponen a riesgos y desafíos diferentes. Plan International advierte que esta distinción todavía necesita reflejarse mejor en la respuesta humanitaria.

Junto con sus socios en territorio, Plan International brinda apoyo psicosocial grupal e individual a niñas, niños y adolescentes, ayuda a las familias a cubrir necesidades urgentes que salvan vidas, y fortalece los servicios de protección de la niñez, con especial atención a las niñas. Esto incluye espacios seguros donde la niñez puede comenzar a procesar lo que ha vivido, así como rutas de derivación hacia servicios especializados de salud mental.

A medida que la respuesta a los terremotos en Venezuela entra en una nueva fase, Plan International reconoce que existe ahora una oportunidad para integrar de forma más cercana el apoyo en salud física y mental en los campamentos de personas desplazadas y las comunidades afectadas. La organización también insta a actores humanitarios y a donantes a recopilar y utilizar datos que distingan entre niñas, niños, adolescentes y personas adultas, para ayudar a que el apoyo se ajuste a sus diferentes necesidades y llegue a quienes están en mayor riesgo.

Plan International Americas

Tel: +503 7885 9315

Email: rodrigo.morales@plan-international.org

*Plan International es una organización independiente humanitaria y de desarrollo que promueve los derechos de la niñez y la igualdad para las niñas. *En colaboración con niñas, niños, jóvenes, seguidores y socios, luchamos por un mundo justo, abordando las causas profundas de los problemas a los que se enfrentan las niñas y los niños en situación más vulnerable. Apoyamos a la niñez desde su nacimiento hasta la edad adulta y los capacitamos para prepararse y responder a las crisis y a la adversidad. Impulsamos el cambio de prácticas y políticas a nivel local, nacional y global gracias a nuestro alcance, experiencia y conocimientos.*

*Durante más de 85 años, hemos reunido a otros optimistas determinados para transformar la vida de todas las niñas y niños en más de 80 países.*

*No nos detendremos, hasta lograr la igualdad.*

reports.title: Venezuela's earthquakes take a hidden toll on children's health
reports.body_text:
Almost one month after the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, the development and humanitarian organisation, Plan International, warns that the physical and mental health of children and adolescents is increasingly affected by conditions in the areas hardest hit by the disaster. Inadequate housing conditions, accumulation of debris, and insufficient care arrangements are deepening the emotional impact of the disaster on children and their families.

According to the report from the UN agency responsible for coordinating humanitarian response ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-26-19-july-2026-time-0900-pm)), 107 transitional camps are currently sheltering more than 23.800 people, close to 86% of their total capacity, while more than 17,900 people remain without housing. As of 19 July, official figures reported 5.208 deaths and 16,740 people injured.

Plan International local partners responding on the ground report that physical complaints with no clear cause are appearing more and more, alongside signs of post-traumatic stress and a constant sense of insecurity, and on closer listening, they reveal weeks of disrupted sleep, jumpiness and accumulated fear.

"When it gets windy I run into my room and hide, and I get scared," says nine year old Victoria in La Guaira. Naomi, who is only five, describes how recurring nightmares are disrupting her sleep: "I was on the beach and a tsunami was chasing me."

Michelle, a 25-year-old mother of three girls, sums up what she sees every day: "They're scared, they're frightened. Right now, the children need psychological support to help them."

Yesica Serrano, Regional Child Protection in Humanitarian Action Adviser at Plan International, is currently in Venezuela and warns that this phase of the emergency demands as much attention as the first.

"Once the immediate shock of the earthquake has passed, the impact does not disappear – it stays with the children and adolescents both in body and mind. A headache, a stomach ache, difficulty sleeping or fear of loud noises can be signs of distress that children are unable to put into words. At this stage of the emergency, children's mental health can no longer be treated as a secondary response. If we don't address both the physical and emotional wellbeing together recovery will be impossible," Serrano said.

She adds that this toll doesn't look the same across ages.

"Children across different ages and development stages don't always have the words or means to explain what they're feeling, and they don't always show it the same way. Younger children may stop eating, struggle to sleep, have occasional crying spells with no apparent reason or startle easily, while adolescents are more likely to withdraw, grow quiet, be more aggressive or pull away from those around them. Being consciously aware of those signals and acting on them, alongside medical care, is just as urgent as rebuilding a roof."

Children and adolescents continue to be grouped into a single category in data collection and needs assessments, even though they experience crises differently and face distinct risks and challenges. Plan International warns that this distinction still needs to be better reflected in the humanitarian response.

With partners on the ground, the organisation is providing group and individual psychosocial support to children and adolescents, helping families meet urgent and lifesaving needs, and strengthening child protection services, with particular attention to girls. This includes safe spaces where children can begin to process what they have experienced, as well as referral pathways to specialised mental health support.

As the earthquake response in Venezuela enters a new phase, Plan International recognises there is now an opportunity for physical and mental health support to be more closely integrated across the displacement camps and affected communities. It also urges humanitarian actors and donors to collect and use data that distinguishes between children, adolescents and adults, helping ensure support is tailored to their different needs and reaches those most at risk.

**ENDS**

**For further information please contact:**

Rodrigo Morales, Regional Communication Officer for Public Relations

Plan International Americas

Tel: +503 7885 9315

Email: rodrigo.morales@plan-international.org

**About Plan International**

Plan International is an independent development and humanitarian organisation that advances children’s rights and equality for girls. We believe in the power and potential of every child but know this is often suppressed by poverty, violence, exclusion, and discrimination. And it is girls who are most affected.

Working together with children, young people, supporters, and partners, we strive for a just world, tackling the root causes of the challenges girls and vulnerable children face. We support children’s rights from birth until they reach adulthood, and we enable children to prepare for and respond to crises and adversity. We drive changes in practice and policy at local, national, and global levels using our reach, experience, and knowledge.

For over 85 years, we have rallied other determined optimists to transform the lives of all children in more than 80 countries.

We won’t stop until we are all equal.

reports.title: Venezuela Emergency Response, Situation Report #4 (9 – 20 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
**OPERATIONAL CONTEXT**

Nearly one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response in Venezuela is rapidly transitioning from the immediate emergency phase to a more structured, large-scale operation. Indeed, humanitarian needs remain immense: over 23,000 people live in transitional camps, thousands more remain displaced in host communities or informal settlements, and damaged housing and basic infrastructure continue to limit access to safe shelter, water, sanitation, healthcare and livelihoods.ii

As aftershocks continue – over 1,300 registered up until now – the humanitarian response continues to expand in scale and complexity. Humanitarian actors are now planning assistance for 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the coming six months, yet significant humanitarian gaps remain, as many communities remain underserved. This requires humanitarian actors that can rapidly identify unmet needs, coordinate effectively with existing response structures and deliver assistance where it is needed most.

Against this backdrop, CESVI has paired rapid operational deployment with early engagement in humanitarian coordination mechanisms, ensuring that field evidence collected from the first days of the emergency directly informed operational planning, strengthened partnerships and supported the targeting of communities that remained outside the initial humanitarian response.

reports.title: One month after earthquakes, Venezuela risks spiraling into deeper crisis without urgent investment in economic recovery
reports.body_text:
Caracas, Venezuela, July 22, 2026 — Nearly one month after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela on June 24, the window is closing to set the country on a sustainable path toward recovery. Without immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support, the disaster risks spiraling into a deeper humanitarian crisis, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns.

Venezuela was already experiencing protracted economic instability long before the ground began to shake, with [over half of the population living in extreme poverty](https://civil-protection-humanitarian-aid.ec.europa.eu/where/latin-america-and-caribbean/venezuela_en). Years of economic hardship drove roughly 8 million people, mainly young adults, to leave the country. This has left a critical gap in the workforce that has impacted search and rescue efforts and will continue to constrain capacity as the vital early recovery phase begins.

Now, the economic situation threatens to unravel further. An initial assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure to cost approximately $37 billion. Nearly 8 million people were in humanitarian need in Venezuela before the earthquakes. In just four weeks that number has grown by 1.4 million. As response efforts scale up, access remains complicated by the indefinite closure of the Simón Bolívar International Airport and continuous aftershocks, with over 1,400 since the initial quakes.

*"Beyond the destroyed buildings and people being pulled from the rubble, there is a quieter economic devastation that is becoming more visible by the day. For reconstruction efforts to have any hope of success, we must focus serious attention on restarting local economies, supporting small businesses, and getting schools back up and running,”* \*\*said IRC’s Emergency Response Lead for the Venezuela Earthquakes, Rafael Velasquez Garcia. “\*\**With millions of futures in the balance, the time to act is now. Absolutely nothing will stop local communities from lifting each other up if they're given the resources to do so."*

The IRC urges the international community to scale up humanitarian funding to support Venezuelans impacted by the earthquakes and the millions who were already in urgent need.

The IRC has been working in Venezuela since 2021 to deliver programs across health, nutrition, protection, education, food security, and livelihoods. As soon as the earthquakes hit, the IRC started scaling up its response to support affected communities, designing and launching ten new programs in tandem with eight local partners on the ground. The IRC will continue its support in the months ahead, providing life-saving assistance and essential protection and early recovery programming to help Venezuela rebuild. Over the past month, the IRC has distributed hundreds of hygiene and water purification kits, supported our partners providing first aid and primary care to 300-400 people every day, and helped reactivate the diagnostic laboratory at the Central University of Caracas to track potential disease outbreaks.

**Media contacts**

Sylvan Foley

**sylvan.foley@rescue.org**

IRC Global Communications

**communications@rescue.org**

reports.title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.5 (Earthquake Response), 13-20 July 2026
reports.body_text:
**Highlights**

- More than three weeks after the earthquakes of 24 June, official figures report 5,208 deaths, 16,740 people injured, and 17,907 people left without housing.1 Humanitarian needs remain significant, particularly among displaced families residing in transitional camps and communities with disrupted access to essential services.
- UNICEF continues to scale up multi-sectoral assistance, focusing on health, nutrition, WASH and child protection services for children and families affected by the earthquakes, reaching over 7,519 people in the initial phase of the response. Health services through mobile health teams have reached around 2,108 people, while vaccination campaigns have reached 6,466 people. More than 2,452 children have been screened for acute malnutrition. WASH services are expanding at temporary shelters reaching 7,180 with critical hygiene supplies and 2,861 benefiting from access to safe drinking water. Psychosocial support and recreational activities have reached more than 2,726 children, adolescents and caregivers. Additionally, more than 4,400 people have been reached with hygiene promotion messages and critical information on available life-saving services.
- UNICEF will reach 150,000 people with critical emergency supplies within the coming weeks, including 49,000 with health supplies, 72,000 with micronutrients, and 29,000 with WASH items. An additional 49 tons of emergency supplies arrived on 14 July to replenish in-country emergency stockpiles.
- In addition to the US$137.6 million requested under the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal and aligned with the addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan 2026, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to respond to the humanitarian impact of the earthquakes.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 28**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**21 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks** since the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck on 24 June.
- Official toll: **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of **1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months, an additional appeal of US$299 million was launched**

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1,405 aftershocks.**

Twenty-four days since the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **5,346 people dead and 16,740 injured since the onset** of the emergency. Authorities also indicated that **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on the management of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, continue implementing multisectoral response activities and scaling up assistance. On 10 July, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher **announced a US$299 million addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan to address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.** The addendum complements the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, increasing the target population from 5.5 million to 6.2 million people and raising total funding requirements from US$632 million to US$931 million.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 28**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**21 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas** desde los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 registrados el 24 de junio.
- Balance oficial: **5.346 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias continúan ampliando la respuesta multisectorial a la emergencia. Para  
     atender las necesidades de **1,3 millones de personas afectadas durante los próximos seis meses, se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$299 millones.**

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.405 réplicas.**

A 24 días de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **5.346 personas fallecidas y 16.740 personas heridas desde el inicio de la emergencia**. Asimismo, indican que **17.907 personas perdieron sus viviendas.**

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en la gestión de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El 10 de julio, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, **anunció una adenda al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria por US$299 millones para atender las necesidades multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.** Esta adenda complementa el Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2026, elevando la meta de personas a asistir de 5,5 millones a 6,2 millones y los requerimientos financieros totales de US$632 millones a US$931 millones.

reports.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake - P8E Distribution: Who? What? Where? As of Tue., 21st July (22/07/2026)
PAHO supports delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen routine immunization in Venezuela
reports.body_text:
Caracas, 21 July 2026 (PAHO/WHO) – A shipment of 1.15 million doses of vaccines donated by Brazil arrived in Venezuela on Monday to strengthen the country's routine immunization programme and help protect communities from vaccine-preventable diseases following the devastating earthquakes on the 24 June.

The shipment includes one million doses of the pentavalent vaccine (which protects children against five serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B and *Haemophilus influenzae* type b), 102,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, and 48,000 doses of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine against tuberculosis. The donation also included 20 vials of anti-arachnid antivenom.

Following disasters, the risk of infectious disease outbreaks can increase as health services are disrupted and many families are displaced into temporary shelters. Maintaining high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent outbreaks of diseases such as measles, diphtheria and pertussis, particularly among children and other vulnerable groups.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) supported the operation by procuring cold boxes for transporting the vaccines, electronic data loggers to continuously monitor temperatures and safeguard the cold chain, and providing additional logistical support to ensure the vaccines arrived safely and remained effective.

This shipment builds on ongoing cooperation between Brazil, Venezuela and PAHO to strengthen immunization efforts. Earlier this year, Brazil's Ministry of Health donated 100,000 doses of yellow fever vaccine and 250,000 canine rabies vaccines to Venezuela's Ministry of Health, with PAHO also providing logistical support to maintain the cold chain throughout transport.

The arrival of these vaccines will support national efforts to restore and sustain essential health services while protecting communities from preventable diseases during the emergency response and recovery phase.

reports.title: VENEZUELA Terremotos — Apoyo internacional mediante cooperación bilateral y coordinación civil-militar (Al 16 de julio de 2026)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
## Panorama

**18 países contribuyentes**

La mayor parte de la asistencia internacional desplegada tras los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio de 2026 ha sido proporcionada mediante **cooperación bilateral directa entre Estados**, incluyendo activos militares, transporte aéreo y marítimo, capacidades de ingeniería, apoyo médico y logística.

**18 países** movilizaron capacidades: **2.200+ efectivos**, **35+ aeronaves de transporte**, **6 buques** y **40+ helicópteros**. **13 países** aportaron evaluación técnica y estructural; **10 países**, maquinaria e ingeniería (apuntalamiento, corte, perforación y rescate técnico). El territorio de **Puerto Rico** contribuye dentro del componente de EE.UU.

Los recursos ingresaron principalmente por el **Aeropuerto Internacional Simón Bolívar (Maiquetía)** y el **Puerto de La Guaira**.

### OCHA / UNDAC

Apoya a las **autoridades venezolanas** facilitando el intercambio de información y el direccionamiento para que los efectivos militares internacionales coordinen sus acciones con las autoridades nacionales.

reports.title: WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies - Mid-Year Update | July 2026
reports.body_text:
## **Overview**

In the first half of 2026, the CFE continued to enable WHO to respond rapidly to health emergencies worldwide. WHO released more than US$ 10 million from the CFE to address the health consequences of 12 emergencies, including five disease outbreaks, three complex crises, and four natural disasters.

As a key source of WHO’s flexible, early financing for emergencies, the CFE ensures that life-saving operations can begin immediately, often before other donor funding is mobilized. Twelve Member States and the UN Foundation have pledged or contributed more than US$ 17 million to the CFE so far this year.

The Fund’s balance, however, remains critically low. Continued support is needed to ensure WHO can act first and fast when new health emergencies strike.

reports.title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #06, 19 July 2026
reports.body_text:
Situation Update  
 • Twenty-five days after the twin earthquakes of 24 June, authorities report 5,208 deaths and 16,740 injuries. Following search and rescue operations, national authorities have shifted the efforts toward relocating displaced populations to transitional camps.  
 • According to authorities, 107 transitional camps have been established, with 23,828 people currently accommodated. As part of the UN-coordinated response, WFP is supporting three camps with two hot meals daily.  
 • WFP Acting Executive Director Carl Skau spoke with Venezuela's Acting President, Delcy Rodríguez, and reaffirmed the organization's commitment to continuing its support to authorities and humanitarian partners in meeting immediate food needs and assisting affected families in their recovery.

reports.title: Situation Report No.6: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 17 July 2026
reports.body_text:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

• More than three weeks after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, affecting at least seven states, the emergency response remains active. While the most acute phase of rescue, trauma care and immediate postdisaster surgery has eased, priorities are now focused on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, supporting temporary camps and preventing public health risks.

• Referral hospitals remain operational, though service delivery is still under strain, most notably in La Guaira, where limited bed availability, structural damage, and a high volume of referrals persist. Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) remain integrated into the national response, providing more than 14,000 consultations while strengthening clinical capacity, referral pathways and continuity of care in the affected states.

• Integrated epidemiological surveillance has been strengthened across affected states through expanded reporting, laboratory support, event-based surveillance and vaccination activities. No large-scale outbreaks have been confirmed to date despite ongoing public health risks in transitional camps.

• The rise to 107 transitional camps heightens protection and public health risks, requiring coordinated action on WASH, mental health, GBV mitigation, and outbreak prevention, alongside stronger support for host communities.

• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through the deployment of its Regional Response Team, covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, risk communication and community engagement, and EMT coordination. In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO is also supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with sixteen EMTs now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua, increasing clinical capacity in the affected areas.

• PAHO/WHO has shipped a total of 33.5 metric tons (MT) of critical medical equipment and supplies to support the response in Venezuela. Of this, supplies have already been distributed to 10 health facilities, with an additional distribution to 18 health facilities and 36 shelters planned in the coming days, including Interagency Emergency Health Kits (IEHK) and Trauma and Emergency Surgery Kits (TESK).

reports.body_text:
The thirteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 15 to 16 July.

**Highlights**

Between 15 and 16 July, IOM expanded its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira, with interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and information management.

To date, IOM has reached 7,290 unique individuals through 11,277 instances of assistance and services, mainly in health, shelter and site coordination, WASH and protection.

At the José María Vargas Sports Centre, IOM maintained essential services for 347 families and supported the relocation of 40 households to other sites in Caracas. At Mare Abajo II, the installation of 200 new bunk beds increased total availability to 350.

**IOM Activities**

IOM continues to support transitory camps and affected communities in La Guaira through shelter, site coordination, WASH, health and mental health, protection, registration, mobility monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

At Mare Abajo II, IOM installed 200 bunk beds with mattresses, prepared a module to partition family spaces and continued works on showers, drainage and site preparation. At Tanaguarena Golf Course, it coordinated service delivery and the distribution of supplies.

IOM will continue strengthening the management and improvement of transitory camps, including the installation of toilets, showers, water systems, lighting and internal partitions, as well as health and mental health care, protection screening and referrals, and measures to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse.

It will also continue updating registration records, conducting multisectoral assessments and monitoring mobility, while consolidating information on services, actors and gaps to improve the coordination of interventions.

reports.body_text:
El decimotercer Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre la respuesta de la OIM a los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela, con información correspondiente al período del 15 al 16 de julio.

**Aspectos destacados**

Entre el 15 y el 16 de julio, la OIM amplió su respuesta multisectorial en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas de La Guaira, con intervenciones en alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, salud, protección, agua, saneamiento e higiene, y gestión de información.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado a 7.290 personas únicas mediante 11.277 asistencias y servicios, principalmente en salud, alojamiento y coordinación de sitios, WASH y protección.

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, la OIM mantuvo servicios esenciales para 347 familias y apoyó la reubicación de 40 núcleos familiares hacia otros espacios en Caracas. En Mare Abajo II, la instalación de 200 nuevas literas elevó la disponibilidad total a 350.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continúa apoyando campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas en La Guaira mediante alojamiento, coordinación de sitios, WASH, salud y salud mental, protección, registro, monitoreo de la movilidad y coordinación interagencial.

En Mare Abajo II, la OIM instaló 200 literas con colchones, preparó un módulo para dividir los espacios familiares y continuó las obras de duchas, drenaje y adecuación del terreno. En el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena, coordinó la prestación de servicios y la distribución de insumos.

En el Estadio César Nieves, la OIM apoyó el suministro de agua, la limpieza y mantenimiento de baños, la instalación de duchas, la gestión de residuos y la entrega de insumos de saneamiento. También distribuyó 30.000 litros de agua en Mare Abajo II y comunidades cercanas.

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas se han realizado 16 jornadas móviles de salud y salud mental, con 1.377 atenciones acumuladas. En Playa Grande se efectuaron 108 consultas médicas y se reforzaron los servicios de odontología, medicina interna y apoyo psicológico.

Los registros alcanzaron 536 familias y 1.605 personas en el Estadio César Nieves; 153 familias y 463 personas en Playa Grande; y 20 familias y 65 personas en el Campo de Golf de Tanaguarena. También avanzó el diseño de una encuesta de hogares y el seguimiento del desplazamiento posterior a los terremotos.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará fortaleciendo la gestión y adecuación de campamentos transitorios, la instalación de baños, duchas, sistemas de agua, iluminación y divisiones internas, así como la atención en salud y salud mental, el triaje y las derivaciones de protección, y las medidas de prevención de la explotación y el abuso sexual.

También continuará actualizando los registros, implementando evaluaciones multisectoriales y monitoreando la movilidad, además de consolidar información sobre servicios, actores y brechas para mejorar la coordinación de las intervenciones.

Latinoamérica y El Caribe Resumen de Situación Semanal al 17 de julio 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**CIFRAS CLAVE**

- 4,9K personas fallecidas tras dos fuertes terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela el 24 de junio
- 26,5K personas retornadas forzosamente a Haití en junio de 2026
- 33K personas afectadas por la temporada de lluvias en Guatemala

**VENEZUELA: TERREMOTO**

Las labores de respuesta continúan casi un mes después de los terremotos del 24 de junio que sacudieron el centro-norte de Venezuela. Al 16 de julio, las autoridades informaron de 4.930 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridas y 17.907 personas que quedaron sin hogar. Las autoridades han registrado más de 1.300 réplicas, mientras que las evaluaciones indican que al menos 856 edificios resultaron dañados, incluidos 190 que se derrumbaron. Más de 21.000 personas permanecen en 107 campamentos transitorios. Los socios humanitarios continúan ampliando la asistencia en materia de salud, alimentación, protección, alojamiento y WASH en los estados más afectados, especialmente La Guaira, Miranda y el Distrito Capital. Las evaluaciones continúan identificando necesidades significativas relacionadas con el alojamiento, el acceso a servicios básicos, la seguridad alimentaria y el apoyo psicosocial, ya que muchas personas afectadas siguen sin poder regresar a casa.

[Apoya aquí al Fondo Humanitario Venezolano](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

Para más información, visita: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**MÉXICO: TERREMOTO**

El 17 de julio, aproximadamente a las 8:49 de la mañana (hora local), un terremoto de magnitud 7,4 sacudió la costa de Chiapas, México, a una profundidad de 10 km. El terremoto, cuyo epicentro se ubicó cerca de Ciudad Hidalgo, cerca de la frontera con Guatemala, se sintió ampliamente en partes de México, Guatemala y El Salvador, lo que provocó evacuaciones y la activación de protocolos de emergencia. El Centro de Alerta de Tsunamis de EE. UU. emitió una alerta de tsunami y las autoridades de protección civil aconsejan a las comunidades costeras que se mantengan alertas. Las autoridades mexicanas informaron de al menos 39 réplicas en las horas posteriores al temblor principal, incluyendo una de magnitud 6,5. Las autoridades no han informado de víctimas ni daños graves, aunque las evaluaciones siguen en curso.

**HAITÍ: VIOLENCIA Y DESPLAZAMIENTO**

La violencia sigue impulsando desplazamientos en el departamento de Artibonite de Haití. En Dessaline y Petite Rivière, los ataques que comenzaron el 6 de julio desplazaron a unas 3.225 personas. La mayoría de las familias (93%) buscaron refugio en comunidades anfitrionas, mientras que el resto se refugia en seis sitios de desplazamiento, incluido uno recién establecido. El 12 de julio, la violencia armada en el municipio de Saint-Marc desplazó al menos a 705 personas, todas ellas alojadas con familias de acogida. Los incidentes reflejan el ciclo continuo de desplazamiento que afecta a comunidades en Haití. Al mismo tiempo, el creciente número de personas migrantes retornadas forzosamente está ejerciendo una presión adicional sobre las comunidades de acogida, con más de 26.500 personas retornadas solo en junio y un aumento del 11% en los retornos durante la primera mitad de 2026 en comparación con el mismo período del año pasado.

**GUATEMALA: TEMPORADA DE LLUVIAS**

La temporada de lluvias en Guatemala, que va de mayo a octubre, sigue afectando a comunidades de todo el país. Al 14 de julio, las autoridades informan de 13 personas fallecidas, una desaparecida y más de 33.000 personas afectadas, con más de 900 emergencias relacionadas con las lluvias registradas en todo el país. Las inundaciones, desbordamientos de ríos, deslizamientos de tierra, árboles caídos y tormentas severas han dañado más de 6.400 viviendas, provocado casi 14.000 evacuaciones y obligado a más de 1.000 personas a refugiarse en albergues temporales. Alta Verapaz sigue siendo el departamento más afectado, con el mayor número de incidentes reportados. Mientras la temporada de lluvias sigue aumentando las necesidades humanitarias, las autoridades y socios humanitarios también se están preparando para los impactos previstos de El Niño, incluyendo un mayor riesgo de sequía y pérdidas de cosechas en el Corredor Seco del país.

reports.title: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 17 July 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**KEY FIGURES**

- 4.9K people dead after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June
- 26.5K people forcibly returned to Haiti in June 2026
- 33K people affected by Guatemala’s rainy season

**VENEZUELA: EARTHQUAKE**

Response efforts continue nearly one month after the 24 June earthquakes that struck north-central Venezuela. As of 16 July, authorities reported 4,930 deaths, 16,740 injuries and 17,907 people left homeless. Authorities have recorded more than 1,300 aftershocks, while assessments indicate that at least 856 buildings were damaged, including 190 that collapsed. More than 21,000 people remain in 107 transitional camps. Humanitarian partners continue to scale up health, food, protection, shelter and WASH assistance across the most affected states, particularly La Guaira, Miranda and the Capital District. Assessments continue to identify significant needs related to shelter, access to basic services, food security and psychosocial support as many affected people remain unable to return home.

[Support the Venezuelan Humanitarian Fund here](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

For more information, visit: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**MEXICO: EARTHQUAKE**

On 17 July at approximately 8:49am (local time), a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Chiapas, Mexico, at a depth of 10km. The earthquake, centred near Ciudad Hidalgo close to the Guatemala border, was widely felt across parts of Mexico, Guatemala and El Salvador, prompting evacuations and the activation of emergency protocols. The U.S. Tsunami Warning Center issued a tsunami advisory and civil protection officials advise coastal communities to remain catious. Mexican authorities reported at least 39 aftershocks in the hours following the main tremor, including one measuring magnitude 6.5. Authorities have not reported any casualties or major damage, although assessments remain ongoing.

**HAITI: VIOLENCE & DISPLACEMENT**

Violence continues to drive displacement across Haiti’s Artibonite department. In Dessaline and Petite Rivière, attacks beginning on 6 July displaced an estimated 3,225 people. Most families (93 per cent) sought refuge with host communities, while the remaining are sheltering in six displacement sites, including one newly established site. On 12 July, armed violence in the municipality of Saint-Marc displaced at least 705 people, all of whom found shelter with host families. The incidents reflect the continued cycle of displacement affecting communities across Haiti. At the same time, growing numbers of forcibly returned migrants are placing additional pressure on host communities, with more than 26,500 people returned in June alone and returns during the first half of 2026 up 11 per cent compared with the same period last year.

**GUATEMALA: RAINY SEASON**

Guatemala’s rainy season, which runs from May to October, continues to affect communities across the country. As of 14 July, authorities report 13 deaths, one missing person and more than 33,000 people affected, with over 900 rain-related emergencies registered nationwide. Flooding, river overflows, landslides, fallen trees and severe storms have damaged more than 6,400 homes, prompted nearly 14,000 evacuations and forced over 1,000 people into temporary shelters. Alta Verapaz remains the hardest-hit department, accounting for the highest number of reported incidents. While the ongoing rainy season continues to heighten humanitarian needs, authorities and humanitarian partners are also preparing for the anticipated impacts of El Niño, including an increased risk of drought and crop losses in the country’s Dry Corridor.

reports.title: IOM Appeals for USD 98 Million to Urgently Support Venezuela Earthquake Response
reports.body_text:
**Geneva/Caracas, 17 July 2026** – The International Organization for Migration (IOM) today launched a USD 98 million appeal to support families and communities affected by the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, causing widespread loss of life, displacement and destruction across the country.

The [IOM Venezuela Earthquake Appeal](https://reliefweb.int/node/4220588/) outlines the Organization’s response for 12 months and seeks funding to provide safe and dignified shelter, life-saving assistance, support early recovery efforts, and help affected communities rebuild in the months ahead.

“The people of Venezuela have shown remarkable resilience, but recovery will take time and sustained support,” said Lia Poggio, IOM Chief of Mission in Venezuela. “This appeal will help ensure that families receive the assistance they need including a place to stay while enabling communities to move beyond the emergency, rebuild essential services, and lay the foundations for a safe and lasting recovery.”

The earthquakes and subsequent aftershocks caused extensive damage across several states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua and Falcón. Thousands of families have been displaced, while damage to homes, health facilities, water systems and other critical infrastructure has severely disrupted access to essential services.

Since the onset of the emergency, IOM has worked alongside Venezuelan authorities, United Nations agencies and humanitarian partners to support people affected by the earthquakes. The Organization has been managing collective shelters, providing health and protection assistance, leading site coordination efforts in collective shelters, and helping displaced families access essential services.

Building on its longstanding presence in Venezuela and operational footprint across affected areas, IOM is scaling up its response through an integrated approach that addresses both immediate humanitarian needs and longer-term recovery priorities.

To date, IOM has assisted nearly 6,000 people in collective sites under its coordination and delivered over 10,000 services, including temporary accommodation, health care, and protection assistance.

The appeal focuses on priority areas including shelter and site coordination, early recovery, and health. Together, these interventions aim to provide immediate relief while helping communities recover safely and with dignity.

IOM’s response will prioritize safety, dignity, accountability and inclusion, ensuring that affected people are at the centre of decision-making and recovery efforts. Working closely with government authorities, local communities, and humanitarian partners, the Organization will support a coordinated, needs-based response that reaches both heavily affected and underserved areas.

The appeal reflects IOM’s broader commitment to supporting people affected by crises and displacement through locally-led, people-centred, and sustainable solutions.
