reports.title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #15 (08 July 2026, Time: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Situation Report No. 15**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**08 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,100 aftershocks.**
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
- Official toll: **3,811 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations' humanitarian chief, called on Member States and donors to turn solidarity into tangible support.**
- An additional appeal for US$296 million was launched to scale up the earthquake response and address the multisectoral needs of 1.3 million people over the next six months.
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**  
 Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1, 102 aftershocks.**

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,811 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher announced an additional US$296 million appeal under the Humanitarian Response Plan to assist 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.

sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 15**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**8 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de 1.100 réplicas.**
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado.
- Balance oficial: **3.811 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, hizo un llamado a los Estados Miembros y donantes para transformar la solidaridad en apoyo concreto.**
- **Se lanzó un llamamiento adicional por US$296 millones para ampliar la respuesta a los terremotos y atender las necesidades**  
    **multisectoriales de 1,3 millones de personas durante los próximos seis meses.**
- El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.102 réplicas.**

A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.811 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas **17.907 personas quedaron sin vivienda**.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. El Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, anunció un llamamiento adicional al Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria de 296 millones de dólares para atender a 1,3 millones de personas afectadas por los terremotos durante los próximos seis meses.

reports.body_text:
The eighth Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts as of 7 July. The second page of the report also includes key funding priorities to sustain and scale up urgent assistance.

**Highlights**

Official figures report 3,685 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,907 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. A total of 856 buildings have also been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses.

A total of 87 transitory camps have been reported, with installed capacity for 20,227 people and 14,634 people currently accommodated. IOM continues supporting shelter, coordination and management of transitory camps, registration, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, community engagement, information management and inter-agency coordination.

To date, IOM has reached 3,638 unique individuals with 6,253 assistance and distribution activities, mainly in health, CCCM/shelter and protection. Urgent additional support is required to improve conditions in transitory camps, expand access to safe water and sanitation, strengthen registration and referrals, and address protection and public health risks.

**IOM activities**

IOM continues supporting the coordination and management of key transitory camps in La Guaira, including Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande. Support focused on site management, registration, community engagement, service coordination, basic assistance, connectivity, protection and the distribution of essential items. At Estadio César Nieves, the delivery of non-food items to 500 families was confirmed, including buckets, plastic sheeting and kitchen sets.

At Polideportivo José María Vargas, which hosts approximately 460 families, IOM supported meetings with community leaders, institutional visits, partial systematization of the community census and protection actions with the Ombudsperson’s Office, Civil Registry and SAIME. A total of 192 consultations were also provided during a health outreach session. Cumulative health assistance represents the largest sectoral volume of IOM’s response, with 3,318 registered assistance activities.

IOM continues supporting the registration of displaced families, the mapping of transitory camps and site assessments to inform operational planning. IOM also strengthened protection, community engagement, safe referrals, initial case support and inter-agency coordination, including the placement of information materials in key areas of the camps.

**IOM planned response**

IOM will continue prioritizing temporary shelter, site coordination and management, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, data and needs assessments. Planned actions include improving shelter conditions through tents, bunk beds, safe covered spaces and site planning; expanding access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene; strengthening medical and psychosocial services; and continuing protection referrals, accountability and risk mitigation for violence against women.

Additional funding would allow IOM to scale up emergency shelter, essential items, WASH, protection, health and mental health services, while strengthening registration, information management, mobility monitoring and coordination in transitory camps and affected communities.

Planned actions include improving shelter conditions through tents, bunk beds, safe covered spaces and site planning; expanding access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene; strengthening medical and psychosocial services; and continuing protection referrals, accountability and risk mitigation for violence against women.

Additional funding would allow IOM to scale up emergency shelter, essential items, WASH, protection, health and mental health services, while strengthening registration, information management, mobility monitoring and coordination in transitory camps and affected communities.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #8 (7 de julio de 2026)
reports.body_text:
El octavo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales al 7 de julio. La segunda página del reporte también incluye prioridades clave de financiamiento para sostener y ampliar la asistencia urgente.

**Aspectos destacados**

Las cifras oficiales reportan 3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridas, 6.462 rescatadas y 17.907 personas sin vivienda tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales.

Se reportan 87 campamentos transitorios, con una capacidad instalada para 20.227 personas y 14.634 personas actualmente alojadas. La OIM continúa apoyando alojamiento, coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, participación comunitaria, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial.

A la fecha, la OIM ha alcanzado 3.638 personas únicas con 6.253 asistencias y distribuciones, principalmente en salud, CCCM/alojamiento y protección. Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar condiciones en campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continúa apoyando la coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios clave en La Guaira, incluidos el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. El apoyo se centró en gestión de sitios, registro, participación comunitaria, coordinación de servicios, asistencia básica, conectividad, protección y distribución de artículos esenciales. En el Estadio César Nieves, se confirmó la entrega de artículos no alimentarios a 500 familias, incluyendo baldes, lonas plásticas y sets de cocina.

En el Polideportivo José María Vargas, que alberga aproximadamente 460 familias, la OIM apoyó reuniones con líderes y lideresas comunitarias, visitas institucionales, sistematización parcial del censo comunitario y acciones de protección con la Defensoría del Pueblo, Registro Civil y SAIME. También se brindaron 192 atenciones durante una jornada de salud. Las asistencias acumuladas en salud representan el mayor volumen sectorial de la respuesta de la OIM, con 3.318 asistencias registradas.

La OIM continúa apoyando el registro de familias desplazadas, el mapeo de campamentos transitorios y las evaluaciones de sitio para orientar la planificación operativa. Asimismo, fortaleció acciones de protección, participación comunitaria, derivaciones seguras, atención inicial de casos y coordinación interagencial, incluyendo la colocación de materiales informativos en áreas clave de los campamentos.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, datos y evaluaciones de necesidades. Las acciones previstas incluyen mejorar condiciones de alojamiento mediante carpas, literas, espacios cubiertos seguros y planificación de sitios; ampliar el acceso a agua segura, saneamiento e higiene; fortalecer servicios médicos y psicosociales; y continuar las derivaciones de protección, rendición de cuentas y mitigación de riesgos de violencia contra la mujer.

El financiamiento adicional permitiría a la OIM ampliar el alojamiento de emergencia, los artículos esenciales, WASH, protección, salud y servicios de salud mental, al tiempo que se fortalecen el registro, la gestión de información, el monitoreo de movilidad y la coordinación en campamentos transitorios y comunidades afectadas.

reports.title: Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: Transitional Camps (06 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
Following the earthquakes that occurred on 24 June 2026, La Guaira State reported some of the most severe impacts and one of the highest levels of population displacement. In support of the response led by national, state and municipal authorities, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is coordinating the management of three transitory camps — Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Estadio Playa Grande — where, together with other humanitarian actors, it provides assistance services. This coordination facilitates the provision of basic services, identification, case assistance and referrals for people with specific needs.

This document presents information on the occupancy and general characteristics of these three temporary accommodation sites. The figures reflect the situation observed at the time of reporting, are preliminary, and are subject to validation and updates as new information becomes available.

IOM Venezuela Flash Appeal: 2026 Earthquake Response (July - December 2026)
reports.body_text:
**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 struck the north-central region of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (henceforth referred to as Venezuela), triggering widespread devastation across several states, including La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, and Falcón. The earthquakes, followed by hundreds of aftershocks, caused significant loss of life, with 3,535 people reported dead and over 16,740 injured, as of 6 July. Damage to more than 2,500 infrastructure assets, including 38 hospitals, has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, water supply, and transport systems, placing considerable strain on national response capacities.

The disaster is unfolding in a context of pre-existing structural vulnerabilities, limited access to basic services, weakened public systems, and protracted humanitarian needs. As a result, the earthquakes have triggered an acute-on-chronic emergency, deepening existing vulnerabilities and increasing humanitarian needs across affected areas. Thousands of families have been displaced and are sheltering in collective centres (e.g. schools, sports centres), spontaneous settlements, self-managed sites, and open spaces due to the destruction or structural damage of homes and continued fear of further collapses.

While initial response efforts by national authorities and international actors have focused on search and rescue, emergency medical assistance, and rapid assessments, significant gaps remain across key sectors. These include safe and adequate shelter, core relief items, access to healthcare and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, protection, site-level coordination and management, and reliable data for operational targeting. Needs are particularly acute in overcrowded and informal displacement settings, where limited infrastructure, weak service provision, and the absence of structured site management increase risks of communicable disease outbreaks, violence against women and girls (VAWG) and other vulnerable groups, family separation, and other protection concerns.

To date, a significant share of the humanitarian response has been concentrated in La Guaira, Distrito Capital, and Miranda, where large-scale interventions have been prioritized. However, Falcón, Aragua, and Carabobo have also reported significant impacts. In these areas, infrastructure damage, service disruption, and comparatively lower operational coverage point to unmet needs and emerging gaps in assistance, particularly among populations in dispersed and hard-to-reach locations. Ensuring that these areas are reached will be critical for a coherent, equitable, and needs-based response, while also laying out the foundation for early recovery and longer-term resilience-building efforts.

reports.title: Atrocity Alert No. 490: Sudan, Lebanon and Venezuela
sources: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
reports.body_text:
## Atrocity Alert is a weekly publication by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect highlighting situations where populations are at risk of, or are enduring, mass atrocity crimes.

### **GROWING RISK OF ATROCITIES AMID ESCALATING CONFLICT IN EL OBEID, SUDAN**

Intensifying clashes in and around El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, are raising serious concerns over the heightened risk of atrocity crimes against civilians. Over the past few weeks, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have reportedly built-up their presence by encircling the city and begun a siege from at least three directions, with a potential offensive appearing imminent. Repeated drone strikes have already led to widespread civilian casualties. Estimates indicate that approximately 500,000 civilians in El Obeid are at risk of large-scale atrocities, including more than 100,000 internally displaced persons.

On 29 June the Yale School of Public Health’s Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) [reported](https://ysph.yale.edu/download-file/76d1775e-de0c-4861-afae-7aa92c4c0228/) satellite evidence covering the period 25 May to 25 June, indicating widespread and escalating damage to protected civilian infrastructure, including electricity generation facilities, fuel storage sites, multiple gas stations and the main market. Yale HRL concludes that the damage “is consistent with intentional bombardment of civilian infrastructure necessary for the sustainment of life.”

Control over El Obeid and the wider region has remained highly contested, with frontlines [shifting repeatedly](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-487/) between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The emerging pattern of encirclement, siege warfare and sustained strikes on civilian infrastructure mirrors RSF tactics previously [documented](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-448/) in El Fasher, North Darfur, where similar methods were used to isolate the city, degrade essential services and intensify pressure on civilian populations through sustained bombardment and encirclement.

During an Enhanced Interactive Dialogue on the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) for the [Sudan’s](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/sudan/) oral update to the UN Human Rights Council (HRC) in June, Norway delivered a statement on behalf of the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention in Sudan and 21 other states, expressing grave alarm at “the urgent risks of atrocities and deliberate killings in Sudan,” and urging all parties “to immediately de-escalate and comply fully with international humanitarian law.” On 20 June the UN Security Council also expressed concern “at the imminent risk of mass atrocities and demanded the RSF immediately halt its assault on El Obeid.”

As atrocities continued to mount, the Global Centre, together with other NGOs, [urged](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/sudan-the-human-rights-council-should-urgently-address-the-situation-in-and-around-el-obeid-north-kordofan-and-take-bold-steps-towards-atrocity-prevention-and-accountability/) the HRC to urgently address the situation in and around El Obeid and take steps towards atrocity prevention and accountability. The HRC convened an urgent debate on 3 July and adopted a resolution on 6 July requesting the FFM to conduct an urgent inquiry.

In light of the rapidly deteriorating situation and the heightened risk of atrocity crimes, all parties must immediately cease attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure and fully comply with their obligations under International Humanitarian Law. The international community should move beyond repeated reactive debates and ensure that investigations and reporting are systematically translated into timely political action. States should base their responses on existing credible findings regarding actors fueling the conflict and ensure that early warning is followed by concrete preventive and accountability measures.

### **NEW FRAMEWORK BETWEEN ISRAEL, US AND LEBANON RAISES JUSTICE CONCERNS**

On 26 June [Lebanon](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/lebanon/), [Israel](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/israel-and-the-occupied-palestinian-territory/) and the United States (US) signed a Trilateral Framework affirming their “shared goal of achieving lasting peace and security.” Brokered by the US after a series of direct talks between Lebanon and Israel, the fourteen-point Framework claims to serve as starting point from which parties will work towards a “full comprehensive peace and security agreement.” However, concerns have been raised over the viability of this Framework and the extent to which its stipulations may undermine justice, accountability and a lasting political resolution. The Framework was signed amid an ongoing ceasefire that has been subject to near-daily violations by Israel, resulting in thousands of casualties.

Despite some of the parties stressing that the Framework does not waive the right of victims to seek justice, clause 13 of the agreement commits Israel and Lebanon to the “cessation of all hostile or adverse actions in international political or legal fora,” which could constrain accountability efforts for Israel’s atrocity crimes in Lebanon, including attempts to revitalize suspended efforts by Lebanon to accept the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC) following [hostilities](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-412-lebanon-haiti-and-venezuela/) with Israel in 2024. Six human rights and press freedom organizations issued a [statement](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/07/lebanon-israel-framework-agreement-betrays-victims-of-war-crimes-in-lebanon/) warning that the agreement “threatens to betray war crimes victims in Lebanon,” including by appearing to obstruct recourse to justice before international courts and “acquiesce to the prolonged and indefinite forced displacement” of residents from the south.

Since 2 March Israeli forces have progressively moved to occupy an estimated six percent of Lebanese territory, including large swathes of southern Lebanon, and established and expanded a [so-called yellow-line](https://www.globalr2p.org/publications/atrocity-alert-no-480/). Dozens of villages have been destroyed and over 1 million people have been forcibly displaced by the occupation.

The Framework upholds measures that would delay and prevent the return of tens of thousands of people who remain displaced. Without explicit mention of the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the Framework effectively conditions the “redeployment” of Israeli forces outside of Lebanese territory on the disarmament of Hezbollah – a task assigned to the Lebanese Armed Forces, which continues to present significant challenges for Lebanon despite efforts to do so since 2024. In the days following the signing of the Framework, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz reportedly instructed forces to prepare for a long-term presence in “security zones” in southern Lebanon.

Parties to the Framework must ensure its implementation neither prevents the return of displaced populations nor impedes recourse to justice for victims of atrocity crimes. Lebanon should finalize earlier moves to grant ICC immediate jurisdiction. States must press for the immediate, unconditional withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, support victims in their pursuit of justice and exert influence on parties to adhere to the ceasefire.

### **CATASTROPHIC EARTHQUAKES DEEPEN VENEZUELA’S MULTIDIMENSIONAL CRISIS**

On 24 June two powerful earthquakes – magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 – struck [Venezuela](https://www.globalr2p.org/countries/venezuela/) less than a minute apart, the strongest to hit the country in over a century. Centered in the state of Yaracuy, the quakes also caused widespread destruction across the Capital District and the states of La Guaira, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo and Falcón, among others. The coastal city of La Guaira, north of Caracas, was among the worst hit, with entire neighborhoods reduced to rubble.

At the time of publication, the official death toll released by Venezuelan authorities has climbed above 3,600, but is estimated to be significantly higher as efforts to recover and identify victims remain ongoing and thousands of people remain unaccounted for. More than 16,700 individuals have been reportedly injured and over 17,000 people left homeless, while at least 1,000 buildings, including hospitals, were damaged or destroyed.

Venezuelan authorities have come under intense criticism for a response widely described as grossly inadequate. Rescue efforts were significantly delayed and under-resourced, leaving families to search for and recover victims from the rubble themselves. National humanitarian organizations, international rescue teams, UN agencies and hundreds of civil society volunteers have since carried out the vast majority of the relief effort. Venezuelan human rights NGO Provea also warned of the deployment of security bodies with no legal competence in disaster response – including the military counterintelligence directorate (DGCIM) and the intelligence service (SEBIN) – which could obstruct relief efforts and give rise to human rights abuses.

The catastrophe has struck a country already gripped by a multidimensional protection crisis that has left populations without reliable access to basic services, including clean water and sanitation, nutrition, health care and electricity for over a decade. Venezuelan civil society platform *HumVenezuela* estimates that 18.2 million people were in need as of January 2026, 12.4 million of whom faced critical humanitarian needs. The authorities’ incompetence is the product of more than two decades of large-scale corruption and the erosion of the rule of law. The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela has documented how state actors, including the DGCIM and SEBIN, have been used as instruments of regime survival, responsible for crimes against humanity and silencing dissent. State-led repression has been accompanied by years of systematic attacks against civic space, including criminalization of civil society organizations and independent media, both of which are central to current relief efforts. These dynamics now threaten to place Venezuelans at even greater risk and further exacerbate unprecedented suffering and despair.

Venezuelan authorities must immediately lift restrictions on civic space, allow full and unrestricted access for humanitarian actors and independent media and guarantee prompt and transparent information on relief efforts. Authorities must also urgently ensure the recovery and identification of the dead, provide families with accurate information on those still missing and ensure that affected communities are able to mourn and bury their loved ones with dignity.

Six human rights and press freedom organizations issued a statement warning that the agreement “threatens to betray war crimes victims in Lebanon,” including by appearing to obstruct recourse to justice before international courts and “acquiesce to the prolonged and indefinite forced displacement” of residents from the south.

Since 2 March Israeli forces have progressively moved to occupy an estimated six percent of Lebanese territory, including large swathes of southern Lebanon, and established and expanded a so-called yellow-line. Dozens of villages have been destroyed and over 1 million people have been forcibly displaced by the occupation.

The Framework upholds measures that would delay and prevent the return of tens of thousands of people who remain displaced. Without explicit mention of the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the Framework effectively conditions the “redeployment” of Israeli forces outside of Lebanese territory on the disarmament of Hezbollah – a task assigned to the Lebanese Armed Forces, which continues to present significant challenges for Lebanon despite efforts to do so since 2024. In the days following the signing of the Framework, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz reportedly instructed forces to prepare for a long-term presence in “security zones” in southern Lebanon.

Parties to the Framework must ensure its implementation neither prevents the return of displaced populations nor impedes recourse to justice for victims of atrocity crimes. Lebanon should finalize earlier moves to grant ICC immediate jurisdiction. States must press for the immediate, unconditional withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, support victims in their pursuit of justice and exert influence on parties to adhere to the ceasefire.

CATASTROPHIC EARTHQUAKES DEEPEN VENEZUELA’S MULTIDIMENSIONAL CRISIS

On 24 June two powerful earthquakes – magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 – struck Venezuela less than a minute apart, the strongest to hit the country in over a century. Centered in the state of Yaracuy, the quakes also caused widespread destruction across the Capital District and the states of La Guaira, Miranda, Aragua, Carabobo and Falcón, among others. The coastal city of La Guaira, north of Caracas, was among the worst hit, with entire neighborhoods reduced to rubble.

At the time of publication, the official death toll released by Venezuelan authorities has climbed above 3,600, but is estimated to be significantly higher as efforts to recover and identify victims remain ongoing and thousands of people remain unaccounted for. More than 16,700 individuals have been reportedly injured and over 17,000 people left homeless, while at least 1,000 buildings, including hospitals, were damaged or destroyed.

Venezuelan authorities have come under intense criticism for a response widely described as grossly inadequate. Rescue efforts were significantly delayed and under-resourced, leaving families to search for and recover victims from the rubble themselves. National humanitarian organizations, international rescue teams, UN agencies and hundreds of civil society volunteers have since carried out the vast majority of the relief effort. Venezuelan human rights NGO Provea also warned of the deployment of security bodies with no legal competence in disaster response – including the military counterintelligence directorate (DGCIM) and the intelligence service (SEBIN) – which could obstruct relief efforts and give rise to human rights abuses.

The catastrophe has struck a country already gripped by a multidimensional protection crisis that has left populations without reliable access to basic services, including clean water and sanitation, nutrition, health care and electricity for over a decade. Venezuelan civil society platform HumVenezuela estimates that 18.2 million people were in need as of January 2026, 12.4 million of whom faced critical humanitarian needs. The authorities’ incompetence is the product of more than two decades of large-scale corruption and the erosion of the rule of law. The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela has documented how state actors, including the DGCIM and SEBIN, have been used as instruments of regime survival, responsible for crimes against humanity and silencing dissent. State-led repression has been accompanied by years of systematic attacks against civic space, including criminalization of civil society organizations and independent media, both of which are central to current relief efforts. These dynamics now threaten to place Venezuelans at even greater risk and further exacerbate unprecedented suffering and despair.

Venezuelan authorities must immediately lift restrictions on civic space, allow full and unrestricted access for humanitarian actors and independent media and guarantee prompt and transparent information on relief efforts. Authorities must also urgently ensure the recovery and identification of the dead, provide families with accurate information on those still missing and ensure that affected communities are able to mourn and bury their loved ones with dignity.

reports.title: Au Venezuela, une urgence humanitaire majeure à la suite de séismes dévastateurs
reports.body_text:
## Deux séismes majeurs ont frappé le nord du Venezuela, faisant des milliers de morts et de disparus. La destruction de nombreuses infrastructures aggrave considérablement un système de santé déjà fragile. Pour répondre à cette crise, Médecins du Monde France vient en appui aux équipes de Médecins du Monde Espagne, déjà déployées sur le terrain.

Le 24 juin 2026, les séismes de magnitudes 7,2 et 7,5 ont particulièrement touché la capitale Caracas et l’État de La Guaira. Alors que **plusieurs milliers de personnes sont toujours portées disparues**, le bilan humain continue de s’alourdir. Les opérations de recherche et de secours sont en cours dans un contexte de répliques possibles et de **dégradation des conditions d’accès aux soins**. En conséquence, les besoins en soins d’urgence, traumatologie et santé mentale abondent.

Sur place, les équipes de [**Médecins du Monde Espagne**](https://www.medicosdelmundo.org/) **sont saines et sauves.** Elles se mobilisent pour évaluer et organiser la réponse en lien avec les autorités locales de santé, avec notamment des besoins en matériel et en médicaments.

**Médecins du Monde France** s’est positionnée en appui de Médecins du Monde Espagne pour intervenir rapidement auprès des populations. Nous sommes prêts à mobiliser rapidement depuis la [Colombie](https://www.medecinsdumonde.org/pays/amerique/colombie/) où nous sommes opérationnels, une équipe de médecins, d’infirmiers, de psychologues et de logisticiens, ainsi que des kits médicaux pouvant **permettre la prise en charge d’environ 1 500 personnes.**

Cette intervention contribuera à :

- Assurer des **soins de santé primaires** en première ligne et **distribuer les médicaments** nécessaires,
- **Stabiliser les urgences** en orientant les patientes et patients vers des **structures adaptées,**
- Fournir un **accompagnement en santé mentale**.

reports.title: CADENA mobilises emergency response for earthquake-affected communities in Venezuela
reports.body_text:
[*CADENA International*](https://cadena.ngo/)*, a HelpAge network member with offices across Latin America, has launched an emergency response in Venezuela following the 24 June earthquakes. Its efforts focus on search and rescue, healthcare, relief distributions, psychosocial support and rapid needs assessments.*

*The organisation has deployed international search and rescue specialists, and is delivering emergency supplies including household water filters and solar lamps, working closely with local authorities and humanitarian partners on the ground.*

## **Reaching older people and other at-risk groups**

Among the estimated 1.8 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, around 250,000 older people are expected to require targeted support. Older people represent approximately 14% of the population and are among those facing the greatest risks following the disaster, particularly those living with disabilities, chronic health conditions, mobility limitations, social isolation, or the loss of caregivers.

## **Responding to urgent needs on the ground**

Initial assessments conducted by CADENA found overcrowded shelters, families sleeping outdoors due to fear of aftershocks, limited access to safe drinking water, shortages of basic medical supplies, and growing protection concerns. Teams also reported that many older people had lost essential assistive devices and were struggling to access services and humanitarian assistance.

To address these needs, CADENA is providing emergency relief items, supporting access to safe water, and helping affected households meet their most urgent basic needs. The organisation is prioritising households with older people, particularly those facing additional risks linked to disability, chronic illness, damaged housing, or lack of family support.

## **Providing healthcare and psychosocial support**

Volunteer medical brigades are providing primary healthcare services in affected communities, while additional medical teams and supplies are being mobilised to strengthen the response. Particular attention is being given to ensuring continuity of care for older people and others who rely on regular medication and treatment for chronic conditions.

At the same time, CADENA is delivering mental health and psychosocial support through specialist staff and trained volunteers. Community-based activities and psychological first aid are helping survivors cope with trauma, grief, stress and uncertainty following the earthquakes. Older people, who may be experiencing heightened isolation and distress, are a key focus of these efforts.

A CADENA team member conducts a psychosocial assessment with an earthquake survivor.

## **Scaling up for recovery**

CADENA is preparing to expand its emergency response in the coming weeks. Planned activities include the distribution of water, hygiene and shelter kits, food assistance, protection activities, disaster risk awareness initiatives, healthcare support, and continued mental health and psychosocial services. The aim is to ensure that older people and other at-risk groups are not left behind as affected communities move from emergency response towards recovery.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Terremoto (24 de junio 2026): ¿Quién hace qué, dónde? (a 7 de julio 2026): al nivel de municipios, en los estados priorizados para la respuesta humanitaria
Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Terremoto (24 de junio 2026) - Equipos Médicos de Emergencia a 07/07/2026
Venezuela on-the-record update #2: Families need safe water and sanitation to reduce health risks | NRC
reports.body_text:
*Media update by Beatriz Ochoa, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s (NRC) Regional Head of Advocacy for Latin America two weeks after earthquakes in Venezuela:*

08. Jul 2026

“Two weeks after the earthquakes struck Venezuela, many families who lost their homes have told me they are concerned about how they will meet their most basic needs. Thousands of people continue to live in temporary shelters, schools, parks and other public spaces. Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services is now becoming increasingly important to prevent health problems and the spread of disease.

“Many families are living in densely populated settings, with limited privacy, exposure to high temperatures and seasonal rains, and sometimes insufficient access to showers, soap and adequate sanitation facilities.

“I have seen families doing everything they can to maintain dignity in extremely difficult conditions. In one temporary shelter, I saw families organising themselves to keep common spaces clean, including through makeshift toilets and basic waste management arrangements. Their determination is remarkable, but families should not have to shoulder this burden alone.

“We urgently need support from international donors so we and other humanitarian organisations can provide access to safe water, toilets, hygiene supplies, and clear public health information to help reduce the risk of diarrhoeal diseases, skin infections and other preventable health problems among displaced families.

“Water is being delivered by tanker trucks to many temporary shelters, but families often lack appropriate containers to store it safely. Access to bottled water, showers and toilets remains limited in some locations. These challenges can be particularly difficult for older people, people with disabilities, pregnant women and families with young children.

"As displacement becomes more protracted, and the days turn into weeks, I have seen families beginning to organise daily life in temporary shelters, including preparing and cooking meals together. In these conditions, access to clean water remains essential to prevent disease and protect people's health.

“Families need basic but essential items, including safe water containers, water purification tablets, soap, chlorine, sanitary pads and tarpaulins.

“NRC has already provided 1,400 displaced people with soap and other hygiene items, water tanks, and jerrycans for safe water storage. We will also be distributing tarpaulins to help protect families protect from exposure to the elements and have supported first responders with personal protective equipment for search and rescue activities.

“As the response evolves, we will work with communities, authorities, and humanitarian actors to establish more suitable solutions, including larger-scale water storage and treatment systems, improved sanitation facilities and community showers that provide greater privacy and dignity.

“The first days of this response were driven by the community. The world should know that this solidarity is not simply a gesture—it is a vital necessity. But it is now time for funding and aid to flow in and support longer-term solutions so people can take the first steps to rebuilding their lives.”

**Notes to editors:**

- Photos and videos from Venezuela are available for use [here](https://visuals.nrc.no?c=15116&k=5b02ed739f).
- At least 3,685 people have been killed and more than 16,740 people injured. The number of dead and injured is likely to rise ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-14-07-july-2026-time-0900-pm)).
- 17,907 people have lost their homes, according to the authorities ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-14-07-july-2026-time-0900-pm)).
- Authorities report at least 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-12-05-july-2026-time-0800-pm)).
- 38 hospitals were damaged by the earthquakes ([OCHA](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/earthquakes-venezuela-situation-report-no-5-28-june-2026-time-500-pm)).
- In 2026, 7.9 million people in the country are in need of humanitarian assistance, 27.7 per cent of the total population (28.5 million people) ([OCHA](https://www.unocha.org/venezuela)). 5.5 million of them have been targeted for assistance.
- The humanitarian response plan in Venezuela is currently 43.4 per cent funded with 274.4 million of the 632.2 million US dollars required having been delivered ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/overview/2026)).
- The 2025 humanitarian response plan in Venezuela was just 20 per cent funded, while the 2024 plan was 28 per cent funded ([OCHA](https://fts.unocha.org/plans/1517/summary)).
- NRC has been working in Venezuela since 2005 providing education, protection, legal guidance, and water and sanitation support. In 2025 we reached more than 71,000 people across four bordering states. NRC has 70 colleagues in Venezuela, and seven local partners. Our teams are working across areas affected by the earthquakes to provide vital supplies, and will be providing water and sanitation support, emergency education and trauma support for children among other services.
- A full family hygiene kit contains: 8 toilet soaps, 4 toothbrush, toothpaste or dental cream, shampoo, washing powder, bleach, toilet paper and deodorant. The family mobility kit includes mosquito repellent, anti-burn cream, sunscreen, among other essential items.

**For more information or to arrange an interview, please contact:**

- NRC global media hotline: media@nrc.no, +47 905 62 329

reports.title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #02 (Reporting period: 01–07 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
*This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.*

**Summary Points**

- On 05 July, an LTC Telecoms Coordinator arrived in Caracas to strengthen in-country coordination, support rapid connectivity assessments, and help identify priority communications needs for the humanitarian response.
- Since 03 July, LTC Telecoms has been conducting a rapid connectivity assessment survey across affected areas to map available communications services, identify coverage gaps, and prioritize shared connectivity solutions for humanitarian partners. Organizations operating in affected areas are encouraged to complete the survey to help identify priority connectivity needs and gaps.
- On 06 July, LTC Telecoms assessed three displacement shelters in La Guaira and identified unreliable power supply and internet connectivity gaps as the main operational constraints. Connectivity support, including Starlink terminals and solar power systems, is being deployed to strengthen communications for responders.

reports.title: Terremotos en Venezuela: Reporte de situación #14 (07 de julio de 2026, Hora: 09:00 pm)
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**Reporte de situación N.º 14**  
**Terremotos en Venezuela**  
**7 de julio de 2026**  
**Hora: 9:00 pm**

**Destacados**

- Tras los sismos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio (18:00 hora local), **las autoridades reportan más de mil réplicas**.
- Al menos siete (7) estados impactados. La Guaira se mantiene como el estado más afectado.
- Balance oficial: **3.685 personas fallecidas y 16.740 heridas.**
- **6.462 personas han sido rescatadas.**
- **Tom Fletcher, jefe humanitario de las Naciones Unidas, inició una visita oficial a Venezuela para apoyar los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.**
- El Sistema de Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en coordinación con el gobierno, responden con acciones multisectoriales y  
     continuarán ampliando la asistencia a las personas afectadas.

**Situación general**

Venezuela enfrenta una emergencia nacional tras dos sismos consecutivos de gran magnitud (7,2 y 7,5) ocurridos el 24 de junio (18:00, hora local) en la región centro-norte, con epicentro sobre el eje San Felipe - Yumare - Montalbán (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Las autoridades reportan 1.076 réplicas.**

A más de una semana de los terremotos, las autoridades reportan un balance de **3.685 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas y 6.462 personas rescatadas** desde el inicio de la emergencia. Asimismo, las autoridades reportan que unas **17.907 personas quedaron sin vivienda**.

La respuesta gubernamental mantiene el foco en las labores de búsqueda, la preparación de los campamentos transitorios y la atención de las personas afectadas. Naciones Unidas y sus organizaciones socias, en articulación con las autoridades, realizan acciones multisectoriales para las personas afectadas y continuarán ampliando la respuesta. En este marco de estos esfuerzos, el Subsecretario General de las Naciones Unidas para Asuntos Humanitarios y Coordinador del Socorro de Emergencia, Tom Fletcher, inició una visita a Venezuela con el fin de conocer de primera mano el impacto de la emergencia y los esfuerzos de respuesta en curso.

**Situation Report No. 14**  
**Earthquakes in Venezuela**  
**07 July 2026**  
**Time: 9:00 pm**

**Highlights**

- Following the 24 June earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 (18:00 local time), **authorities report more than 1,000 aftershocks.**
- At least seven (7) states have been impacted. La Guaira remains the most affected state.
- Official toll: **3,685 people dead and 16,740 injured.**
- A total of **6,462 people have been rescued.**
- **Tom Fletcher, the United Nations humanitarian chief, began an official visit to Venezuela to support ongoing response efforts.**
- The United Nations system and its partner organizations, in coordination with the Government, are responding with multisectoral actions and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people.

**Situation overview**

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive high-magnitude earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5) that struck on 24 June (18:00 local time) in the north-central region, with the epicentre located along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). **Authorities report 1.076 aftershocks.**

More than a week after the earthquakes, authorities report a toll of **3,685 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued** since the onset of the emergency. Authorities also reported that approximately **17,907 people lost their homes.**

The Government response remains focused on search and rescue operations, the preparation and expansion of transitional camps and the assistance to affected populations. The United Nations and its partner organizations, in coordination with the authorities, are implementing multisectoral response activities and will continue to scale up assistance to affected people. In this context, United Nations Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher began a visit to Venezuela to gain first-hand insight into the impact of the emergency and the ongoing response efforts.

reports.title: UNFPA Flash Update: Earthquakes in Venezuela (26 June-6 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
Venezuela is facing a severe humanitarian emergency following two powerful earthquakes that struck the country's central-northern region on 24 June. At least 3,342 people have been killed and 16,470 injured. With tens of thousands of people still unaccounted for, the death toll is expected to increase as search and rescue efforts continue.

An estimated 36,700 pregnant women have been affected by the earthquakes, including approximately 4,000 who are expected to give birth in the next month. The health system is under severe strain, with 38 health facilities damaged, significantly limiting access to essential maternal health services for women and newborns. Maintaining emergency obstetric and newborn care is therefore an urgent humanitarian priority.

The disruption of essential services, overcrowded shelters, family separation, and rising psychosocial distress are exacerbating protection risks, particularly for women, adolescent girls, persons with disabilities, and older persons. In addition, more than 10,000 people are currently residing in temporary shelters, where privacy, lighting and protection measures remain insufficient. Strengthening gender-based violence prevention and ensuring safe access to survivor-centred services is critical.

UNFPA is scaling up its responses to ensure continued access to maternal health services, emergency obstetric care, family planning, clinical management of rape, and gender-based violence prevention and response services. Initial shipments of reproductive health supplies and essential equipment are being mobilized to support affected communities. UNFPA estimates it requires approximately US$10 million to sustain life-saving reproductive health and protection interventions for the first three months of the emergency response.

reports.title: Venezuela, Americas | Earthquake: Emergency Appeal - Operational Strategy (MDRVE015)
sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
reports.body_text:
## DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession, with preliminary magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5. Authorities have reported more than 302 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. They were also felt in parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and Brazil, reaching as far as Martinique and the Brazilian Amazon, more than 1,700 km from the epicentres.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency and designated La Guaira a disaster zone, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations is concentrated. According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS), an estimated 9.73 million people have been affected, including approximately 530,000 exposed to extreme earthquake intensity.

According to the initial statistical model developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), there was a 50 per cent probability that the number of casualties (deaths and injuries) would range between 1,000 and 10,000, and a 30 per cent probability that it would exceed 10,000. International response teams from at least 17 countries have deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the 2 OCHA Situation Report No. 9 Earthquakes in Venezuela coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG).

According to OCHA, as of 2 July2, 2,595 people had been confirmed dead and 12,400 injured. A further 12,841 people had been displaced after their homes were severely damaged. In total, 2,501 structures were affected, including 38 hospitals, 189 buildings that collapsed completely, and 855 buildings that either partially collapsed or sustained significant damage. La Guaira remains the worst-affected state.

reports.title: Venezuela (República Bolivariana de): Respuesta a Terremotos - Reporte de Situación #7 (6 de julio de 2026)
reports.body_text:
El séptimo Reporte de Situación presenta una actualización sobre el impacto de los terremotos del 24 de junio en la República Bolivariana de Venezuela y resume la respuesta en curso y planificada de la OIM en apoyo a las poblaciones afectadas y a los esfuerzos nacionales al 6 de julio. La segunda página del reporte también incluye prioridades clave de financiamiento para sostener y ampliar la asistencia urgente.

**Aspectos destacados**

Las cifras oficiales reportan 3.535 personas fallecidas, 16.740 personas heridas, 6.462 personas rescatadas y 17.854 personas sin vivienda tras los terremotos del 24 de junio. También se reportan 856 edificios afectados, incluidos 190 colapsos totales.

Se reportan 82 campamentos transitorios. Las últimas cifras disponibles indican una capacidad instalada para 14.599 personas, con 10.702 personas actualmente alojadas. La OIM continúa apoyando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, registro, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, participación comunitaria, gestión de información y coordinación interagencial.

Se requiere apoyo adicional urgente para mejorar las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios, ampliar el acceso a agua segura y saneamiento, fortalecer el registro y las derivaciones, y abordar riesgos de protección y salud pública.

**Actividades de la OIM**

La OIM continúa apoyando la coordinación y gestión de campamentos transitorios clave en La Guaira, incluidos el Polideportivo José María Vargas, el Estadio César Nieves y Playa Grande. El apoyo se centró en mejoras del sitio, coordinación de servicios, registro, conectividad, participación comunitaria, derivaciones de protección y distribuciones de artículos esenciales, incluida la asistencia a 360 familias en el Estadio César Nieves y comunidades aledañas.

El 6 de julio, los equipos de salud y SMAPS apoyados por la OIM brindaron 353 atenciones médicas y psicosociales en los tres sitios. La OIM también continuó apoyando el mapeo de campamentos transitorios y el registro para orientar la planificación operativa, al tiempo que fortaleció las actividades de protección, orientación legal, derivaciones y sensibilización sobre riesgos de protección en emergencias.

**Respuesta planificada de la OIM**

La OIM continuará priorizando alojamiento temporal, coordinación y gestión de sitios, WASH, salud y SMAPS, protección, registro, datos y evaluaciones de necesidades. Las acciones previstas incluyen fortalecer servicios seguros y con rendición de cuentas en campamentos transitorios, ampliar el apoyo médico y psicosocial, mejorar WASH y las derivaciones de protección, y generar datos oportunos para orientar una asistencia focalizada.

El financiamiento adicional permitiría a la OIM ampliar el alojamiento de emergencia, los artículos esenciales, WASH, protección, salud y servicios de SMAPS, al tiempo que se mejoran las condiciones en los campamentos transitorios y las comunidades afectadas.

reports.title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #7 (6 July 2026)
reports.body_text:
The seventh Situation Report provides an update on the impact of the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and summarizes IOM’s ongoing and planned response in support of affected populations and national efforts as of 6 July. The second page of this also includes key funding priorities to sustain and scale up urgent assistance.

Highlights

Official figures report 3,535 fatalities, 16,740 injuries, 6,462 people rescued and 17,854 people without housing following the 24 June earthquakes. A total of 856 buildings have been reported as affected, including 190 total collapses.

A total of 82 transitory camps have been reported. The latest available figures indicate installed capacity for 14,599 people, with 10,702 people currently accommodated. IOM continues supporting temporary accommodation, site coordination and management, registration, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, community engagement, information management and inter-agency coordination.

Urgent additional support is required to improve conditions in transitory camps, expand access to safe water and sanitation, strengthen registration and referrals, and address protection and public health risks.

IOM activities

IOM continued supporting coordination and management of key transitory camps in La Guaira, including Polideportivo José María Vargas, Estadio César Nieves and Playa Grande. Support focused on site improvements, service coordination, registration, connectivity, community engagement, protection referrals and essential item distributions, including assistance to 360 families at Estadio César Nieves and surrounding communities.

On 6 July, IOM-supported health and MHPSS teams provided 353 medical and psychosocial consultations across the three sites. IOM also continued supporting camp mapping and registration to inform operational planning, while strengthening protection activities, legal orientation, referrals and awareness on protection risks in emergencies.

IOM planned response

IOM will continue prioritizing temporary accommodation, site coordination and management, WASH, health and MHPSS, protection, registration, data and needs assessments. Planned actions include strengthening safe and accountable services in transitory camps, expanding medical and psychosocial support, improving WASH and protection referrals, and generating timely data to guide targeted assistance.

Additional funding would enable IOM to scale up emergency accommodation, essential items, WASH, protection, health and MHPSS services, while improving conditions in transitory camps and affected communities.

reports.title: Latinoamérica y El Caribe Resumen de Situación Semanal al 7 de julio 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**CIFRAS CLAVE**

- 3,5K personas fallecidas tras dos poderosos terremotos que sacudieron Venezuela el 24 de junio
- 6,4K personas rescatadas tras dos poderosos terremotos que azotaron Venezuela el 24 de junio
- 750K personas podrían necesitar asistencia alimentaria entre junio y agosto en Honduras

**VENEZUELA: TERREMOTO**

Más de una semana después de los terremotos de magnitud 7,2 y 7,5 del 24 de junio en la región centro-norte de Venezuela, las autoridades informan de 3.535 personas fallecidas, 16.740 heridas y 6.462 rescatadas, con casi 1.000 réplicas registradas. Al menos siete estados se han visto afectados, siendo La Guaira la zona más afectada. Aproximadamente 17.845 personas han perdido sus hogares, y 80 campamentos transitorios —concentrados en Caracas, Miranda y La Guaira— operan ahora al 73% de su capacidad. La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano fue transferida formalmente de equipos internacionales a la Protección Civil de Venezuela, aunque varios equipos internacionales siguen desplegados para apoyar los esfuerzos de recuperación. El 1 de julio comenzó un período de luto nacional de siete días.

Las necesidades prioritarias siguen concentradas en la protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH) y seguridad alimentaria, especialmente entre las familias desplazadas y aquellas en las zonas más cercanas al epicentro. La respuesta humanitaria sigue ampliándose en todos los sectores, con servicios de salud, protección y apoyo psicosocial que llegan a varios cientos de personas afectadas a través de consultas, asesoramiento y gestión de casos en los campamentos transitorios. Los socios de WASH están ampliando la infraestructura de saneamiento y la distribución de kits de higiene, mientras que continúan las mejoras en los campamentos transitorios. La evaluación inicial del UNDRR estima que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura ascienden a aproximadamente 37.000 millones de dólares, mientras que la estimación preliminar del PNUD sobre los daños físicos directos es de 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalente al 6% del PIB.

Apoya [aquí al Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

Más información en: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**ECUADOR: INUNDACIÓN**

El 3 de julio, fuertes lluvias provocaron el desbordamiento del río Zamora, lo que desencadenó graves inundaciones en Guadalupe, en el municipio de Zamora, en la provincia amazónica de Zamora Chinchipe. Los informes preliminares de la Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos de Ecuador (SNGR) indican 5 personas fallecidas, 10 desaparecidas y 38 heridas, incluidos bomberos implicados en operaciones de evacuación y rescate. Se estima que 300 personas han sido afectadas y 200 desplazadas, con daños en viviendas, carreteras, suministro de agua, electricidad, telecomunicaciones, cultivos y medios de vida. Las autoridades nacionales y locales han activado mecanismos de coordinación de emergencia, establecido un albergue temporal para familias desplazadas y lideran operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y la prestación de asistencia humanitaria.

**CENTROAMÉRICA: SEGURIDAD ALIMENTARIA**

FEWS NET pronostica precipitaciones por debajo de la media y condiciones secas persistentes en la mayor parte de Centroamérica hasta principios de julio, a pesar del aumento de las precipitaciones a principios de junio, que no compensaron los déficits a largo plazo. Se prevé que la mayoría de las zonas productoras de granos básicos reciban no más del 45% de la precipitación media histórica entre el 16 de junio y el 10 de julio, con los déficits más pronunciados, de hasta el 65%, concentrados en Guatemala y Nicaragua. En Honduras, ya se han registrado resultados de Crisis (Fase 3 de la CIF) en el Corredor Seco y en el departamento de Choluteca, en la costa del Pacífico. FEWS NET estima que entre 500.000 y 749.999 personas necesitarán asistencia alimentaria humanitaria a nivel nacional, con picos entre junio y agosto. Los servicios meteorológicos regionales prevén que una canícula prolongada (periodo seco a mediados de verano) afecte aún más al Corredor Seco, y pronostican temperaturas entre 2-4 °C por encima de la media en la vertiente del Pacífico de la región.

La coordinación de las operaciones de Búsqueda y Rescate Urbano fue transferida formalmente de equipos internacionales a la Protección Civil de Venezuela, aunque varios equipos internacionales siguen desplegados para apoyar los esfuerzos de recuperación. El 1 de julio comenzó un período de luto nacional de siete días.

Las necesidades prioritarias siguen concentradas en la protección, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, salud, alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene (WASH) y seguridad alimentaria, especialmente entre las familias desplazadas y aquellas en las zonas más cercanas al epicentro. La respuesta humanitaria sigue ampliándose en todos los sectores, con servicios de salud, protección y apoyo psicosocial que llegan a varios cientos de personas afectadas a través de consultas, asesoramiento y gestión de casos en los campamentos transitorios. Los socios de WASH están ampliando la infraestructura de saneamiento y la distribución de kits de higiene, mientras que continúan las mejoras en los campamentos transitorios. La evaluación inicial del UNDRR estima que los daños directos a viviendas e infraestructura ascienden a aproximadamente 37.000 millones de dólares, mientras que la estimación preliminar del PNUD sobre los daños físicos directos es de 6.700 millones de dólares, equivalente al 6% del PIB.

Apoya aquí al Fondo Humanitario de Venezuela

Más información en: ReliefWeb Response

ECUADOR: INUNDACIÓN

El 3 de julio, fuertes lluvias provocaron el desbordamiento del río Zamora, lo que desencadenó graves inundaciones en Guadalupe, en el municipio de Zamora, en la provincia amazónica de Zamora Chinchipe. Los informes preliminares de la Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos de Ecuador (SNGR) indican 5 personas fallecidas, 10 desaparecidas y 38 heridas, incluidos bomberos implicados en operaciones de evacuación y rescate. Se estima que 300 personas han sido afectadas y 200 desplazadas, con daños en viviendas, carreteras, suministro de agua, electricidad, telecomunicaciones, cultivos y medios de vida. Las autoridades nacionales y locales han activado mecanismos de coordinación de emergencia, establecido un albergue temporal para familias desplazadas y lideran operaciones de búsqueda y rescate, evaluaciones rápidas de necesidades y la prestación de asistencia humanitaria.

CENTROAMÉRICA: SEGURIDAD ALIMENTARIA

FEWS NET pronostica precipitaciones por debajo de la media y condiciones secas persistentes en la mayor parte de Centroamérica hasta principios de julio, a pesar del aumento de las precipitaciones a principios de junio, que no compensaron los déficits a largo plazo. Se prevé que la mayoría de las zonas productoras de granos básicos reciban no más del 45% de la precipitación media histórica entre el 16 de junio y el 10 de julio, con los déficits más pronunciados, de hasta el 65%, concentrados en Guatemala y Nicaragua. Los servicios meteorológicos regionales prevén que una canícula prolongada (periodo seco a mediados de verano) afecte aún más al Corredor Seco, y pronostican temperaturas entre 2-4 °C por encima de la media en la vertiente del Pacífico de la región.

reports.title: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 7 July 2026
sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
reports.body_text:
**KEY FIGURES**

- 3.5K people dead after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June
- 6.4K people rescued after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela on 24 June
- 750K people may require food assistance between June-August in Honduras

**VENEZUELA: EARTHQUAKE**

More than a week after the 24 June magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes in Venezuela’s north-central region, authorities report 3,535 people dead, 16,740 injured, and 6,462 rescued, with nearly 1,000 aftershocks recorded. At least seven states have been affected, with La Guaira remaining the hardest hit. Approximately 17,845 people have lost their homes, and 80 transitional camps - concentrated in Caracas, Miranda, and La Guaira - are now operating at 73 per cent capacity. Coordination of Urban Search and Rescue operations has formally transferred from international teams to Venezuela’s Civil Protection, though several international teams remain deployed to support recovery efforts. A seven-day national mourning period began on 1 July.

Priority needs remain concentrated in protection, mental health and psychosocial support, health, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security, particularly among displaced families and those in areas closest to the epicentre. The humanitarian response continues to scale up across sectors, with health, protection, and psychosocial support services reaching several hundred affected people through consultations, counselling, and case management in transitional camps. WASH partners are expanding sanitation infrastructure and hygiene kit distribution, while shelter improvements continue across camp sites. UNDRR’s initial assessment puts direct damage to housing and infrastructure at approximately US$37 billion, while UNDP’s preliminary estimate of direct physical damage stands at US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.

[Support the Venezuelan Humanitarian Fund here](https://crisisrelief.un.org/en/donate-venezuela-crisis)

For more information, visit: [ReliefWeb Response](https://response.reliefweb.int/es/venezuela/terremoto-junio-2026)

**ECUADOR: FLOODING**

On 3 July, heavy rainfall caused the Zamora River to overflow, triggering severe flooding in Guadalupe, in Zamora municipality in the Amazonian province Zamora Chinchipe. Preliminary reports from Ecuador’s National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR) indicate 5 people killed, 10 missing, and 38 injured, including firefighters involved in evacuation and rescue operations. An estimated 300 people have been affected and 200 displaced, with damage to homes, roads, water supply, electricity, telecommunications, crops, and livelihoods. National and local authorities have activated emergency coordination mechanisms, established a temporary shelter for displaced families, and are leading search and rescue operations, rapid needs assessments, and the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

**CENTRAL AMERICA: FOOD SECURITY**

FEWS NET forecasts below-average rainfall and persistent dry conditions across most of Central America through early July, despite increased rainfall in early June that failed to offset long-term deficits. Most basic grain-producing areas are expected to receive no more than 45 per cent of historical average rainfall between 16 June and 10 July, with the steepest deficits, up to 65 per cent, concentrated in Guatemala and Nicaragua. In Honduras, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes have already emerged across the Dry Corridor and the Pacific coastal department of Choluteca. FEWS NET estimates 500,000–749,999 people will need humanitarian food assistance nationally, with needs peaking between June and August. Regional meteorological services expect an extended canícula (mid-summer dry spell) to further affect the Dry Corridor, and forecast temperatures 2-4°C above average across the Pacific side of the region.

reports.title: AMDA Emergency Relief #1: Earthquakes in Venezuela - 06 July 2026
sources: Association of Medical Doctors of Asia
reports.body_text:
In response to the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June, AMDA has dispatched its emergency relief team to reach out to people in affected areas.

The team comprises four members, including AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato, one nurse, and two physicians from AMDA Peru.

At around 6:00 p.m. on 24 June local time, two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 struck northwestern Venezuela in succession. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), the earthquakes had claimed 2,295 lives, injured 11,267 people, and affected more than 26,000 people (as of 1 July).

As of now, an advance team of two physicians from AMDA Peru and a Japanese nurse from the U.S. has already arrived in Venezuela since 5 July. Upon arrival, the team held a meeting with local counterparts in Caracas to coordinate relief efforts.

Meanwhile, AMDA President Dr. Takushi Sato departed from Okayama, Japan, on 6 July to join the mission. He is expected to arrive at Arturo Michelena International Airport in the city of Valencia the next day, where he will join AMDA’s local partners.

Prior to the personnel deployment, an AMDA coordinator paid a courtesy visit to the Embassy of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in Tokyo to report on the project implementation. During his visit, Venezuelan Ambassador to Japan His Excellency Seiko Luis Ishikawa Kobayashi expressed his full support for AMDA's medical relief activities.

While bracing for possible aftershocks, AMDA hopes to deliver consistent assistance to those affected by the quakes.

reports.title: Todas las ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español responden a las necesidades de la población en Venezuela tras los terremotos
reports.body_text:
Las 8 ONG del Comité de Emergencia, Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision, se han volcado en la respuesta a los terremotos que sufrió Venezuela el pasado 24 de junio que dejan, hasta el momento según las últimas cifras oficiales, 235 personas fallecidas y 4.300 heridas.

Ante una primera evaluación y análisis de la situación, y una vez garantizada la seguridad e integridad de sus equipos, el objetivo principal de estas organizaciones es atender a la población más vulnerable, junto con las organizaciones locales, que tienen presencia y arraigo en Venezuela para poder prestarles apoyo, de manera coordinada con los actores humanitarios y estructuras de coordinación que ya existen en el país.

El objetivo fundamental de las organizaciones es dar soporte a personas enfermas, niños, niñas y mujeres, cubriendo sus necesidades más inmediatas en las áreas de trabajo en las que suelen trabajar como alimentación e higiene, refugio y atención sanitaria y psicológica.

La afectación de los seísmos se concentra en la franja centro-norte del país —incluyendo Caracas, Valencia y estados cercanos—, una de las zonas más densamente pobladas de Venezuela. Las autoridades han confirmado daños estructurales y colapsos parciales de edificios en distintas zonas de Caracas y en el estado Aragua, así como afectaciones en infraestructuras clave como hospitales.

Respuesta a las necesidades humanitarias urgentes

Las principales necesidades identificadas en estos momentos incluyen:

- Alojamiento seguro para familias cuyas viviendas han quedado dañadas o inhabitables.
- Acceso a agua potable, saneamiento e higiene y materiales de primera necesidad como mantas o ropa.
- Protección infantil en entornos inseguros y necesidad de espacios seguros.
- Apoyo psicosocial frente al miedo, la incertidumbre y las pérdidas.
- Atención sanitaria, traslado a clínicas móviles, personal y material médico.
- Continuidad educativa ante posibles daños en escuelas.

“La experiencia pasada en otras emergencias humanitarias demuestra que ante una catástrofe como el terremoto en Venezuela, la coordinación y el llamamiento unánime a la ciudadanía es fundamental para conseguir ayuda urgente y salvar más vidas. Esta unión, entre la sociedad y las organizaciones es fundamental para que las ONG en terreno puedan actuar de forma rápida y atender algunas de las necesidades más urgentes que surgen tras una emergencia”, explica la directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira.

Empresas y medios de comunicación también se solidarizan con las víctimas

Los grupos y empresas que son parte del Comité de Emergencia están volcados y colaborando ya en la recaudación de fondos, activando sus planes de llamamiento a la ayuda.

En estas primeras horas ya se han unido a la respuesta Allianz Partners, Atresmedia, Atrevia, CaixaBank, Correos España, Editorial Santillana, Exterior Plus, Forética, Fundación Quirónsalud, Iberdrola, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, PayPal, Prisa, Televisión Canaria, Televisión de Galicia, TuMedio, RTVE, Tragsa, Unidad Editorial, Vivir Ediciones, Vocento y Worldcoo, cediendo sus espacios en medios de comunicación, publicidad, digital, programas de televisión y radio y soportes publicitarios para difundir el llamamiento que desde el Comité de Emergencia Español se está realizando.

La respuesta ciudadana está siendo ejemplar y confirma la capacidad de movilización que podemos alcanzar juntos.
